yamauchi-kazutoyo: Yamauchi Kazutoyo, whose name is also pronounced Yamanouchi, was the son of Yamauchi Moritoyo, a descendant of Fujiwara no Hidesato. Moritoyo was a senior retainer of the Iwakura Oda clan, which opposed Oda Nobunaga, and lord of Kuroda Castle in Owari Province at the end of the Sengoku period. Kazutoyo's life spanned the closing years of the Sengoku period, the Azuchi–Momoyama period and the beginning of the Edo period.

While still a lord of only 400 koku, he was entrusted with the teaching of boys who later rose high, among them Kuroda Nagamasa, then a hostage of Oda Nobunaga, and Toyotomi Hidetsugu. He fought on the Oda side at the Battle of Anegawa in 1570. After the Siege of Odawara in 1590, when Toyotomi Hideyoshi forced Tokugawa Ieyasu to exchange his lands in the Tōkai region for the Kantō, Kazutoyo received Kakegawa Castle from Hideyoshi.

His rise owed much to his wife Yamauchi Chiyo, a daughter of Endo Morikazu, lord of Gujo-Hachiman Castle. She is said to have spent all her money on a fine horse so that he could impress his superiors, and to have risked her life to send him secret information while they were apart during the war. Their daughter, Yonehime, was killed in the Tenshō earthquake of 1586. After the Battle of Sekigahara he held the title Tosa no kami.

Kazutoyo died on 1 November 1605, four years after he became lord of Tosa, aged around 60 and without children of his own. He was succeeded by his nephew Yamauchi Tadayoshi, whom he had adopted. His life and that of Chiyo were dramatised in Kōmyō ga Tsuji, the 45th NHK Taiga drama, broadcast in 2006 from a story by Shiba Ryōtarō, with Nakama Yukie as Chiyo and Takaya Kamikawa as Kazutoyo; it tells how a wise wife helped her husband rise from an ordinary samurai to the governor of a whole province.
yamuna: The Yamuna rises in the Yamunotri Glacier on the south-western slopes of the Bandarpunch peaks of the Lower Himalaya in Uttarakhand. It enters Himachal Pradesh and then flows into the Indo-Gangetic plains of Haryana and Uttar Pradesh, passing Delhi, and drains an area of 366,223 square kilometres, 40.2 per cent of the Ganges Basin. It meets the Ganges at the Triveni Sangam in Prayagraj, a site of the Kumbh Mela, which is held every 12 years. Its tributaries include the Tons, its largest, the Chambal, the Sindh, the Betwa and the Ken. With the Ganges it forms the fertile Ganges–Yamuna Doab.

The earliest mention of the Yamuna is in the Rig Veda, composed in the Vedic period, and it also appears in the Atharvaveda and in Brahmanas such as the Aitareya and Shatapatha. Greek sources know it as Iomanes, in the surveys of Seleucus I Nicator, who visited India in 305 BCE. In the Mahabharata the Pandava capital of Indraprastha stood on its banks, at the site of modern Delhi.

The river's waters have long been used for irrigation. Some canals date to the Tughlaq dynasty in the 14th century, which built the Nahr-i-Bahisht, or Paradise canal, parallel to the river. The Mughals restored and extended it in the first half of the 17th century under the engineer Ali Mardan Khan, to near the capital Shahjahanabad, the present Delhi.

In Hinduism the river is venerated as the goddess Yamuna, daughter of the sun god Surya and his wife Saranyu and twin sister of Yama, the god of death. According to tradition, bathing in her waters frees one from the torments of death, and the Padma Purana says they cleanse the mind of sin. The Rig Veda counts the Yamuna among the seven sacred rivers, and in Gupta art she and the Ganges appear on temple doorjambs to purify those who pass through.

The Yamunotri temple, dedicated to the goddess near the river's source, is among the holiest shrines of Hinduism. The river is closely associated with Krishna: the Puranas tell how he subdued the Naga Kaliya, who had terrorised the people of Braja, and the river is a centre of pilgrimage for his devotees.
yamunanagar-district: Yamunanagar district lies at the north-eastern tip of Haryana and covers 1,756 square kilometres. It is bounded by Himachal Pradesh to the north, Uttar Pradesh to the east, Karnal district to the south, Kurukshetra district to the south-west and Ambala district to the west. The land is plain, with the Siwalik hills on the northern side. Its hilly part, Kalesar, borders the Sirmaur district of Himachal Pradesh and contains Kalesar National Park. Monsoon rainfall averages 892 millimetres, much higher than the state average of 462.

The district came into existence on 1 November 1989, and the town of Yamunanagar is its headquarters. Within its bounds stands Lohgarh Fort, the capital of the First Sikh Empire under Baba Banda Singh Bahudur, and the towns of Sadhaura and Mustafabad, the scene of his first victories, also lie in the district.

The district has three sub-divisions, Jagadhri, Radaur and Bilaspur, and four tehsils. The main towns are Bilaspur, Chhachhrauli, Radaur, Jagadhri and Yamunanagar, a municipal corporation; Jagadhri lies next to Yamunanagar and is the older of the twin cities. At the census of 2011 the district had a population of 1,214,205, and 38.94 per cent of the people lived in urban areas. Hindi was the first language of 88.28 per cent, Punjabi of 7.24 per cent, Haryanvi of 1.75 per cent and Urdu of 1.20 per cent.
yamunotri: Yamunotri stands at an altitude of 3,293 metres in the Garhwal Himalayas, about 150 kilometres north of Uttarkashi, on a flank of the Bandarpunch mountain, and is the westernmost shrine of the Garhwal Himalayas. The river's actual source, a frozen lake of ice and glacier about 1 kilometre further up, is not generally visited because it cannot be reached, so the shrine was placed at the foot of the hill.

From its source the Yamuna crosses Uttarakhand, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh and Delhi before merging with the Ganges at the Triveni Sangam in Prayagraj. For Hindus the Yamuna, like the Ganges, has the status of a divine mother, held responsible for nurturing and developing Indian civilisation.

A small shrine stood at the site before the present temple was built by a ruler of Tehri Garhwal. The temple stands at 3,235 metres on the left bank of the Yamuna near its source, and its image of the goddess is made of black marble.

Worship centres on the temple and the hot springs near it, of which Surya Kund is the most important. Beside it lies a rock called Divya Shila, worshipped before the goddess herself. Devotees tie rice and potatoes in muslin cloth and cook them by dipping them in the springs, taking the cooked rice home as prasada. Because the approach to the source is extremely difficult, pilgrims offer puja at the temple itself. Yamunotri is one of the four sites of the Chota Char Dham pilgrimage.
yan-ying: Yan Ying was born around 578 BCE in what is now Gaomi, Shandong, the son of Yan Ruo, a minister of Qi, whose post he took on his father's death in 556 BCE. In his lifetime he used the courtesy name Zhong, and after his death he received the posthumous title Ping. He was said to be short and very ugly but a nimble debater, and for that reason he was often sent to other states as a diplomat. He was an elder contemporary of Confucius.

When Duke Zhuang was killed by the men of the minister Cui Zhu in 548 BCE, Yan Ying went unguarded into Cui's house to mourn over the body. Cui spared him because the people looked up to him, and Yan Ying refused the oath of loyalty Cui forced on others under the new ruler, Duke Jing. Stories of his missions passed into folklore, though their historicity is uncertain. Sent to King Ling of Chu, he refused a small side door made to mock his height, and when shown a thief said to be from Qi he answered that oranges grown south of the Huai River turn bitter north of it.

Other stories tell how he saw through a Jin envoy's test with the duke's wine cup, so that Jin gave up an attack, which Confucius praised; how he saved Duke Jing's bird keeper, Zhu Zou, by listing his crimes so that the duke saw his own unreason; and how two peaches offered to three arrogant generals, Gongsun Jie, Tian Kaijiang and Gu Yezi, led all three to kill themselves.

Mortally ill around 500 BCE, he sealed a letter in a pillar of his house for his son, warning him not to exhaust cloth and silk, livestock, worthy men or the state's resources. His tomb is in Zibo, Shandong. The Yanzi Chunqiu, compiled in the Warring States period, gathers stories of his advice to three dukes, and Sima Qian devoted a chapter of the Records of the Grand Historian to him and Guan Zhong. Several of the stories became sayings, among them southern oranges are bitter in the north.
yanakuna: The Quechua word yana means black or servant and may come from the verb yanapa, to help; in Qosqo Quechua it can also mean partner, spouse or paramour. The suffix -kuna marks the plural, so that yanakuna, if yana is read as servant, means servants. The Hispanicized forms are yanacona and yanaconas.

The word servant is misleading about the yanakuna of the Inca Empire, who were not forced to work as slaves. Some were born into the status, some chose to leave their ayllus and some were selected by nobles. They differed from the mitmaqkuna, who were moved in large groups as labour for great projects: yanakuna were relocated one by one and stood outside any ayllu. The mitmaqkuna built Machu Picchu, while yanakuna lived there and served the Inca.

When the Spanish arrived, yanakuna helped them take control of the empire. Under the encomienda system they stood apart from the ayllu-based tribute, and while the indios de encomienda did the most menial work in the silver mines of Potosí, yanakuna served there as skilled artisans or worked as free wage labourers from the 1540s.

The reforms of Viceroy Francisco de Toledo (1569-1581) replaced the encomienda with the mita, a labour draft of about one seventh of the tribute-age men of the villages around Potosí. Yanakuna grew in importance: in 1603 only 5,100 of the 58,800 Indians working at Potosí were mita draftees.

Spanish farmers too came to prefer yanakuna to draftees and to African slaves, since they knew indigenous and European methods and did not have to be bought, and the historian Steve J. Stern has shown settlers of the Huamanga region relying more and more on contracted yanakuna for farming, mining, ranching and manufactures. In the towns yanakuna owned and handed down property and kept a privileged place as skilled craftspeople. The term was also used in the conquest of Chile and in the New Kingdom of Granada, and in Chile its use in the press has led to legal action.
yanam: Yanam lies in the delta of the Godavari River, at the confluence of the Koringa River, nine kilometres from the Bay of Bengal on the Circar coast. The town is entirely surrounded by Andhra Pradesh. The Bank Canal, which begins at the Dowleswaram headworks of Sir Arthur Cotton's barrage on the Godavari, brings irrigation and drinking water; it is popularly called the French Channel because it was built under a 1949 agreement between the French government and the government of India.

The French established a trading post at Yanaon in 1723, the third French colony in India, but gave it up in 1727 after commercial operations proved unsuccessful. Governor-General Dupleix seized it again in 1731, and the Nizam of Hyderabad confirmed the French hold in 1751. Until the end of the Napoleonic wars Yanam passed intermittently under British control, and it was finally restored to France in 1814. Its Tuesday market drew Telugu people of the Madras Presidency, who came to buy foreign and smuggled goods.

On 13 June 1954 a coup in Yanam joined it to the Republic of India. The de facto transfer of the four enclaves of Pondicherry, Yanam, Mahé and Karikal took place on 1 November 1954. A treaty of cession was signed on 28 May 1956, but the legal transfer waited until the end of the Algerian War: the French parliament ratified the treaty in May 1962, and on 16 August 1962 the instruments of ratification were exchanged. The enclaves became the Union Territory of Pondicherry on 7 January 1963. After the liberation about 10,000 people in Yanam chose French nationality.

Yanam is a district of the Union Territory of Puducherry. The 1956 treaty kept the former colonies' special administrative status, and French remains an official language of the territory alongside Telugu and English. The town blends French and Telugu culture, which gave it the nickname Frelugu. Its population was 31,362 at the census of 2001. Among its monuments is the Vishnalayam, a 15th-century temple to Venkateswara.
yanan: Yan'an is a prefecture-level city in the Shaanbei region of Shaanxi province, on the Loess Plateau. It borders Shanxi to the east across the Yellow River and Gansu to the west across the Ziwu Ridge. The land is hilly, ranging from 388.8 to 1,809.8 metres above sea level, and the Yellow River, the Yan River and the Luo River flow through it. Yaodong, cave dwellings cut into the hillsides, are traditional homes of northern Shaanxi.

The area was populated at least as early as the Xia dynasty. After the Qin dynasty was established in 221 BCE it formed part of Shang Commandery, and the Sui dynasty organised it as Yan'an Commandery with a military base. Under the Song it was a border fortress against the Tangut-led Western Xia, and in 1080 the polymath Shen Kuo was sent to Yan Prefecture to aid its defence; in autumn 1081 he defended Song territory and captured several nearby fortified towns. In 1221 combined Mongol and Western Xia forces defeated a Jin army of 30,000 in the east of the present-day area.
Before the Dungan Revolt of 1862-1877 much of rural Yan'an was inhabited by Chinese Muslims, many of whom were killed or forced to move; Bao'an had 51,000 people in 1823 but only 170 in 1868.

In October 1935, after the Long March, the Chinese Red Army arrived in the area from Jiangxi. In January 1937 it entered Yan'an without a fight, after local warlords handed the town over, and on 6 September 1937 Yan'an became the seat of the communist government of the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region. Thousands of intellectuals travelled there, party members and troops were trained, and in 1941 Mao Zedong launched training programmes that began the Yan'an Rectification Movement.

Japanese bombing destroyed almost every building except a pagoda, and most inhabitants lived in yaodongs. From 1944 to 1947 the United States Army Observation Group, the Dixie Mission, was stationed there. Kuomintang forces briefly captured the city in the Chinese Civil War, after the Communist leadership learned of the attack and withdrew; the People's Liberation Army retook it on 21 April 1948.

Yan'an is regarded by Chinese communists as the birthplace of the revolution, and the Yan'an Revolution Memorial Hall draws visitors who come to learn the party's history. Yan'an University is based in the city. Oil has been extracted from the Changqing Oil Field, part of the Ordos basin, since the early 1970s.
yancai: The Chinese name Yancai is usually rendered as Vast Steppe. Its people are generally considered Iranian, of the Sarmatian group. They first appear in chapter 123 of the Shiji of Sima Qian, which draws on the travels of the 2nd-century BCE diplomat Zhang Qian. It places Yancai some 2,000 li, about 832 km, north-west of Kangju, beside a great shoreless lake, and credits the country with more than 100,000 archer warriors.

According to Chinese sources Yancai lay on the Northern Route of the Silk Route, and the Chinese sent embassies there and promoted trade. Its people are often linked with the Aorsi of Roman records, who held the lands between the Don and the Aral Sea and were both a wealthy mercantile people and a strong military power. The historian Y. A. Zadneprovskiy dates Yancai's subjection to Kangju to the 1st century BCE; the westward expansion of Kangju drove many Sarmatians west and contributed to the Migration Period in Europe.

The Hou Hanshu, the chronicle of the Later Han completed in the 5th century, reports that Yancai had changed its name to Alanliao and was a dependency of Kangju. The 3rd-century Weilüe, the last source to mention it, says that Yancai was also called Alan, bordered Roman territory to the west and Kangju to the south-east, and was no longer Kangju's vassal. In the 1st and 2nd centuries CE the Alans became the leading people among the Sarmatians, moved west into southern Russia and often raided the Parthian and Roman empires.

Chinese writers describe the people of Yancai as nomads whose customs and dress resembled those of Kangju. The Hou Hanshu says the climate was mild and that wax trees, pines and aconite, called white grass, were plentiful. The Weilüe adds that they raised cattle, moved about in search of water and fodder, lived close to a large shoreless lake and were known for their sables.
yang-di-pertuan-agong: The title Yang di-Pertuan Agong means He who is made Lord. The office was established in 1957, when the Federation of Malaya gained independence from the United Kingdom. On 31 August 1957 the Conference of Rulers rejected the suggested title Yang di-Pertuan Besar in favour of Yang di-Pertuan Agong and elected the first occupant. By seniority the first in line was the 84-year-old Sultan Ibrahim of Johor, who declined because of age.

The next, the Sultan of Pahang, Abu Bakar, was rejected five times by his fellow electors, in part because his various marriages to celebrities and cabaret dancers were seen as unbecoming. Tuanku Abdul Rahman of Negeri Sembilan, who had been elected to his state throne in 1933, was chosen by eight votes to one.

The Yang di-Pertuan Agong is the constitutional monarch and ceremonial head of state, and the Federal Constitution and Acts of Parliament define his powers. The Constitution vests the federal executive power in him, but with few exceptions he must act on the advice of the Cabinet, and the day-to-day work of government is done by the Cabinet. His discretionary powers concern chiefly the appointment of the prime minister, withholding consent to a dissolution of Parliament and calling meetings of the Conference of Rulers on the privileges and dignities of the rulers. Under the Westminster system he appoints a prime minister who commands the confidence of a majority of the Dewan Rakyat.

He also appoints senior judges, the governors of Penang, Malacca, Sabah and Sarawak and 44 senators, is Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces under Article 41, and is Head of Islam in his own state, the governed states and the federal territories.

The king is elected by secret ballot to a five-year term by and from the nine rulers of the Malay states, who form the Conference of Rulers; the four governors attend but cannot vote. A nominee needs five votes. A ruler who has served may not stand again until all the others have served. Minors are disqualified, and the Conference may declare a ruler unsuitable by a secret ballot of at least five. The office rotates in practice, following the order set by the first cycle of nine kings, 1957 to 1994, which began with the ruler of Negeri Sembilan.

Because it is elective there is no line of succession. In 1993 constitutional amendments removed the legal immunity of the king and the state rulers in their personal capacity, and a Special Court was established to hear proceedings against a ruler.
yang-guozhong: Born Yang Zhao, at an unknown date, he came from a family of Pu Prefecture that traced its line to the Han official Yang Zhen. In his youth he was known as a drinker, gambler and wastrel, looked down on by his own clan. He joined the army at Yi Prefecture, became magistrate of Xindu County and depended on the help of a rich local man, Xianyu Zhongtong. His rise began after his second cousin Yang Yuhuan, later Yang Guifei, became Emperor Xuanzong's favourite consort in 744, when the military governor Zhangqiu Jianqiong sent him to Chang'an with gifts for her family.

Welcomed at court through the consort's sisters and cousins, Yang became an imperial censor and helped the chancellor Li Linfu bring false accusations that destroyed several hundred households. As a financial official he reported record surpluses, and in 750 the emperor renamed him Guozhong, faithful to the state. He hid from the emperor the defeat of Xianyu's army by the Kingdom of Nanzhao in 751, with 60,000 dead, and pressed on with a campaign whose Tang death toll reached 200,000. In 752 he engineered the fall of Li Linfu's allies and, after Li's death, his posthumous disgrace, and became leading chancellor.

As chancellor he held more than 40 posts, decided matters at home without consulting colleagues and lived in extreme luxury with the consort's sisters. He quarrelled with An Lushan, military governor of Fanyang, Hedong and Pinglu, and repeatedly accused him of plotting rebellion; in 755 he had An's friends arrested and executed in secret, deepening An's fears. When An rebelled that winter, Yang believed the revolt would be crushed quickly.

Distrusting the general Geshu Han, who held Tong Pass, Yang had the emperor order him to give battle. The Tang army was crushed and the pass fell on 10 July 756, and on 14 July the court left Chang'an secretly for Jiannan. At Mawei Station the next day, unfed and angry imperial guards, claiming that Yang was plotting treason with Tibetan envoys, killed him with his son Yang Xuan and others of his family. The Old Book of Tang blamed the whole disaster on Yang Guozhong.
yang-maosou: Yang Maosou, also called Yang Wusou in some records, was the founding ruler of Chouchi during the Sixteen Kingdoms period. His ancestors had lived in Qingshui County in Lüeyang Commandery, in modern Tianshui, Gansu, and moved to the Chouchi region under Yang Ju in the early 3rd century, later returning to Lüeyang as the forces of Yang Feilong grew. Feilong had no son of his own and adopted the son of his sister, Lady Linghu, renaming him Yang Maosou. When Feilong died in 296, Maosou succeeded him as chief.

In the same year the Di chieftain Qi Wannian led a tribal rebellion against Jin which, coinciding with famine, devastated the Guanzhong region and created many refugees. Yang Maosou led around 4,000 families to Chouchi to escape the turmoil and declared himself General Who Upholds the State and Worthy Prince of the Right. Other refugees joined him; he welcomed them, and gave those who wished to leave supplies for the road.

Emperor Min of Jin later confirmed his authority, appointing him General of Agile Cavalry and Worthy Prince of the Left, and his son Yang Nandi was made General Who Attacks the South by Sima Bao, Prince of Nanyang. Maosou also sent tribute to the neighbouring Ba Di state of Cheng-Han as its vassal.

In 313, when the Jin Inspector of Liang, Zhang Guang, campaigned against the refugee rebel Yang Hu, both sides sought Maosou's alliance, and he chose Zhang Guang. Nandi, sent to help, changed sides, defeated Zhang Guang and briefly held Hanzhong until a local revolt drove him back to Chouchi in 314. Yang Maosou died in 317. Nandi, his eldest son, succeeded him but chose to rule Chouchi jointly with his brother Yang Jiantou.
yang-pu: Yang Pu was born in 900, the fourth son of the warlord Yang Xingmi, military governor of Huainan Circuit, by his concubine Lady Wang. In 919, under his brother Yang Longyan, he was made Duke of Danyang. When Yang Longyan fell ill in 920, the regent Xu Wen, wary of the third brother Yang Meng, summoned Yang Pu to the capital Jiangdu, and on Yang Longyan's death he became King of Wu. He is known posthumously as Emperor Rui.

Xu Wen held real power. In 921 Yang Pu sacrificed to heaven and earth, claiming the Mandate of Heaven. In 923, when Later Tang destroyed Later Liang, he answered Emperor Zhuangzong's letter as an equal while showing deference. In 924, reviewing the fleet at Baisha, he complained to Xu Wen of Zhai Qian, the overseer who spied on his movements, and had him exiled. In 925 Wu broke off relations with Wuyue after its ruler Qian Liu accepted the title King of Wuyue. After Xu Wen died in 927, Yang Pu declared himself emperor in keeping with Xu Wen's last wishes.

In 929 Xu Wen's adopted son Xu Zhigao detained his rival Xu Zhixun and took over his army, and from 930 he ran the government from Jinling. That year Yang Pu made his eldest son Yang Lian crown prince. Xu Zhigao prepared his own accession: Yang Pu granted him great titles in 934 and 935 and the Principality of Qi with ten prefectures. Yang Meng, fearing the end of the dynasty, fled custody in 937 but was captured and executed. Yang Pu then issued an edict passing the throne to Xu Zhigao, by then named Xu Gao.

Emperor Liezu of Southern Tang still addressed him as a subject and left him his palace and insignia. To ward off suspicion, Yang Pu wore feather robes and studied Taoist disciplines, but he asked to leave the old palace, and he and his clan were moved under heavy guard to Danyang Palace at Run Prefecture. He died soon afterwards; it was commonly believed that he had been killed on the new emperor's orders, though proof was lacking.
yang-tong: Yang Tong was the second of the three sons of Yang Zhao, the crown prince of Emperor Yang of Sui, by his concubine Consort Liu. When Yang Zhao died in 606, Emperor Yang named none of his sons heir and made Yang Tong Prince of Yue. In 613, during the second campaign against Goguryeo, the eight-year-old prince was left nominally in charge of the eastern capital Luoyang, with the official Fan Zigai holding real authority, when the general Yang Xuangan rebelled nearby. In 616 Emperor Yang left for Jiangdu, and the rebels Li Mi and Zhai Rang seized the granaries near Luoyang, leaving the city short of food.

After Emperor Yang was killed in a coup led by Yuwen Huaji in 618, the officials at Luoyang declared Yang Tong emperor. Government passed to seven officials, the seven nobles, who made peace with Li Mi against Yuwen. Wang Shichong objected, and when Yuan Wendu planned to ambush him, Wang struck first, killed Lu Chu and surrounded the palace. Yang Tong handed Yuan over, and Yuan told him, "If I die in the morning, Your Imperial Majesty will die in the evening." From then on Wang held all power.

In the autumn of 618 Wang crushed Li Mi at the Battle of Yanshi, and for a time rebel leaders such as Du Fuwei and Dou Jiande nominally submitted to Yang Tong. Wang grew arrogant, stopped seeing the emperor after a bout of food poisoning he blamed on the palace, and by the spring of 619 had himself made Prince of Zheng. When Yang Tong refused to yield the throne, Wang placed him under house arrest and issued an edict of abdication in his name.

Made Duke of Lu, Yang Tong became the focus of a plot by Pei Renji and others to restore him; it leaked, and the conspirators and their families were killed. Wang Shiyun then persuaded his brother to put him to death. Before drinking the poison sent to him, Yang Tong prayed that he might never again be reborn into an imperial household; when it did not kill him, he was strangled. Wang honoured him as Emperor Gong, but because the Book of Sui was written under the Tang, who gave that name to his brother Yang You, his standing as a Sui emperor became ambiguous in traditional histories.
yang-xingmi: Yang Xingmi, born Yang Xingmin, came from Lu Prefecture, in modern Hefei, of a family of farmers. Strong in youth, he became a bandit during the Qianfu era (874–879) and was captured, but the prefect Zheng Qi, impressed by him, set him free. As a soldier of the prefecture's militia he distinguished himself; when his wary commander sent him away on a mission, Yang killed him and took command. The prefect, unable to control him, recommended him as his own replacement, and Emperor Xizong, at the recommendation of Gao Pian, military governor of Huainan, made him prefect.

In 883 the sorcerer Lü Yongzhi, who ran Huainan in Gao Pian's name, falsely warned Yang that two officers meant to attack Lu; Yang ambushed and killed them. In 887 Bi Shiduo rebelled and besieged Huainan's capital, Yang Prefecture, and Yang marched to its aid on the advice of his strategist Yuan Xi. In 888 and 889 he crossed the Yangtze, besieged Xuan Prefecture and, after its governor Zhao Huang was expelled and captured, was made governor of Xuanshe by Emperor Zhaozong, later its military governor when it was renamed Ningguo. He executed Zhao and sent his head to Zhu Quanzhong, who had asked for his release.

Years of war had stripped Huainan of people and wealth. Yang was frugal, promoted farming, cut taxes and encouraged trade with neighbouring circuits, and within several years the circuit was said to have recovered. He formed 5,000 soldiers of his rival Sun Ru who had submitted to him into the elite Heiyun Corps, his advance guard in battle.

In 899 he attacked Xu Prefecture but withdrew as Zhu Quanzhong approached, and in 900 Emperor Zhaozong gave him the honorary title of Shizhong. In 901, on a false rumour of Qian Liu's assassination, he sent Li Shenfu against Zhenhai Circuit; Li captured the general Gu Quanwu but withdrew with a large payment. Yang died on 24 December 905. His lands came to cover most of modern Jiangsu and Anhui and parts of Jiangxi and Hubei.
yang-xiuqing: Yang Xiuqing came from a farming family of Xincun near Jintian in Guangxi. His father died when he was five and his mother when he was nine, and the uncle who raised him could not send him to school, so he remained illiterate. He made his living by farming, logging and burning charcoal; imperial reports add that he later organised convoys to protect goods carried through the area from bandits. His brother Yang Fuqing also became a Taiping commander.

In April 1848, while Feng Yunshan and Hong Xiuquan were away in a neighbouring province, Yang took the lead in the God Worshipping Society. He said he had been struck deaf and mute and then healed at a meeting, and began to enter trances in which God the Father was said to speak through him. Hong and Feng investigated these claims on their return in 1849 and accepted them, and Hong gave Yang the title Holy Spirit Wind. Historians doubt that Yang believed in the trances himself, since speaking as God gave him authority even over Hong.

In 1851 Hong made Yang, who had no military experience, commander-in-chief of the army and East King, one of five kings. Yang built a wide network of spies and proved an able strategist and organiser. After the Taiping took Nanjing in 1853 he controlled the city, ended the killing by threatening to execute any officer who entered a private home, sent residents back to work and kept men and women apart. As Hong withdrew from politics, Yang became prime minister, and many of the kingdom's basic laws were issued under him.

In August 1856 Yang broke the government army besieging Nanjing by drawing off its forces and then attacking in strength. He quarrelled with Hong over Confucianism, which Yang thought compatible with Taiping Christianity and Hong wanted eradicated. Yang demanded the imperial title Wansui. Hong recalled Wei Changhui, Shi Dakai and Qin Rigang, and on 1 September 1856 Wei arrived with three thousand troops; he and Qin stormed the palace and killed Yang, then his family and, over three months, his remaining followers in the city. The rebellion's fortunes declined in the intrigues that followed.
yangban: The term first appeared in the late Goryeo period and came into wide use under Joseon. The yangban succeeded the Goryeo nobility, who had been educated in Buddhist and Confucian learning, and the early Joseon state joined former Goryeo nobles and a new class of agrarian bureaucrats in their ranks. The gwageo examinations, modelled on the imperial examinations, tested the Confucian classics, history and poetry. In theory anyone but the nobi, the baekjeong and the children of concubines could sit them, yet with at most 100 posts open to thousands of candidates, family ties came to count for more than merit.

From the 16th century the word came more and more to mean wealthy local families believed to descend from high officials. After the wars of that century and the disasters of the Little Ice Age left the treasury short, the government sold offices through the Gongmyeongcheop, and descent rather than office became the proof of rank. Provincial families of this kind were called jaejisajok, the country families, and by the late Joseon period people could buy the status with a minor post or a jokbo, a noble pedigree, so that the word lost its lustre and even took on a mocking tone.

The court's rival factions, the Northern, Southern, Eastern and Western, watched each other for corruption until the reign of King Sunjo, when the Andong Kim clan and related grandee families took full control; such powerful houses were called sedoga. After the status lost its legal standing in 1894, some yangban kept their wealth by working with the Japanese colonial government and moved into printing, textiles, brewing and later heavier industry.

Yangban were often exempt from laws, including those on taxes, and the monarchy and the class lived on the labour of the lower orders. Dress marked rank. Men of the class wore the long gown called dopo, a cylindrical hat, the gat, a headband, the mang-geon, whose side buttons, the kwan-ja, showed rank by their material and size, and leather shoes, while commoners wore cotton or hemp and straw shoes or clogs. Deep red cloth, dyed with madder, cost more than four times as much as white cloth.
yangikent: The town's many names, Jankent, Dzhankent, Yenikent and others, all mean New Town in Turkic. Its ruins stand on the left bank of the lower Syr Darya, about 25 kilometres southwest of Kazaly in Kyzylorda province, in the dried-out river delta. Walls up to 7 metres high enclose 16 hectares in a broadly rectangular circuit given a T shape by an eastern cross-bar, with gates in the east and west walls, a separately walled citadel in the north-western corner and a semicircular annexe on the north wall.

Arab geographers of the 10th century, among them Al-Masudi and Al-Idrisi, mention an Oghuz town called Jengi-Kent, and Ibn Rustah and Ibn Hawqal call it the seat of the Oghuz Yabgu. The orientalist V. V. Bartold identified it with Jankent in the 1920s. The town is also held to be the home of the Kazakh cultural hero Korkyt Ata, reputed inventor of the kobyz lute.

Excavators suggest that the first settlement was founded in the 7th century by people of the Dzhetyasar culture from further upriver, as trade began along a northern branch of the Silk Road. The walled town was built in the 9th or 10th century, after the Oghuz arrived. Its finds point to a mixed population of Oghuz nomads, settled Dzhetyasar people and people of the Khorezmian civilisation, and it probably served as a trading and craft centre where the Silk Road met the caravan route from the Volga to Khorezm. It was abandoned between the 12th and 14th centuries, for reasons unknown.

Jankent is a scheduled monument. Russian army topographers first recorded it in the early 19th century, and the Chorasmian Expedition surveyed and photographed it from the air in 1946. Systematic excavation since 2005 by Russian, Kazakh and German teams has found living quarters, a possible metal workshop and, in 2019, a 9th- or 10th-century pot holding three eggs inscribed in Arabic.
yangon: Yangon stands in Lower Burma where the Yangon and Bago Rivers meet, about 30 km from the Gulf of Martaban, on the delta of the Irrawaddy. The name comes from the Burmese words yan, meaning enemies, and koun, meaning run out of, and is usually translated as End of Strife. The English form Rangoon is based on the Rakhine dialect. In 1989 the military government changed the city's English name to Yangon, along with many other transliterations; many Burmese did not accept the changes, and neither did a number of publications and foreign governments.

The settlement was founded as Dagon by the Mon people, who then inhabited Lower Burma, in the early 11th century (c. 1028-1043). From the 14th century, under the Hanthawaddy kingdom, it became an important pilgrimage town around its pagoda. Princess Maha Dewi governed it from 1364 to 1392, and her grandniece Shin Saw Pu, later the only female queen regnant in Burmese history, built a palace beside the Shwedagon Pagoda in 1460 and lived there until her death in 1471.

The British captured Yangon and all of Lower Burma in the Second Anglo-Burmese War of 1852 and made the city the commercial and political centre of British Burma, moving the capital there from Moulmein. On a design by the army engineer Lt. Alexander Fraser, they laid out a new city on a grid plan on delta land, bounded on the east by the Pazundaung Creek and on the south and west by the Yangon River. After the Third Anglo-Burmese War of 1885 it became the capital of all British-ruled Burma. By the 1890s prosperous suburbs had grown north of Royal Lake (Kandawgyi) and Inya Lake, and the British had founded hospitals and colleges, among them Rangoon General Hospital and Rangoon University.

After independence in 1948 many colonial names of streets and parks were replaced by Burmese ones. The city's area grew from 72.52 square kilometres in 1901 to 208.51 in 1974 and 598.75 in 2008, as it spread north towards the airport.

Yangon is the capital of the Yangon Region and the largest city of Myanmar, with about 5.16 million people at the 2014 census, and its main commercial centre. It was the national capital until the government moved its administration to the purpose-built Naypyidaw in 2005-2006. Its colonial-era core, centred on the Sule Pagoda, holds the largest number of colonial-period buildings in Southeast Asia, among them the former High Court, the former Secretariat and the Strand Hotel. The gilded Shwedagon Pagoda is the most sacred Buddhist pagoda of Myanmar. The main religions practised in the city are Buddhism, Christianity, Islam and Hinduism.
yangtze-river: The Yangtze, called Chang Jiang, or Long River, in Chinese, rises in the Tanggula Mountains of the Tibetan Plateau and flows for 6,300 kilometres in a generally easterly direction to the East China Sea. Its drainage basin comprises one-fifth of the land area of China. The source the Chinese government has traditionally recognised is the Tuotuo tributary at the base of a glacier on Geladandong Mountain, while the hydrologically longest source, at Jari Hill, was discovered only in the late 20th century. The river has over 700 tributaries, among them the Min, Jialing, Han and Gan, and it passes Chongqing, Wuhan and Nanjing on its way to Shanghai.

Unlike the Yellow River, whose mouth has shifted north and south of the Shandong peninsula, the Yangtze has remained largely static. Human activity is verified in the Three Gorges area as far back as 27,000 years ago. By the 5th millennium BCE the lower Yangtze was a major population centre of the Hemudu and Majiabang cultures, among the earliest cultivators of rice, followed in the 3rd millennium BCE by the Liangzhu culture. What is thought of as Chinese culture developed along the Yellow River, and the Yue of the lower Yangtze, who tattooed their bodies and cut their hair short, were considered barbarous by northerners.

Steamers came late to the upper river between Yichang and Chongqing, where the Three Gorges posed hazards of crosscurrents and whirlpools, and junks were pulled upriver by 70 to 80 trackers. The river was a major barrier between northern and southern China, and until 1957 there was no bridge across it from Yibin to Shanghai. The Central China floods of 1931 were among the deadliest natural disasters ever recorded.

The Yangtze basin is home to nearly one-third of China's population, and the river is the longest in Asia and the largest entirely within a single country. Tens of millions of people live in its floodplain, which floods naturally every summer and is habitable because dikes protect it. The Three Gorges Dam is the largest hydroelectric power station in the world by installed capacity. The basin has 416 known fish species, 178 of them found only there, and the Yangtze river dolphin, or baiji, was declared functionally extinct in 2006.
yangzhou: Yangzhou is a prefecture-level city in central Jiangsu Province, on the north bank of the Yangtze. It borders the provincial capital Nanjing to the south-west, Huai'an to the north, Yancheng to the north-east and Taizhou to the east, and Zhenjiang lies across the river. It stands on a plain with many streams and lakes, and the Grand Canal crosses the prefecture from north to south. The name means Rising Prefecture and refers to its former position as the capital of the ancient Yangzhou prefecture. The climate is subtropical monsoon, with winters of about four months.

In the Spring and Autumn period Fuchai, the hegemon of Wu, built the Han Canal to improve supply lines from the region of present-day Suzhou to the North China Plain, where he was fighting Qi. By 486 BCE the canal joined the Yangtze at present-day Yangzhou to the Huai River at present-day Huai'an. The next year Fuchai founded a fortress, Hancheng, to guard its southern end. It was a square of 3 li by 3 li raised about 12 metres above the water on the Yangtze's northern bank, with the canal forming a moat on two sides.

Under the Eastern Han the area formed the Guangling Commandery of Xu Province, whose seat, also called Guangling, lay near the meeting of the Yangtze and the Han Canal. Historically Yangzhou was one of the wealthiest cities in China, known at various periods for its great merchant families, poets, artists and scholars. From the Taiping Rebellion in 1853 to the 1980s it declined through war damage, the neglect of the Grand Canal as railways replaced it, and stagnation. It endured eight years of Japanese occupation in the Second Sino-Japanese War, and in 1943 about 1,200 Allied civilians from Shanghai were interned there.

Yangzhou had a population of 4,559,797 at the 2020 census. The Runyang Yangtze River Bridge carries the road to Zhenjiang, and the harbour at the junction of the Grand Canal and the Yangtze handles passengers and freight for northern Jiangsu, eastern Anhui and south-east Shandong. Yangzhou Railway Station opened in 2004.
yanji: Yanji lies in the east of Jilin Province, among foothills. The main urban area occupies a small, very flat area ringed by mountains dotted with remote farming communities. It lies between 42°50' and 43°23' north and between 129°01' and 129°48' east. The climate is humid continental with long, very cold winters and short, warm, humid summers; the average temperature ranges from about −13 °C in January to about 21.7 °C in August, and most of the annual rainfall of 531 mm falls in summer.

In the 1800s the Qing rulers of China encouraged migration into the area from China proper as part of the Chuang Guandong policy, which aimed to populate Manchuria and stem Russian expansion. From 1934 to 1943 the city was the seat of Jiandao Province in the Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo. In 1943 it was renamed Jiandao and made part of the Dongman Consolidated Province.

After the Second World War the city, again called Yanji, was nominally part of a new Songjiang Province. With the communist seizure of power in 1949 the province's borders were changed and Yanji became part of Jilin Province. Yanbian University was founded there in 1949. The railway station was built in 1924. The Korean population grew to become the largest of any Chinese city: the 1990 census placed the ethnic Korean population at over 170,000.

Yanji is a county-level city and the seat of the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture, which lies in eastern Jilin. It is the political, economic and cultural centre of the prefecture, with a population of about 400,000, of which a significant part is ethnic Korean. Both Chinese and Korean are official languages, and official signs are bilingual. The city is a hub of transport and trade between China and North Korea, and in 2009 the Changchun-Yanji Expressway opened.

Yanbian University, the Yanbian University of Science and Technology and the Yanbian Medical College are in the city. An annual Korean folk festival takes place each September, and the North China Travel Fair has been held there every year since 1996.
yankee-doodle: Yankee Doodle is a traditional song and nursery rhyme whose early versions predate the Seven Years' War and the American Revolutionary War. Rumour holds that its earliest words came from a Middle Dutch harvest song on the same tune, supposedly dating to 15th-century Holland.

The word doodle first appeared in English in the early 17th century and is thought to derive from the Low German dudel, meaning playing music badly, or Dödel, meaning fool. In British conversation, Yankee doodle dandy implied an unsophisticated imitation of upper-class fashion, and the fashion historian Peter McNeil claims that the British were insinuating that the colonists were lower-class and lacked masculinity.

According to the usual account, the song was sung by British officers to mock the colonial soldiers who served with them in the French and Indian War. It is said to have been written at Fort Crailo around 1755 or 1758 by the British Army surgeon Richard Shuckburgh, perhaps after seeing the troops of Colonel Thomas Fitch. The date of the earliest known version is disputed. Its first verse tells of Brother Ephraim, who sold his cow, bought a commission and proved a coward in Canada. The tune also appeared in 1762 in The Disappointment, a comic ballad opera from Pennsylvania.

American troops embraced the song and added verses mocking the British and hailing George Washington, and by 1781 it had become a song of national pride. After the Battle of Lexington and Concord, a Boston newspaper reported a British officer saying that the Minutemen had made them dance to the tune until they were tired. The song was played at the British surrender at Saratoga in 1777. According to the Online Etymology Dictionary, the current version seems to have been written in 1776 by Edward Bangs, a Harvard sophomore and Minuteman.

The full version describes a boy who goes with his father to camp, sees Captain Washington on a stallion and flees home to his mother's chamber. It served as one of the de facto national anthems of the United States, with Hail, Columbia and My Country, 'Tis of Thee, until The Star-Spangled Banner was adopted on 3 March 1931, and it is the state song of Connecticut. Its tune is shared by the nursery rhymes Simple Simon, Jack and Jill and Lucy Locket, and by the Japanese dōyō Alps Ichiman Jaku.
yao-chang: Yao Chang, courtesy name Jingmao, was the 24th of the 42 sons of Yao Yizhong, a Qiang chief and general of Later Zhao. After Yao Yizhong died in 351, his son Yao Xiang led the family's troops, rebelled against the Jin in 352 and tried to make himself ruler of the Luoyang region, with Yao Chang among his strategists. Defeated by the Jin general Huan Wen in 356, Yao Xiang turned west against Former Qin and was captured and killed in 357. Yao Chang surrendered, and was spared at the intercession of Fu Jiān.

Fu Jiān took the Former Qin throne that year and made him a general. Yao Chang served under Wang Meng against Jing Province in 366 and against the Qiang rebels of Lian Qi in 367, became governor of Longdong and later of Ning Province, and took part in the conquest of Former Liang in 376 and the siege of Xiangyang in 378. He was one of the few generals who favoured Fu Jiān's great attack on Jin in 383, and was given the title General Longxiang, which Fu Jiān himself had once held.

In 384, after Fu Rui was killed against Murong Hong and Fu Jiān executed the messengers who brought the news, Yao Chang feared for his life, gathered the Qiang and declared himself King of Qin of 10,000 Years. He kept his forces mobile, based at Beidi, while Western Yan besieged Chang'an. At Xinping in 385 he promised the governor Gou Fu safe passage, then had the 5,000 people who left the city slaughtered. When Western Yan abandoned Chang'an, he made it his capital, claimed the imperial title and named his son Yao Xing crown prince.

His main rival was Fu Deng, who used the killing of Fu Jiān to good effect and won many battles that decided little. In 389 Yao Chang desecrated Fu Jiān's tomb and whipped his body, then made and worshipped an image of him before cutting off its head. Later that year he took Fu Deng's base at Dajie in a night attack, killing his sons and executing his wife, Empress Mao, after she cursed him; Fu Deng never again threatened the state.

Ill in 392, he still faced Fu Deng at Anding and drew off so skilfully that his rival marvelled at the old Qiang. The Book of Jin records that before his death around the new year 394 he was haunted in dreams by Fu Jiān's spirit, went mad and died of blood loss after a guard accidentally wounded him, still begging Fu Jiān's forgiveness. Yao Xing succeeded him. Because Fu Jiān had once saved his life, many historians regard Yao Chang as a traitor and murderer.
yao-hong: Yao Hong was born in 388, in the reign of his grandfather Yao Chang, the eldest son of Yao Xing. His father made him crown prince in 402 only after much hesitation, for he was described as loving and kind but weak and often ill, and as a lover of arts and literature. He was left in charge of the capital while his father campaigned, and in 409 he defeated the rebel Liu Jue, though he declined to have the victory proclaimed, saying that preventing rebellion was his duty and defeating one nothing to be proud of.

His brother Yao Bi, favoured by their father for his talents, schemed for years to replace him, and when Yao Xing was ready to execute Yao Bi in 412, Yao Hong pleaded for his life. In 416, as Yao Xing lay dying, Yao Bi's allies plotted to kill Yao Hong and seize the palace; Yao Xing had Yao Bi forced to commit suicide and died the next day. Yao Hong executed the remaining conspirators and took the full imperial title rather than his father's title of Heavenly King.

Yao Hong relied on his uncle Yao Shao against attacks from Jin and Xia and against brothers and cousins who rebelled one after another: Yao Yi at Puban in late 416 and Yao Hui at Anding in 417 were both quickly defeated. Seeing the state's unrest, the Jin general Liu Yu attacked in the autumn of 416 and took its eastern half, including Luoyang. His generals Tan Daoji and Shen Linzi defeated Yao Shao, who died of illness. Leading tens of thousands against them, Yao Hong turned first on a force of fewer than 1,000 under Shen Tianzi at Qingni and was beaten, and his army collapsed.

When Liu Yu's fleet under Wang Zhen'e landed at Chang'an, Yao Hong's troops broke without fighting. His 10-year-old son Yao Fonian urged suicide, since they would be executed anyway; when his father refused, the boy leapt from a wall to his death. Yao Hong surrendered with his empress and was sent to Jiankang, where he was executed, as were most of the Yao clan who were captured or surrendered, and the Later Qin came to an end.
yao-xing: Yao Xing, courtesy name Zilüe, was born in 366, when his father Yao Chang was a general of the Former Qin emperor Fu Jiān. His mother is uncertain: the later Empress She is named, but he afterwards honoured his father's concubine Consort Sun as empress dowager. He served as an assistant to Fu Jiān's crown prince Fu Hong, and when Yao Chang rebelled in 384 he fled from Chang'an to join him. Made crown prince in 386, he often guarded the home base and was known for his study of literature.

Soon after his accession Fu Deng attacked, but his army, short of water near Mawei, was routed; Yao Xing then ambushed, captured and executed him, and Later Qin took nearly all of Former Qin's remaining lands. Historians describe these years as diligent and efficient rule. His brother Yao Chóng captured Luoyang from Jin in 399, and the same year, after astrological signs of disaster, Yao Xing gave up the imperial title for that of Heavenly King.

In 400 he defeated Qifu Gangui of Western Qin and took most of his cities, and in 401 the siege of Guzang brought the submission of Later Liang, while Southern Liang, Northern Liang and Western Liang declared themselves vassals. His campaign against Northern Wei ended in 402 when Yao Ping's army was captured at Chaibi. Under the influence of Kumārajīva he became a devout Buddhist; the monk translated more than 300 sutras at his request, and he built many towers and temples.

Later Qin then stopped expanding. In 407 the general Liu Bobo, later Helian Bobo, rebelled and founded Xia, wearing down Later Qin with guerrilla attacks, and in 408 Qi Nan's whole army was captured, costing all of modern northern Shaanxi. Qifu Gangui restored Western Qin in 409, and Jin destroyed Southern Yan in 410 and Western Shu in 413, both of them Later Qin vassals.

His last years were troubled by his son Yao Bi, who plotted against the crown prince Yao Hong and was twice forgiven. In 416, as Yao Xing returned ill from Huayin, Yao Yin and the attendant Yin Chong attacked the palace; Yao Xing appeared in person, his son's troops deserted, and he ordered Yao Bi to commit suicide. He died the next day. Yao Hong faced revolts by his brothers and attacks by Xia and Jin, and by 417 Later Qin had fallen to Jin.
yaounde: Yaoundé lies in the Centre Region of Cameroon at an elevation of about 750 metres, between the Nyong and Sanaga rivers at the northern edge of the area's forests. It is thermally equatorial, with a narrow range of temperatures through the year, and has a long wet season from March to November with a lull in July. Two trans-African highways pass through it, and railway lines run west to the port of Douala and north to N'Gaoundéré.

The outpost of Epsumb, or Jeundo, was founded by the German explorers Lt. Richard Kund and Hans Tappenbeck, with the agreement of the chiefs of Ela Esono. From December 1889 to May 1895 the German botanist Georg August Zenker occupied it as an agricultural research station, which he named Jaunde after the local Yaunde or Ewondo people. It served as a base for the rubber and ivory trade, buying from local people in exchange for imported clothing and iron.

In 1895 Major Dominik set up a military garrison at the site, which made possible a Pallotine mission and religious school at nearby Mvolyé. During the First World War Jaunde was occupied by Belgian troops from the Congo. After Germany's defeat France held eastern Cameroon as a mandate of the League of Nations, and Yaoundé was chosen as the capital of the colony in 1922. Douala long remained the more important settlement, but Yaoundé grew rapidly after 1958, because of the cocoa crisis and unrest along the coast, and it has been the seat of government of the Republic of Cameroon since independence.

Yaoundé has more than 2.8 million inhabitants and is the second-largest city in Cameroon after Douala. Its economy is centred on the civil service and the diplomatic services, with tobacco, dairy products, beer, clay, glass goods and timber among its industries. Its landmarks include the Presidential Palace in the Etoudi district, the Palais des Congrès and the Reunification Monument. Cameroon is bilingual, with English and French both official, and the city has schools in both systems.
yap-ah-loy: Yap Ah Loy, also known as Yap Tet Loy and Yap Mao Lan, was born on 14 March 1837 in a poor village of Canton province, a Hakka of the Fui Chiu clan whose parents lived at Danshui in Huizhou prefecture. He left China by way of Macau in 1854. At Malacca a clansman, Yap Ket Si, sheltered him; he worked four months at a tin mine in Durian Tunggal and a year in a relative's shop at Kesang. Sent towards home through Singapore, he lost all his money there and walked instead to Lukut, arriving in 1856.

He worked as a miner and petty trader until his friend Liu Ngim Kong became the second Kapitan Cina of Kuala Lumpur in 1862, a post of leadership among the Chinese and of liaison with the Malay rulers. Yap became Liu's trusted lieutenant and, after Liu's death, his successor. Rivals rallied under Chong Chong, and the Hakka Hai San and Cantonese Ghee Hin fought for the tin trade. In 1870 Yap drove Chong Chong from Kanching, where 12 Chinese and 8 Malays were killed, and in the Selangor Civil War Raja Mahdi's forces under Syed Mashhor took Kuala Lumpur in 1872 before Tengku Kudin's side recaptured it in March 1873.

The town had been gutted and the mines flooded. Yap rebuilt it, improved its roads and revived mining, though a slump in tin prices in the mid-1870s left him nearly bankrupt until prices rose in 1879. After fire and flood in 1881, the British Resident Frank Swettenham required brick and tile, and Yap set up the brickworks that gave Brickfields its name. He came to own a third of the town's buildings, presided over a small claims court with a police force of six, built a prison for 60 and opened the town's first school.

His independence waned after a British resident was posted to Kuala Lumpur in 1879, though none of his successors approached his power. He fell ill with bronchitis and a lung abscess at the end of 1884 and died on 15 April 1885, and was buried in the Kwong Tong Cemetery. Kuala Lumpur became capital of the Federated Malay States in 1896 and later of Malaysia. Jalan Yap Ah Loy in Chinatown bears his name, and the historian J. M. Gullick wrote that if you seek his memorial you should remember that you are in Kuala Lumpur.
yapahuwa: The citadel lies in the North Western Province, midway between Kurunegala and Anuradhapura, around a granite rock that rises abruptly above the surrounding lowlands. Its original name was Yapawwa. A stupa, a Bodhi tree enclosure and a rock shelter used by monks on the summit, and caves at its foot, one with a shrine of Buddha images and one with a Brahmi inscription, show that the site had earlier been a Buddhist monastery, like many boulders and hills of the area.

The king moved the capital here from Dambadeniya in the face of invasions from South India, bringing the Sacred Tooth Relic with him, and built the palace and fortress in the style of the Sigiriya rock fortress. The relic was kept in a Tooth Temple at the top of the third staircase, following the tradition that whoever held the Tooth ruled the land. After the king's death the Pandyans invaded and carried the relic to South India. Parakramabahu III recovered it in 1288 through negotiation and the threat of war, and placed it for safety at Polonnaruwa. Yapahuwa was then largely abandoned and left to Buddhist monks and ascetics.

The ornamental stairway rises in three flights at about 70 degrees, a design meant to give the defenders the high ground. Its third and best-known flight has a stone portal, or vahalkada, and makara balustrades with dwarfs and lion-like creatures; local folklore holds that a treasure can be seen where the lions gaze. Of the Tooth Temple only its outline and platform remain. At the southern foot of the rock a fortification with two moats and ramparts encloses ruined buildings, and the Yapahuwa Rajamaha Vihara, built in the Kandyan period, has murals of that time.
yaqub-al-mansur: Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Yusuf ibn Abd al-Muʾmin al-Mansur was the third Almohad caliph, known also as Moulay Yacoub. His father was Abu Yaqub Yusuf, and his mother was a Christian concubine called Sahir. The historian Rom Landau, a specialist in Arabic, describes his mother as a Negro slave. He later acquired the name Yaqub the Victorious. He succeeded his father in 1184 and died on 23 January 1199.

His father was killed in Portugal on 29 July 1184, and al-Mansur, on reaching Seville with the body on 10 August, was proclaimed caliph at once. He vowed revenge, but fighting against the Banu Ghaniya delayed him in Africa. In 1190 his siege of Tomar, centre of the Portuguese Templars, failed. In 1191 he recaptured Paderne Castle and its territory near Albufeira in the Algarve, held by the Portuguese army of King Sancho I since 1182, and returned to the Maghreb with three thousand Christian captives. The Christians then retook cities including Silves, Vera and Beja, and he came back to defeat them again.

On 18 July 1195 he defeated the army of Castilian King Alfonso VIII at the Battle of Alarcos. It was said that his forces killed 150,000 and took spoils beyond calculation, and after this victory he took the title al-Mansur Billah, Made Victorious by God. He built a monumental gate at the Kasbah of the Udayas in Rabat and a royal citadel and palace complex in Marrakesh, with the Kasbah Mosque and the gate of Bab Agnaou. In Rabat he began a still larger fortified capital and attempted to build what would have been the world's largest mosque.

He was religiously learned, favoured the Zahirite school of jurisprudence in line with Almohad doctrine, and wrote his own book on the recorded sayings and actions of the Prophet Muhammad. He protected the philosopher Averroes. On inheriting the throne he ordered the chief judge Ibn Maḍāʾ to carry out the burning of non-Zahirite religious books, which Ibn Maḍāʾ and his father had banned. The Bimaristan of Marrakesh, the first hospital in Morocco, is counted among his works.

He died in Marrakesh and was buried temporarily in his palace before being taken to Tinmal, where earlier Almohad caliphs and Ibn Tumart were buried. Work on the Rabat mosque and citadel stopped after his death, leaving a large part of the minaret now known as the Hassan Tower. The victory at Alarcos was remembered for centuries and is recounted by Ibn Abi Zar in his Rawd al-Qirtas of 1326.
yaqub-ibn-al-layth-al-saffar: Ya'qub was born on 25 October 840, of eastern Iranian origin, in the small town of Karnin, east of Zaranj, in what is now Afghanistan. Information about his genealogy is lacking, and sources describe him as extremely poor. His family moved to Zaranj because of sectarian violence between Sunnis and Kharijites, and there he worked as a coppersmith, the trade that gave him the name Saffar. With his brothers he later joined the ayyars under Salih ibn al-Nadr, who opposed the Abbasids. By 854 the ayyars had expelled the Tahirid governor of Sistan, and in 861 Ya'qub overthrew another ayyar leader, Dirham ibn Nasr, and took the title of Emir.

Ya'qub first fought Kharijites in Sistan, and in 865 he defeated and killed their leader Ammar ibn Yaser. His armies took Kabul and Bamiyan from the Hindu Shahis, and by 870 the whole of Khorasan was under his control. In 867 he sent the caliph al-Mu'tazz a poem claiming the inheritance of the kings of Persia. In 873 he ousted the Tahirids from Nishapur and captured their ruler Muhammad ibn Tahir, which led to conflict with the Abbasid caliphate. He took Fars in 875.

In 876 al-Muwaffaq offered him the governorship of Khurasan, Tabaristan, Fars, Gurgan and Ray; Ya'qub refused and advanced towards Baghdad. The armies met at Dayr al-Aqul on 8 April 876. His troops numbered about ten thousand, and the Abbasids were superior in numbers. The Saffarid army, somewhat reluctant to fight the caliph, broke and fled, and many men drowned in flooded land. Ya'qub withdrew from Iraq.

Ya'qub suffered from colic and refused treatment. He died at Gundeshapur on 5 June 879, and his brother Amr succeeded him. Accounts of his religion differ: some sources call him a Kharijite, a Christian or an Ismaili, while the historian D. G. Tor presents evidence that he was a devout Sunni warrior. During his rule Persian was introduced as an official language, and he reportedly did not know Arabic. He has the status of a popular folk hero because his court revived the Persian language, and poets traced his genealogy to the Iranian king Jamshid of tradition. His campaigns also marked an early stage in the decline of caliphal political unity.
yaqub-ibn-killis: Abu'l-Faraj Ya'qub ibn Yusuf ibn Killis was born in Baghdad into a Jewish family. He came to Egypt as a young man, in 943 according to one account, and entered the service of Kafur, the power behind the Ikhshidid regime, where he rose as an expert in finance and took charge of the household and property. He converted to Islam in 967, which pleased Kafur but roused the jealousy of the vizier Ibn al-Furat. When Kafur died in 968 Ibn al-Furat arrested his companions; Ya'qub, it is said, bribed his jailer and escaped to Ifriqiya, where he entered the service of the Fatimid Caliph al-Mu'izz.

Al-Mu'izz gave him charge of the economy. After the Fatimid conquest of Egypt in 969 he went there, by one account with Jawhar as-Siqilli and by another with the caliph in 972, and when Ibn al-Furat resigned in 974 the administration passed to him. Under al-Aziz he became chief minister, Wazir al-Adjall, a title the earlier Fatimid caliphs' assistants had not borne. He set up departments of state anew, promoted agriculture, reformed trade and stabilised the currency, and the treasury was fuller than ever before. In 983/4 he fell from favour and was fined 20,000 gold dinars for reasons unknown, but within months he was back in office.

He was also a scholar who lectured at his palace every Friday night to judges, theologians, grammarians and poets, and a work on theology compiled with 40 theologians, the Risalat al-Waziria, is attributed to him. His annual income was put at 100,000 dinars, and he kept a private force of 4,000 young men.

He fell seriously ill on 10 January 991, and al-Aziz, visiting him, offered to give away the state's wealth or his own son for his recovery. He died on 22 February 991 and was mourned throughout Egypt. According to Ibn Khallikan, 100 poets composed laments for him, each rewarded by the caliph, and a district of Cairo was named the Vizier's Quarter in his honour.
yaqub-shpata: Yaqub, in Albanian Jakup Bua Shpata, was a grandson of Gjon Bua Shpata, the first Albanian ruler of Arta, through Gjon's daughter Irene and an unknown member of the Shpata family. He had a brother, Muriq, and two half-siblings from his mother's second marriage, Charles and Maddalena de' Buondelmonti. He was raised at the Ottoman court of Sultan Mehmed I, where he converted to Islam and took his name.

On Muriq's death in 1414/15 he claimed the succession and, with his mother's support, took Arta itself, while his half-brother Charles became ruler of nearby Rogoi. His Muslim faith soon provoked opposition, as the people feared he would deliver them to the Ottomans: they rose, imprisoned him and installed Charles Marchesano in his place. Released, Yaqub won the sultan's aid, returned with an Ottoman army under a leader named Ismail, retook Arta after a brief siege, exiled his half-brother and executed the leading men of the city.

He then faced Carlo I Tocco, Count palatine of Cephalonia and Zakynthos, who already held Ioannina and the northern half of the old Despotate of Epirus and, posing as the champion of the local Greeks against the Albanian lords, now sought the lands around Arta. Yaqub and his father-in-law Maurice, who had defected from Tocco service, tried to take Carlo's base at Vobliana. The Spatas were heavily defeated by Leonardo II Tocco at Mazoma near ancient Nicopolis, but held Arta against a later attack.

Carlo lured Yaqub into an ambush near Vobliana, where he was captured and at once executed on 1 October 1416. The magnates of Arta then took control from his mother and offered to surrender the city if their rights and privileges were respected. Carlo accepted and entered Arta on 4 October, while Leonardo took Rogoi. The order of the earlier fighting is uncertain, as the main source, the Chronicle of the Tocco, does not follow a strict chronology.
yaqui: The Yaqui call themselves Hiaki or Yoeme, their word for person, and their homeland Hiakim. They speak Yaqui, or Yoem Noki, a Cahitan language of the Uto-Aztecan family spoken by about 16,000 people. When the Spanish first met them in 1533 they numbered an estimated 30,000 people in 80 villages along the lower Yaqui River, most of them farming beans, maize and squash on land the river flooded each year, while others fished near its mouth or hunted and gathered in the deserts and mountains.

After defeating the Spanish in two battles in 1608 and making peace in 1610, the Yaqui invited Jesuit missionaries in 1617. Over some 120 years most converted to Christianity while keeping many traditional beliefs, and the Jesuits gathered them into eight towns, among them Vícam, Pótam and Tórim. Encroachment on their land led to a revolt with the Mayo in 1740 in which one thousand Spanish and 5,000 Native Americans were killed.

After Mexican independence the Yaqui refused to pay taxes. Juan Banderas led a revolt in 1825 and was executed in 1833, and Cajemé led the struggle until his execution in 1887; in 1868 the army burned 150 Yaqui to death inside a church. By 1908 at least 5,000 Yaqui had been sold into slavery on plantations, where most died, two thirds within a year of arriving. The last major battle was fought at Cerro del Gallo in 1927. In 1937 President Lázaro Cárdenas reserved 500,000 hectares of ancestral land on the river's north bank and ordered a dam built for irrigation.

Today there are eight Yaqui pueblos in Sonora. Yaqui who fled the violence formed the Pascua Yaqui Tribe of Arizona, based in Tucson, which received 817,000 square metres of land in 1964 and federal recognition on 18 September 1978.

Many Yoeme hold that the universe is made of overlapping worlds, the aniam, such as the flower world and the wilderness world. The deer dance, accompanied by the deer song, joins three of them, and many believe the world depends on their yearly Lenten and Easter rituals. Flowers, held to have sprung from the blood shed at the crucifixion, are seen as the manifestation of souls.
yaqut-al-hamawi: Yaqut, meaning ruby or hyacinth, was the kunya of Ibn Abdullah, "son of Abdullah". He was born in Constantinople, the Byzantine capital called al-Rum in Arabic, whence his nisba al-Rumi. Captured in war and enslaved, he became the mawali of Askar ibn Abi Nasr al-Hamawi, a trader of Baghdad, from whom he received the laqab al-Hamawi. As Askar's apprentice he learned accounting and commerce and travelled as his envoy, twice or three times, to Kish in the Persian Gulf. In 1194 Askar stopped his salary over some dispute, and Yaqut worked as a copyist and studied under the grammarian al-Ukbari. Five years later he made another mission to Kish for Askar.

On his return to Baghdad Yaqut set up as a bookseller and began to write. He then spent ten years travelling in Iran, Syria and Egypt. His importance as a scholar lies in his testimony to the great, largely lost literary heritage held in libraries east of the Caspian Sea, since he was one of the last visitors before the Mongol invaders destroyed them. He gained much material from the libraries of Merv, where he had studied for two years, and of Balkh. About 1222 he was working on his Geography in Mosul and he completed the first draft in 1224. In 1227 he was in Alexandria, and he moved from there to Aleppo, where he died in 1229.

The Mu'jam al-Buldan, "Dictionary of Countries", was composed between 1224 and 1228 and completed a year before his death. It is classed as a literary geography: an alphabetical index of place names from the literary corpus of the Arabs, with their vocalisations, their Arabic or foreign derivation and their location. Yaqut supplements the geographic descriptions with historical and ethnographic material, accounts of Muslim conquests, names of governors, monuments and local celebrities, and so preserves much early literary, historical, biographical and geographic material, in prose and poetry.

His Mu'jam al-Udaba, the "Literary Encyclopedia" of 1226, is also known as the Irshad al-Arib. Another work, al-Mushtarak, is a lexicon of geographical homonyms, edited by Ferdinand Wüstenfeld in 1846. Wüstenfeld also edited the Mu'jam al-Buldan in six volumes, published at Leipzig.
yarim-lim-i: Yarim-Lim, also written Yarimlim, was the second king of the Amorite kingdom of Yamhad, the son of its first king Sumu-Epuh and his queen Sumunna-Abi. He came to the throne at a time of danger: Shamshi-Adad I of the Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia had surrounded Yamhad through alliances with Carchemish and Urshu to the north and Qatna to the south, and had conquered Mari to the east, placing his son Yasmah-Adad on its throne. Sumu-Epuh was killed campaigning against him. Yarim-Lim's wife was Gashera, whose parents are unknown, and their daughter Shibtu married Zimri-Lim of Mari.

Yarim-Lim held out against Shamshi-Adad. Around 1777 BCE he conquered the city of Tuttul, and when Shamshi-Adad died around 1776 BCE he helped Zimri-Lim, the heir of Mari, drive out Yasmah-Adad and take the throne. Zimri-Lim called him father and acted under the guidance of Hadad, the chief god of Yamhad, whose mediator Yarim-Lim was. The tablets of Mari show this dependence: Yarim-Lim refused to hand over men Zimri-Lim asked for, giving way only at the Mari ambassador's third request, and Zimri-Lim turned down a peace offer from Ibal-pi-el II of Eshnunna three times when Aleppo withheld its consent.

Ibal-pi-el later allied with Elam, the enemy of Yarim-Lim's ally Hammurabi of Babylon. Yarim-Lim's influence reached Ugarit, and his armies campaigned as far as Elam. A tablet found at Mari holds his declaration of war on Dēr and Diniktum, reminding the king of Dēr that Yarim-Lim had given him military help for 15 years and had kept 500 warships of Aleppo at Diniktum for 12 years.

Yarim-Lim died around 1764 BCE and was succeeded by his son Hammurabi I. His widow Gashera outlived him and remained a strong-willed figure in the politics of the kingdom after his death. The historian William Hamblin called Yarim-Lim at the height of his power "the mightiest ruler in the Near East outside of Egypt".
yarim-lim-of-alalakh: Yarim-Lim was a son of Hammurabi I of Yamhad, who appointed him governor of a northern district whose main city was Irridu. He kept the district under his elder brother, Abba-El I. When Zitraddu, governor of Irridu, rebelled, Abba-El destroyed the city, and as compensation he made a treaty granting Yarim-Lim the city of Alalakh as a hereditary kingdom under the suzerainty of Aleppo. This happened fifteen years into Abba-El's reign, around 1735 BCE.

Yarim-Lim ruled through the rest of his brother's reign, that of his nephew Yarim-Lim II of Yamhad and the first years of his great-nephew Niqmi-Epuh. He died around 1700 BCE and was succeeded by his son Ammitakum, and the cadet branch of the Yamhadite dynasty he founded lasted until the Hittite king Hattusili I conquered Alalakh.

His identity is disputed. Moshe Weinfeld suggested that he and Yarim-Lim II of Yamhad were one man, a natural son of Hammurabi I adopted by Abba-El, a view with little support. Nadav Na'aman, pointing to the very long reigns of Yarim-Lim and Ammitakum across five Yamhadite kings, proposed a second Yarim-Lim of Alalakh, a grandson of the first; Dominique Collon and Erno Gaál support this, while Horst Klengel and Marlies Heinz reject it, and no evidence for him has been found.

Leonard Woolley found the Palace of Yarim-Lim in excavations begun in 1936. The burial lay in a pit 15 metres deep with a central shaft of nine metres holding the funeral urn; the shaft was filled with stones and the pit with successive layers of ceremonial buildings, each burned and then built over. A royal chapel above it held a diorite statue of Yarim-Lim. Woolley took the statue to represent Yarim-Lim I of Yamhad, but readings of the Alalakh tablets showed it to be the king of Alalakh, his grandson.
yarkand: Yarkand, or Yarkant County, lies on the southern rim of the Taklamakan Desert in the Tarim Basin, at an altitude of 1,189 metres, and is administered under Kashgar Prefecture. The oasis is fed by the Yarkand River, which flows north from the Karakorum and through the Kunlun Mountains. It now covers 3,210 square kilometres but was probably far more extensive before a period of desiccation that began from the 3rd century CE. The oasis farmland produces cotton, wheat, corn, pomegranates, pears, apricots and walnuts.

The Book of Han of the 1st century BCE first mentions the territory as Shaju, probably related to the name of the Iranian Saka tribes. In the 1st century CE the kingdom of Suoju was the most powerful in the Western Regions. Its king Xian, given the seal of Protector General in 41 CE and then denied it, conquered Kucha and other kingdoms, until Guangde of Khotan captured him in 61 CE and killed him. The Han general Ban Chao defeated Suoju in 86 CE, and in 130 CE Yarkand sent tribute to the Chinese emperor along with Ferghana and Kashgar.

Little is recorded for many centuries after that. Yarkant became the main base of Chagatai Khan, who inherited Kashgaria after Genghis Khan died in 1227. Marco Polo described it in 1273 as a province where people followed the law of Mahomet, with some Nestorian Christians, and rich in cotton. In 1509 the Dughlats rebelled against Moghulistan, and five years later Sultan Said Khan conquered them and set up the Yarkent Khanate, with Yarkand as its capital. The Jesuit Benedict Göez reached the city in 1603 and called it a mart of much note, where the Kabul caravan ended and a new one formed for Cathay.

The Qing dynasty gained control of the region in the middle of the 18th century. By the 19th century trade with Ladakh and foreign merchants made it the largest and most populous state of Kashgar. In the 1860s Yakub Beg made Yarkant the capital of his Turkic state of Yettishar and received embassies from England in 1870 and 1873. The Qing defeated him in 1877, and he committed suicide. Yarkant is now predominantly Uyghur, with a small Tajik minority.
yarkent-khanate: The Yarkent Khanate, also called the Yarkand Khanate and the Kashghar Khanate, was a Sunni Muslim khanate ruled by Turkified Mongol descendants of Chagatai Khan, son of Genghis Khan. Its ruling house belonged to the Eastern Chaghatayid, or Moghul, dynasty. The Chagatai Khanate collapsed in the first half of the 14th century. Its western part became the Empire of Timur in 1370, and its eastern part became Moghulistan, created by Tughluk Timur Khan in 1347 with its capital at Almalik, in the Ili River Valley. Moghulistan comprised the settled lands of eastern Kashgaria and the regions of Turpan and Kumul.

The Dughlats had ruled Kashgaria as vassals since 1220, when Chagatai Khan granted them most of it. In 1509 they rebelled against Moghulistan. Sultan Said Khan, a brother of the Khan of Eastern Moghulistan, or the Turpan Khanate, then conquered them, took Kashgar, Yarkent and Hotan from Mirza Abu Bakr Dughlat and set up his own khanate. Yarkent was its capital until its fall in 1705, as it had been for the Dughlat state.

The khanate was predominantly Uyghur and Turki, and its populous cities included Hotan, Yarkent, Kashgar, Yangihissar, Aksu, Kucha, Karashar, Turpan and Kumul. Its conquest of the Dughlats ended their dominance in Kashgaria and made it the foremost power of the region. Said Khan's reign was heavily influenced by the khojas, and he had a close relationship with his cousin Babur, founder of the Mughal Empire. He campaigned in Bolor in 1527 to 1528, raided Badakhshan in 1529, and led looting expeditions into Ladakh and Kashmir in 1532. He reportedly died in 1533 at Daulat Beg Oldi of high-altitude pulmonary edema while returning from Ladakh and Kashmir.

His successor Abdurashid Khan, who ruled from 1533 to 1565, began by executing a member of the Dughlat family.
