Han forces under Huangfu Song, Zhu Jun and Lu Zhi fought the main rebel armies. By the start of 185 the rebellion had mostly been suppressed, and in mid-February the emperor changed his era name to Zhongping, meaning pacification achieved. Remnants rose again for two decades. The White Wave Bandits appeared in 188, and in 192 hundreds of thousands of Yellow Turban remnants who entered Yan Province surrendered to Cao Cao, who made the best of them into the elite Qingzhou Army.

The rebellion destroyed major government buildings, killed high officials and fragmented the dynasty's territory. Rebel deaths numbered in the hundreds of thousands, and many civilians were left homeless or destitute. The court's weakness and the rising political influence of regional military governors who helped suppress it led to warlord dominance and the Three Kingdoms period. After Emperor Ling died in 189, Dong Zhuo took control of the young heir and the capital, and the Han dynasty collapsed completely by 220. The revolt also marks an important point in the history of Taoism, and it is the inciting event of the 14th-century novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms.
yelu-bei: Yelü Bei, also called Yelü Tuyu, was the first son of Yelü Abaoji and his wife Shulü Ping, and the History of Liao describes him as intelligent and studious in youth. When his father proclaimed himself emperor in 916, as Emperor Taizu, he made Yelü Bei crown prince. Asked which spirit should first receive sacrifice, Yelü Bei named Confucius rather than the Buddha, and Taizu built a Confucian temple where the heir made offerings twice a year. He led the vanguard against the Wugu and the Tangut and is said to have drafted the plan to conquer Balhae.

As King of Dongdan he bore the title Imperial King of Men. When Taizu died at Fuyu soon after its capture, Empress Shulü, who favoured her second son Yelü Deguang, let the chieftains choose by taking the rein of the son they backed; they took Deguang's, and he became Emperor Taizong. Yelü Bei tried to flee with several hundred soldiers but was stopped at the border and sent back to Dongdan. Taizong moved its capital to Dongping and set guards over him, and Emperor Mingzong of Later Tang secretly urged him to come south.

In 930 he sailed with his concubine Lady Gao and his library to Deng Prefecture, leaving behind his wife, Queen Xiao, who ruled Dongdan until 940, and his eldest son Yelü Ruan, later Emperor Shizong. Mingzong named him Li Zanhua and gave him military governorships whose work others did. Accounts call him cruel to his household, drinking his concubines' blood, so that his new wife, Lady Xia, divorced him to become a Buddhist nun, but also gifted in medicine, music and writing in Khitan and Han; he translated the Huangdi Yinfujing into Khitan, and his paintings of Khitan horsemen reached the Song palace collections.

He kept up contact with his mother and brother and is said to have urged Taizong to invade after Li Congke seized the Later Tang throne in 934. When Shi Jingtang rebelled with Khitan aid in 936, an official proposed making Li Zanhua emperor of the Khitan to open a second front, but the plan came to nothing. As Later Jin's troops neared Luoyang, Li Congke prepared to die in his burning palace; Li Zanhua refused to join him and was killed by the officer Li Yanshen. Shi Jingtang mourned him and sent his body home.
yelu-chucai: Yelü Chucai was born on 24 July 1190 near Zhongdu, the capital of the Jin dynasty, a descendant of Yelü Bei of the Khitan Yelü clan. His father, Yelü Lu, rose from translator to minister under Emperor Zhangzong of Jin but died when his son was two, and his scholarly mother saw to his education. Offered a post in the Jin civil service at seventeen through his father's rank, he chose instead to sit the imperial examinations and came first, and by 1213 he was prefect of Kaizhou.

By the time of the 10-month Mongol siege of Zhongdu in 1213 he had been recalled to the city with the title of Auxiliary Secretary of the Boards of Right and Left. The siege caused him a mental crisis, and from 1215 he studied Chan Buddhism under Wansong Xingxiu for three years while serving as a scribe to the new rulers.

In 1218 he was summoned to the Mongol court between the Tuul and Kherlen rivers. Genghis Khan told him he had avenged the Liao on the Jin, and Yelü Chucai answered that his father and grandfather had served the Jin and that he could not count his sovereign and his father as enemies. The khan was impressed by the reply and by the tall, long-bearded man, called him Urtu Saqal, Long Beard, and took him into his retinue as scribe-secretary and court astrologer. He helped arrange Genghis Khan's meeting with the monk Qiu Chuji.

Under Ögedei Khan he was put in charge of tax reform in North China in 1229 and made head of the Great Imperial Secretariat. He separated civil from military powers and argued that an empire might be conquered on horseback but could not be ruled on horseback. When some Mongol commanders urged the razing of Kaifeng and the killing of its people, he persuaded the Mongols to rule and tax them instead. He used his office to shield Confucian scholars and to find them posts as officials and tutors to the princes.

He died on 20 June 1244, during the regency of Töregene Khatun, still treated with respect. He was buried by Kunming Lake in Beijing, where a temple to his memory stood until Red Guards razed it in 1966 during the Cultural Revolution. He is the last person recorded as able to speak the Khitan language and read the Khitan large and small scripts.
yelu-dashi: Yelü Dashi was a minor member of the imperial Yelü clan of the Liao dynasty and an eighth-generation descendant of the Emperor Taizu of Liao. His courtesy name was Zhongde. The History of Liao describes him as well versed in Khitan and Chinese scripts, excellent at riding and archery, and a graduate of the highest imperial examination in 1115. In the dynasty's last years he held increasingly important administrative and military posts, including the governorship of Taizhou and Xiangzhou.

The Jurchens established the Jin dynasty in 1115 and allied with the Song dynasty against the Liao; by 1122 the Jin held much of Liao territory. After the Liao emperor Tianzuo fled west, his uncle Prince Yelü Chun formed the short-lived Northern Liao at Liao Nanjing, now Beijing.

Under Dashi and Xiao Gan, the Liao army repelled Song attacks, but the Jin took the city in 1123. Dashi was captured, escaped after five months and rejoined the emperor. When Tianzuo planned to attack the Jin, Dashi thought it folly and in 1124 led a band of officials northwest to the garrison town of Kedun. Tianzuo was captured in 1125 and the Liao dynasty ended.

On 13 March 1130 Dashi set out west with fewer than 20,000 men and established a base on the Emil River. The ruler of Qocho welcomed him, but an attack on Kashgar in 1131 failed. In 1132 his followers proclaimed him Gurkhan. In 1134 he deposed the Eastern Karakhanid ruler of Balasaghun, Ibrāhīm II, and made it his capital. He took control of what is now Xinjiang and in May 1137 defeated a Western Karakhanid ruler at Khujand.

In 1141 Dashi met the Seljuk sultan Ahmad Sanjar at the Battle of Qatwan and won a decisive victory. Sanjar barely escaped, and his wife was captured. Seljuk power declined sharply, and Khwarazm and the Karakhanids became vassals of the Qara Khitai. Dashi died in 1143, and his empress Xiao Tabuyan became regent. His dynasty lasted until Kuchlug usurped it and Genghis Khan conquered its lands in 1218. His victory and his good relations with Nestorian Christianity led to his link with the legend of Prester John, first chronicled by Bishop Otto of Freising in 1145.
yelu-deguang: Born on 25 November 902, before the Liao state was founded, Yelü Deguang was the second son of the Yelü clan chieftain Yelü Abaoji and his wife Shulü Ping. In 922 his father made him Generalissimo of All Forces and put him in charge of raids on the Former Jin; in 923 his troops took Ping Prefecture and defeated the Huxun tribe of the Xi. After the campaign of 926 against Balhae, Abaoji made his elder son Yelü Bei king of the new Dongdan Kingdom and gave Deguang the title of Generalissimo Crown Prince and charge of the capital Linhuang.

As emperor he honoured his mother as empress dowager and was said to be so devoted to her that he would not eat when she was too ill to eat. In 930 he named his younger brother Yelü Lihu crown prince, and Yelü Bei, passed over again, fled to the Later Tang. When Shi Jingtang, military governor of Hedong, rebelled in 936 and asked for help, offering to serve him as a father and to cede Lulong Circuit and the prefectures north of the Yanmen Pass, Taizong agreed. He made You Prefecture a southern capital to govern the sixteen prefectures, modelled his government on Chinese states and made Zhao Yanshou chancellor.

Relations soured after Shi Chonggui succeeded in Later Jin and wrote to him as grandson, not subject; Liao merchants were arrested and killed at Kaifeng. Taizong invaded in 944 but was held at the Yellow River crossing at Majiakou, and his troops slaughtered captured Han civilians. In 946 a feigned defection by Zhao Yanshou drew the Later Jin army north, where Taizong surrounded it at Zhongdu Bridge and won its commanders Du Wei and Li Shouzhen over with a promise of the throne. The capital, left undefended, surrendered.

Taizong declared himself emperor of China, broke his promises to Zhao and Du, and sent Shi Chonggui into exile as the Marquess of Fuyi. Han rebellions spread, and after he left Daliang the Yellow River ford of Heyang fell. He blamed three errors: taking money from the circuits, letting his soldiers forage, and keeping the military governors from their posts. He died on 18 May 947. His sons included Yelü Jing, later Emperor Muzong.
yemelyan-pugachev: Pugachev was the youngest son of a small Don Cossack landowner and was born in the stanitsa of Zimoveyskaya, in present-day Volgograd Oblast. He enlisted at 17, married a Cossack girl, Sofya Nedyuzheva, within the year, and joined the Russian army in Prussia during the Seven Years' War. He returned home in 1762 and reached the Cossack rank of khorunzhiy. At the siege of Bender in 1770, during the Russo-Turkish War, he first showed a flair for impersonation by telling comrades that his sword was a gift from his godfather, Peter I.

In 1770 he left the army and became a fugitive. He was arrested and escaped several times, spent time among the Cossacks of the Terek, and returned to Russia in the autumn of 1772 with the help of Old Believers. He settled near present-day Volsk and probably heard there of the rebellion of the Yaik Cossacks.

The idea of posing as the dead Emperor Peter III came to Pugachev early; Peter III had been overthrown and murdered in 1762 by supporters of his wife, the future Catherine II. Pugachev promised to restore privileges to the Cossacks and the Old Belief, and in 1773 he began an open revolt, proclaiming an end to serfdom. His army overran much of the region between the Volga and the Urals, and he gained the support of industrial peasants in the Urals. He set up a College of War with four judges to organise his army, and it paid wages and bounties to the Cossacks. In 1774 his chief success was the capture of Kazan, where the city was burned to the ground.

General Pyotr Panin was slow to act against him, because of transport difficulties and indiscipline among his poorly paid soldiers. In August 1774 General Michelsohn crushed the rebels near Tsaritsyn, and about ten thousand were killed or taken prisoner. Panin carried out savage reprisals after the capture of Penza. On 14 September 1774 Pugachev's own Cossacks handed him over at Yaitsk.

Alexander Suvorov had him placed in an iron cage and sent to Simbirsk and then to Moscow. He was executed publicly in Bolotnaya Square on 21 January 1775, beheaded and then quartered. Catherine II had been trying to reform the provincial administration, but the horrors of the revolt made her drop other reforms, in particular attempts to emancipate the serfs. Alexander Pushkin wrote a history of the rebellion and used it in his novel The Captain's Daughter (1836).
yemen: Yemen lies in southern Arabia and covers 455,503 square kilometres, with a coastline of about 2,000 kilometres. It borders Saudi Arabia to the north and Oman to the northeast, and its territory includes the Socotra Archipelago and several Red Sea islands, among them the Hanish Islands, Kamaran and Perim. Socotra lies east of the Horn of Africa and is geographically and bio-geographically associated with Africa.

The country divides into four main regions: the coastal plains in the west, the western highlands, the eastern highlands and the Rub' al Khali in the east. The Tihamah, a very arid and flat plain along the Red Sea coast, ends abruptly at the escarpment of the western highlands. These highlands are heavily terraced and receive the highest rainfall in Arabia, from about 760 millimetres a year at Taiz to over 1,000 millimetres at Ibb.

Large settlements existed in the mountains of northern Yemen from about 5000 BCE. The four major kingdoms of South Arabia were Saba, Hadhramaut, Qataban and Ma'in. Saba, thought to be the biblical Sheba, was the most prominent, and its rulers took a title generally thought to mean unifier. It built the Great Dam of Marib around 940 BCE. A Roman army of 10,000 men under Aelius Gallus was defeated before it reached Marib.

By the third century BCE Qataban, Hadhramaut and Ma'in had become independent of Saba, which regained its hegemony after Qataban collapsed in 50 BCE. The Himyarites annexed Sanaa around 100 CE, and by 275 Shammar Yahri'sh had conquered Hadhramaut, Najran and Tihamah, unifying Yemen under Himyarite rule. By 515 Himyar was divided along religious lines, and civil turmoil brought an intervention from Aksum.

Islam spread rapidly in the seventh century, and for centuries Yemen was a primary producer of coffee, exported through the port of Mokha. In the nineteenth century the country was divided between the Ottoman and British empires. The Kingdom of Yemen was established after the First World War and became the Yemen Arab Republic in 1962. South Yemen became independent in 1967, and the two states united in 1990.

Sanaa is the constitutional capital and largest city. Modern Standard Arabic is the official language and Islam the state religion. The country has an estimated population of about 34.7 million. The old city of Sanaa, with its tower-houses of mud-brick and stone, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. Yemen is a member of the Arab League, the United Nations and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.
yemeni-civil-war-2014-present: Islam in Yemen takes mainly Sunni and Shia forms, and among the Shia the Ismaili and Zaydi sects historically competed for influence. After the Ayyubid expansion most of the Hamdan tribe converted to Zaydism, and during the Rasulid period, from 1229 to 1454, Shafi'i Sunni Islam gained popularity. From the 1960s Zaydis faced discrimination under governments that favoured Sunni Islam. The Houthis, or Ansar Allah, are a Zaydi group from the Sa'dah Governorate on Yemen's northern border with Saudi Arabia, who led a low-level insurgency against the government from 2004 after their leader, Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi, was killed in a military crackdown.

After weeks of street protests against the administration of President Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi, which had cut fuel subsidies, the Houthis fought army forces under General Ali Mohsen al-Ahmar and in a battle of a few days took Sanaa in September 2014. Hadi negotiated an agreement under which the government resigned and the Houthis gained more influence over state institutions than ever before.

On 21 March 2015 the Houthi-led Supreme Revolutionary Committee declared a general mobilisation. With forces loyal to the former president Ali Abdullah Saleh, the Houthis fought in Lahij Governorate and by 25 March had reached the outskirts of Aden, where Hadi's government sat. Hadi fled the country the same day. A coalition led by Saudi Arabia began air strikes and other operations to restore the government. Aden was recaptured, but the conflict settled into a protracted stalemate.

Saleh was assassinated in 2017 after his alliance with the Houthis broke down. The Southern Transitional Council, formed in 2017 and backed by the United Arab Emirates, captured Aden in 2018, and clashes followed between it and forces loyal to Hadi, who were backed by Saudi Arabia. The Stockholm Agreement of December 2018 sought a ceasefire around Hodeida. A United Nations truce began in April 2022.

The war brought a severe humanitarian crisis. The United Nations reports more than 150,000 people killed, and estimates of more than 227,000 further deaths from famine and the lack of health care. Yemen meets 90% of its food needs through imports, and a blockade disrupted deliveries, while cholera cases rose from 2015. The UN Security Council imposed an arms embargo on the Houthis in 2015.
yemeni-socialist-party: The party grew out of the National Liberation Front, formed in the Aden Protectorate in 1963, which fought the British and defeated its rival, the Front for the Liberation of Occupied South Yemen. The British withdrew on 30 November 1967 and handed power to the NLF. In the Corrective Move of 22 June 1969 its left wing under Abdul Fattah Ismail and Salem Rubai Ali overthrew President Qahtan Muhammad al-Shaabi, and in 1975 the front joined left-wing Ba'athists and Marxists in a unified organisation. Abdul Fattah Ismail founded the YSP from it and from the Yemeni Popular Unity Party of North Yemen, and became its first General Secretary.

Its charter took scientific socialism as its theory and a unified democratic Yemen with a socialist perspective as its goal, and in December 1978 it won all 111 seats in parliament. Factional quarrels marked its rule. In 1980 Ismail resigned under pressure and went into exile in Moscow, and Ali Nasser Mohammed, seen as more moderate, sought better relations with Arab neighbours and the West. The conflict between the factions led to the South Yemen Civil War of 1986, in which Ismail was killed; Ali Salem al-Beidh took over the party and Haidar Abu Bakr al-Attas became president.

The YSP helped bring about unification and multi-party politics in May 1990. In 1993 it won 56 of 301 seats and joined a coalition with the General People's Congress and al-Islah. After the 1994 civil war, in which its leaders proclaimed a Democratic Republic of Yemen in the south, its property was confiscated and its members were arrested and tortured. It boycotted the 1997 elections, joined the Joint Meeting Parties in 2002 and won 3.8% of the vote in 2003.

Membership rose from 19,198 members and candidates in December 1980 to 32,786 by June 1985, over half of them office workers and soldiers. Once a Marxist–Leninist vanguard party, it later moved to pan-Arab nationalism and social democracy. In the Yemeni Civil War it split: one faction, calling itself YSP – Anti-Aggression, declared loyalty to the Houthis, while leaders such as Abdulrahman al-Saqqaf and Yasin Said Numan went into exile in Riyadh and backed the government of Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi.
yemoja: Her name is a contraction of the Yoruba words iye, a dialect form of ìyá, mother; ọmọ, child; and ẹja, fish. Roughly rendered as mother of fish children, it expresses the breadth of her motherhood and fertility and her rule over all living things. In traditional Yoruba belief she is a mother spirit and the patron of women, especially pregnant women. Besides the Ogun River, other rivers across Yorubaland are dedicated to her, and she is worshipped at almost any stream, creek or spring, and at wells.

Among the river deities of Yorubaland, with Ọ̀ṣun, Erinlè̩, Ọbà and Yewá, she is counted a leader, while the role of sea deity belongs to Olókun. In some beliefs, when her waters broke they caused a great flood that made the rivers and streams, and the first mortal humans came from her womb.

Carried across the Atlantic, her worship changed its emphasis: in West Africa she is a high-ranking river deity, but in Brazil and Cuba she is honoured mainly as a deity of the sea. In Candomblé and Umbanda in Brazil, Yemanjá is one of the seven Orixás, the Queen of the Ocean, patron of fishermen and of survivors of shipwreck, and the spirit of moonlight. Her day is Saturday, her colours light blue and crystal, and white roses are offered to her. In Brazil she is also identified with Our Lady of Navigators and Our Lady of the Conception.

In Cuban Santería, or regla de ocha, Yemayá is the mother of all living things and owner of the oceans and seas. She has many roads, or aspects, among them Okute, Asesú, Achabá and Mayelewo, all marked by blue; her number is seven, and her necklace has seven blue and seven crystalline beads.

Her festivals draw large crowds. Every 2 February in Salvador, Bahia, thousands bring flowers, perfume, combs and mirrors to her shrine at Rio Vermelho, and fishermen carry the offerings out to sea. On New Year's Eve millions of Brazilians of all religions, dressed in white, throw flowers into the sea for her. In Havana she is honoured on 7 September with a procession in Regla, a tradition begun by the cabildos of enslaved people, and in Montevideo worshippers launch small boats of offerings from Ramírez Beach every 2 February.
yen-bai-mutiny: The Vietnamese Nationalist Party (VNQDĐ), modelled on the Chinese Kuomintang of Chiang Kai-shek, had been badly damaged by the colonial government's first large-scale crackdown in 1929, which also strengthened the violent tendencies of what remained. Its leaders hoped that a military attack in the Red River Delta would inspire a wider uprising to overthrow colonial rule and create an independent Vietnamese republic. Most of them seem to have judged their chances poor: at best they might trigger a spontaneous uprising, at worst French reprisals would make them anti-colonial martyrs.

At about 1:30 a.m. on 10 February 1930, some 50 soldiers of the Second Battalion of the Fourth Regiment of Tonkinese Rifles, joined by about 60 civilian party members, attacked the garrison's 29 French officers and warrant officers. Five Frenchmen were killed and three seriously wounded. The rebels took the armoury, raised the party's flag and sent a patrol into the town, falsely claiming that the entire French officer corps was dead. Most Vietnamese soldiers of the garrison stayed loyal, and the mutiny failed within 24 hours. An attack on the barracks at Hưng Hóa the same night was repelled, and other attacks across the delta had little effect.

Governor General Pasquier created the Criminal Commission of Tonkin on 12 February, presided over by Jules Bride. During 1930 it prosecuted 547 people and handed down 80 death sentences, not all of them carried out, 102 life sentences of forced labour and 243 deportations, to places such as Poulo Condore and French Guiana. The party's leaders were killed or sentenced to death, and its remnants fled to China. In the long run Yên Bái allowed the Indochinese Communist Party of Ho Chi Minh to take the VNQDĐ's place as the leading anti-colonial movement.

The army also took steps against another mutiny. According to Maurice Rives, 10,000 Vietnamese troops, more than 80 per cent of Tonkin's tirailleurs, were transferred to other zones; 2,000 soldiers returning from France were sent on indefinite leave; military intelligence was tied more closely to the Sûreté; and in a compromise adopted by Pasquier one regiment of Tonkinese Rifles was disbanded.
yen-chia-kan: Yen Chia-kan was born on 23 October 1905 in Mudu, to the Yan family of Dongshan, a prestigious and moderately wealthy Soochow family. He began formal schooling in 1910 and in 1926 graduated from St. John's University in Shanghai with a Bachelor of Science degree in chemistry. In 1931 he began work as a manager of the Shanghai railway administration.

During the Second World War Yen directed the finance department of the Fuchien and Kwangtung provincial governments. He initiated a land tax paid in agricultural produce, which was then adopted nationwide. In Fuchien he abolished more than 70 miscellaneous taxes and balanced the provincial budget. He later became procurement director of the War Production Board, in charge of supplies from American Lend-Lease and from British and Canadian loans.

He reached Taiwan in October 1945. As chairman of the Bank of Taiwan he began issuing the New Taiwan dollar on 15 June 1949 to replace the old currency, which was suffering hyperinflation during the Chinese Civil War, and he imported 10,000 tons of rice from Southeast Asia. After serving as Minister of Economic Affairs and Minister of Finance, he became Governor of Taiwan in 1954, and was later again finance minister until 1963. Together with Yin Chung-jung and Yang Chi-tseng he formed the "Yin–Yen–Yang iron triangle" of finance. He became Premier on 16 December 1963 and was elected Vice President in 1966 with 55.23 percent of the votes, and re-elected in 1972 with 83.78 percent.

Chiang Kai-shek died on 5 April 1975, and Yen was sworn in as President on 6 April. He declared a month of mourning and kept the vice-presidency vacant out of respect. As the first civilian president he enacted reforms, among them the shift from Literary Chinese to the written vernacular in government documents. The oil crisis of 1973 had pushed Taiwan's inflation to 61.5 percent in March 1974; austerity measures, higher interest rates and restricted credit brought it to 0.13 percent by October 1976. In July 1977 he visited Saudi Arabia. His term ended on 20 May 1978, and he did not seek re-election; Chiang Ching-kuo succeeded him.
He later chaired the Chinese Cultural Renaissance movement. He had been bedridden since a brain haemorrhage in 1986, suffered a second in 1992, and died in Taipei on 24 December 1993, aged 88.
yen-the-insurrection: From 1865 to 1885 the northern mountains of the Empire of Annam were troubled by armed groups from Guangxi, driven out after the Taiping Rebellion collapsed, whom the local authorities of the Nguyễn dynasty could not remove. Refugees from the lowlands who settled the western hills of Bắc Giang province had to unite to defend themselves, and they traded with these groups for goods and weapons, above all with the Black Flag Army, whose soldiers used the hills to ambush the French in the Red River Delta. Local leaders, mostly heading bands of farmers, took titles such as đề đốc, provincial military commander, which the Nguyễn court did not recognise.

Yên Thế Thượng was at first held by Đề Hả (Lương Văn Nắm) and Đề Sặt (Đỗ Văn Hùng), who sided with the Black Flag Army against the Yellow Flag Army. In March 1892 about 2,200 French soldiers under General Voron attacked the Yên Thế camps and defeated them, and some leaders surrendered. Đề Hả died in April 1892; French documents gave dysentery as the cause, but the insurgents suspected that Đề Sặt had helped the French kill him.

In 1893 Đề Hả's adopted son Trương Văn Nghĩa took charge and had Đề Sặt killed, his head displayed in Nhã Nam market. From then on he led the insurgents under the title Đề Thám. Several French campaigns through the mountains failed to end the resistance, so the colonial authorities turned at times to truces, ceding four cantons to his control. Đề Thám fought by guerrilla raids on local patrols and at times by full attacks. By the early 20th century his area of operations had narrowed, and the movement collapsed when an agent working for the French killed him in 1913.

The revolt was one of the longest chapters of resistance to French rule in Vietnam, and Đề Thám, called the Sacred Panthera of Yên Thế, has been a subject of Vietnamese art since the 1920s. The ruins of his camp at Phồn Xương are kept as the Yên Thế Uprising relic area, and the Yên Thế Festival, held on 16 March every year since the 1980s, is recognised as national intangible cultural heritage.
yenangyaung: Yenangyaung lies on the Irrawaddy River in the Magway Region, 135 miles from Mandalay, surrounded by oil fields that were long the most productive in the country. Besides petroleum the area produces cooking oil, and its farmers grow sesame, groundnut, onion, sunflower and beans. The city is divided into 14 main quarters, with Myoma Market and Yadanar Market at its centre and an industrial zone to the north.

Oil was dug by hand here long before the colonial era. Some claim the industry began as early as the 10th century, but the earliest surviving record dates from 1755, when the English captain George Baker described an earth oil town of 200 families by the river. In 1795 Major Michael Symes described the wells of petroleum, and the following year Captain Hiram Cox, the East India Company's Resident in Rangoon, found 520 wells registered by the government.

The fields at Twingon and Beme belonged to a hereditary corporation of 24 families, each headed by a twinzayo, with inheritance passing from male to male and female to female. An elected head, the twingyimin, approved every new well site, and British rule recognised these hereditary rights in the Executive Instructions of 1893.

In the Second World War Yenangyaung had a strategically important refinery. As the Japanese advanced through Burma, retreating Allied forces blew up the oil fields and refinery on 16 April 1942. The demolition team, among them Arthur Herbert Virgin, formerly of the 2nd Bombay Pioneers, escaped nearly 1,000 miles through enemy-held territory to Imphal and Kohima. The Japanese still worked the fields, which Allied bombers badly damaged in the last year of the war. Yenangyaung was the capital of Minbu Division and of Yenangyaung District until 1974, when the division became the Magway Region, the district was abolished and the capital moved to Magway.

The area produces most of Myanmar's oil and natural gas. The city had 45,120 people at the 2014 census, the fourth-largest in the Magway Region, and is home to Yenangyaung University. Aung San, the leader most responsible for Burmese independence, went to high school here.
yenisei-river: The Yenisei is the fifth-longest river system in the world and the largest to drain into the Arctic Ocean. The river proper is 3,487 km long, measured from the meeting of the Great Yenisei and Little Yenisei at Kyzyl to its mouth in the Kara Sea. Its basin covers 2,580,000 km2 and includes Lake Baikal, the world's deepest lake. It divides the Western Siberian Plain from the Central Siberian Plateau and flows through Tuva, Khakassia and Krasnoyarsk Krai. The basin holds 55 native fish species, two of them endemic.

Nomadic peoples such as the Ket and the Yugh have lived along the banks since ancient times, and the region is the home of the Yeniseian language family. The Ket, about 1,000 in number, are the only survivors of those who once lived throughout central southern Siberia, and were politically absorbed into Russia between the 17th and 19th centuries. Some of the earliest evidence of Turkic origins was found in the valley, in stelae and memorial tablets of the seventh to ninth centuries.

The river's first written mention, as Kem, dates to the 7th century in Tang dynasty China, at the time of contact with the Yenisei Kyrgyz, and the word Käm appears in 8th-century Orkhon inscriptions. The origin of the name Yenisei remains unclear. Dutch navigators knew the river by the end of the 16th century. Russians reached the lower river from the north-west by 1600, when the Tobolsk Cossacks built Fort Mangazeya, and the upper river in 1605, travelling from the Ob by way of the Ket.

River steamers first came to the Yenisei in 1864, brought across the Kara Sea from the Netherlands and the United Kingdom. The Thames overwintered in 1876 and was wrecked, while the Frazer and Express succeeded in 1878. The Dalman reached Yeniseisk in 1881. Captain Joseph Wiggins sailed the Orestes with rails in 1893 during the building of the Trans-Siberian Railway.

The route proved very difficult, since the long estuaries of the Ob and Yenisei are shallow, ice-bound and prone to high winds, and several ships were lost. After the railway was completed, river traffic fell to local service, as the Arctic route was too indirect. Radioactive discharges from a plutonium plant at the secret city of Krasnoyarsk-26, now Zheleznogorsk, contaminated the river.
yennenga: Yennenga, who is placed in the 12th century, is described in oral histories as the daughter of Nedega and Napoko, king and queen of her kingdom in the early 12th century. Her name means the slim and refers to her beauty. Her father raised her as a skilled hunter and fighter, and from the age of 14 she fought in his battles against the neighbouring Malinkés. She was skilled with javelins, spears and bows, an excellent horsewoman, and commanded a battalion of her own. Her story has entered legend, though it may have a core of truth.

When she reached marriageable age Nedega refused to choose a husband for her or let her marry, because of her value as a warrior. To show her unhappiness she planted a field of wheat and let the crop rot, explaining that this was how she felt. Nedega was unmoved and locked her up. One of the king's horsemen helped her escape on her stallion, with her disguised as a man; the versions of the escape differ. The Malinkés attacked, her companion was killed, and she rode on alone to the north.

One night, exhausted from crossing a river, she was carried by her stallion into a forest, where she met a solitary elephant hunter named Rialé. He saw through her disguise, and they fell in love. They had a son, Ouedraogo, whose name means stallion. Ouedraogo later visited his grandfather Nedega, who had been searching for his daughter for years. Nedega held a feast and sent delegates to bring her home, and Yennenga and Rialé returned to his open arms. He had his grandson trained and gave him cavalry, cattle and other goods, which Ouedraogo used to found the Mossi kingdom.

The Mossi people regard Yennenga as the mother of their empire, and many statues of her stand in Ouagadougou, the capital of Burkina Faso. A golden stallion statue, the Étalon de Yennenga, is the first prize of the biennial Panafrican Film and Television Festival of Ouagadougou, and the national football team is nicknamed Les Étalons in reference to her stallion. In March 2017 an international competition was held to design a new city called Yennenga, 15 km from Ouagadougou, which Hardel Le Bihan Architectes won.
yeon-gaesomun: Yeon Gaesomun was the first son of Yŏn T'aejo, who held the office of Mangniji, comparable to prime minister, under King Pyeongwon and King Yeongyang; his grandfather Yŏn Chayu had held it too. Tang records call him Ch'ŏn, because his family name was also the given name of the Tang founder, Emperor Gaozu, and the Nihon Shoki calls him Iri Kasumi. Little is known of his early life before he became Western Governor, when he oversaw the building of the Cheolli Jangseong, a chain of garrisons defending Liaodong against the Tang.

In the winter of 642, learning that King Yeongnyu and his officials were plotting to kill him, he invited about a hundred opponents to a banquet, killed them all and then murdered the king in his palace. He placed the king's nephew Bojang on the throne, took the title Tae Mangniji and ruled Goguryeo until his death. Traditional historians saw in the coup a thirst for power; many modern Korean historians see an attempt to take a harder line against Tang China than the king had.

After a brief conciliatory approach to the Tang, including a request in 643 for Taoist teachers, relations broke down when Goguryeo attacked Silla. In 645 Emperor Taizong took several border fortresses but was held for months at Ansi, while Yeon Gaesomun defeated the marine force sent against Pyongyang. Taizong retreated in winter with heavy losses and was defeated again in 647 and 648. Under Emperor Gaozong, Yeon Gaesomun's forces destroyed the army of the Tang general Pang Xiaotai at the Sasu River in 662, and Su Dingfang was forced back from Pyongyang.

Yeon Gaesomun died of natural causes, most likely in 665, the year recorded on the tomb stele of his eldest son Yŏn Namsaeng; the Samguk sagi gives 666 and the Nihon Shoki 664. His sons and younger brother then fought over the succession, Namsaeng defecting to Tang, and Goguryeo fell to the Tang and Silla in 668. Tang and Silla sources portrayed him as a brutal and arrogant dictator, and Joseon historians blamed him for Goguryeo's fall, while the nationalist historian Shin Chae-ho placed him above every other hero of Korean history. In Chinese opera and legend he appears as the adversary of the Tang general Xue Rengui.
yeon-namsaeng: Namsaeng is said to have become Tae Mangniji, the highest office of Goguryeo, before his father's death, when Yŏn Kaesomun stepped down and took an honorary title. After his father died, Namsaeng prepared for war with the Tang and set out to inspect the border fortresses in Yodong and other strongholds of the kingdom, leaving his younger brothers Yŏn Namgŏn and Yŏn Namsan in charge of Pyongyang.

In his absence the brothers seized Pyongyang and the royal court, accused him falsely of treason and forced King Bojang to order his arrest. Urged by his son, who had escaped death at the hands of his uncles, Namsaeng went over to the Tang and was given a high position in its army. He helped lead the Tang campaign into Goguryeo that destroyed the kingdom in 668.

Namsaeng died in the lands of the Protectorate General to Pacify the East, the Andong Duhufu, set up by the Tang at Pyongyang after the fall of Goguryeo to govern its former domains. He was buried on Mt. Mang at Luoyang, the eastern capital of the Tang.

His tomb stele and that of his brother Namgŏn have been found. His biography appears in book 110 of the Xin Tangshu, the New History of Tang, under the family name Quan, or Cheon. Chinese sources avoided the name Yŏn, read Yuan in Chinese, because it was the given name of Emperor Gaozu of Tang, Li Yuan, and was therefore taboo. In recent times he has been portrayed in Korean television series, among them Dae Jo-yeong of 2006-2007 and The Blade and Petal of 2013.
yeondeunghoe: The festival's origin is thought to lie in the Palgwanhoe, begun in 551, in the 12th year of the reign of King Jinheung of Silla. Records mention the event at Hwangnyongsa Temple in Gyeongju in 866. In Silla the lantern festivals combined Buddhist lantern offerings with ancestral rites to the dragon god, held to protect farmers and the nation. The name has been rendered in English as Lotus Lantern Festival or as lighting a lantern, and the lanterns are said to stand for light, hope and unity.

Today the festival falls on the eighth day of the fourth month of the Korean lunar calendar, the Buddha's Birthday. It opens with the ritual bathing of a sculpture of the Buddha as a baby, water being spooned over its head and shoulders with a ritual ladle. Lanterns hang in temples and private homes and are carried in parades. The lotus is the commonest design; in Buddhism the flower is associated with dignity, the sublime and the awakening of the devotee's true nature. Other lanterns take the form of drums, cranes, fish, dragons, tigers and phoenixes.

A crafted lantern has a frame of split bamboo or wire covered with hanji, a traditional Korean paper handmade from mulberry bark whose overlapping fibres make it strong, or with silk. Simple lotus lanterns are made in community workshops and family homes by twisting tissue paper petals onto a white spherical lantern. Candles once lit them; battery-powered lights are now used as safer.

Yeondeunghoe was listed as a South Korean intangible cultural property in 2011. Religious events are normally excluded from UNESCO's list, but the committee's decision rested on the festival's inclusivity and on the way it removes social boundaries between those who attend. The best-known celebration is in Jongno District of Seoul, home of Jogyesa, the chief temple of the Jogye Order. There the festival was cancelled four times after 1960: under martial law in 1961 and in 1980, when the city refused a street permit in 1970, and during the Coronavirus pandemic in 2020.
yeongjo-of-joseon: Yeongjo, personal name Yi Geum, was the second son of King Sukjong, and his life was marked by political infighting and by resentment over the low birth of his mother, Concubine Suk. When his elder half-brother Gyeongjong became king in 1720, the Noron faction unsuccessfully pressed Gyeongjong to step down in his favour.

A few months later Prince Yeoning was named Crown Prince Brother, which sharpened the power struggle and led to the Shinim literati purge of 1721. When Gyeongjong died on 11 October 1724, the Soron accused Yeoning of involvement, though many historians now think food poisoning more likely. He took the throne on 16 October 1724.

Early in his reign the Noron faction regained its position, and a coalition of radical Namin and excluded Soron began Yi In-jwa's Rebellion, which started on 15 March 1728 with the seizure of Cheongju Castle. The royal army defeated the rebels as they marched towards Hanyang, and Yi In-jwa and his family were executed. Yeongjo pursued the Tangpyeong policy of recruiting equally from the factions, believing factional strife harmful. He halved the military service tax, replacing the lost revenue with taxes on fisheries, salt and vessels and an additional land tax, adopted an accounting system for the state's finances and encouraged coinage.

He distributed books in Hangul, including the Book of Agriculture, and had rain gauges made and sent to local offices. Trade grew in Hanseong, and guilds and monopolies expanded. In 1758 he outlawed Catholicism, the first king to act against it. He valued Park Mun-su, whom he made a secret royal inspector to arrest corrupt local officers.

The Annals of the Joseon dynasty record him reducing the dishes on his table in years of flood or famine. In July 1762 he ordered his son Crown Prince Sado into a wooden rice chest, where Sado died on the eighth day; the memoirs of his widow and the Annals report that Sado suffered from mental illness.

Yeongjo was in poor health for much of his life and took many precautions to protect it. He died on 22 April 1776 and is buried with his second wife, Queen Jeongsun, at Wonneung in Guri. His grandson Yi San, the son of Sado, succeeded him as King Jeongjo.

Yeongjo had registered the boy as the son of the late Crown Prince Hyojang to protect his claim. Confucianization was at its height under Yeongjo and Jeongjo, and the economy recovered from the wars of the late 16th and early 17th centuries, but his policies could not hold back the social change that followed.
yeongnyu-of-goguryeo: Yeongnyu was a son of the 25th king, Pyeongwon, and a younger half-brother of the 26th, Yeong-yang, whom he succeeded on his death in 618. That same year the Tang dynasty replaced the Sui in China. Goguryeo was still recovering from the Goguryeo–Sui War, and the new Tang emperor was still completing the unification of his own realm, so neither side was in a position to begin new hostilities.

Goguryeo and Tang exchanged envoys, and at the Tang request the two carried out a prisoner exchange in 622. In 624 the Tang court formally presented Taoism to Goguryeo, which sent scholars the following year to study Taoism and Buddhism. As Tang grew stronger, however, it sent a small force in 631 to destroy a monument to Goguryeo's victory over the Sui. Goguryeo answered by beginning the Cheolli Jangseong, a defensive wall along its western border, a project of fifteen years supervised by Yeon Gaesomun.
In the south Goguryeo went on fighting the Korean kingdom of Silla to win back lost territory, and in 629 Kim Yu-sin of Silla took the Goguryeo fortress of Nangbi.

Yeongnyu and some officials planned to kill the most powerful military officers, beginning with Yeon Gaesomun, whose power and influence were overtaking those of the throne. Yeon Gaesomun discovered the plot, went at once to Pyongyang and killed the plotters, the king among them, in 642. He then placed Yeongnyu's nephew Bojang on the throne. Yeongnyu had at least two sons, Prince Hwangwon and Prince Bokdeok, and two daughters. He has been portrayed in the Korean television series Yeon Gaesomun (2006–2007) and The Blade and Petal (2013).
yeonsangun-of-joseon: Yeonsangun, personal name Yi Yung, was born on 2 December 1476, the eldest surviving son of King Seongjong and the Deposed Queen Yun. Lady Yun had been Seongjong's concubine and was chosen as his second wife for her beauty. She was jealous of the other concubines, poisoned one of them in 1477, and in 1479 struck the king and left scratch marks. Seongjong's mother ordered her into exile, officials later petitioned for her execution, and she died in 1482, ordered to drink poison. The crown prince grew up believing that he was the son of Queen Jeonghyeon, his father's third wife.

In his early years on the throne Yeonsangun was an able administrator who strengthened the national defence and aided the poor. When he learned the truth about his mother he tried to restore her titles, but officials of the Sarim faction opposed him. In 1498 a passage critical of King Sejo's coup of 1455 was put into the royal records, and the king ordered the execution of many Sarim officials and the mutilation of the remains of Kim Chong-jik: the First Literati Purge.

In 1504 Im Sa-hong showed him a blood-stained garment from his mother's death. Yeonsangun beat to death two of his father's concubines, and had officials who had backed his mother's execution put to death, and even those merely present at court: the Second Literati Purge.

He closed the royal university Sungkyunkwan and the temple Wongaksa and made them pleasure grounds, gathering young girls from the eight provinces, and evicted 20,000 residents of the capital to clear hunting grounds. He abolished the Office of Censors. On 19 July 1504 three notices in Hangul mocking his tyranny were found, and he banned the learning and use of the script and ordered those using it beheaded. The author was never caught, and the ban was short-lived.

In September 1506 a group of officials, among them Pak Wŏnjong, Sŏng Hŭian and Yu Sunjŏng, deposed him and set his younger half-brother Grand Prince Jinseong on the throne. Demoted to Prince Yeonsan, he was exiled to Ganghwa Island, where he died after two months. His four young sons were made to take poison. As a much-despised overthrown king he received no temple name.
yerba-mate: The Guaraní and some Tupi communities first cultivated and consumed yerba mate before European colonisation. Its use was at first confined to the natives of two regions of what became Paraguay, Amambay and Alto Paraná. The Guaraní name for the plant is kaʼa, meaning herb, while mate comes from the Quechua mati, a word for a container for a drink and for a gourd. The French botanist Augustin Saint-Hilaire named the plant.

Consumption became widespread under Spanish colonisation, particularly in the colony of Paraguay in the late 16th century, among settlers and Guaraní alike. It became Paraguay's main commodity, above tobacco, and the labour of indigenous peoples was used to harvest wild stands. In the mid-17th century the Jesuits domesticated the plant and set up plantations in their reductions in Misiones, Argentina. After their expulsion in the 1770s the plantations decayed and their methods of domestication were lost.

Ilex paraguariensis begins as a shrub and matures into a tree up to 15 metres tall. Its evergreen leaves have serrated margins and contain caffeine and related alkaloids, with caffeine making up between 0.7% and 1.7% of dry weight. The flowers are small and greenish-white, and the fruit is a small red drupe. When the plant is harvested the branches are often dried over a wood fire, which gives a smoky flavour. The War of the Triple Alliance (1864–1870) devastated Paraguay's economy, and Brazil and Argentina later became the main producers.

Mate is made by filling a container, traditionally a small hollowed-out gourd, up to three-quarters with dry leaves and adding water at 70 to 80 °C, hot but not boiling. With cold water the infusion is called tereré, and the Guaraní drank it in this form, without ice. Drinking mate is a common social practice, often a communal ritual, in Paraguay, Uruguay, Argentina, southern Brazil and southern Chile. Friends and family share one gourd and drink through the same straw, called a bombilla. The brewer refills the gourd and passes it round clockwise, and it is also popular in Syria and Lebanon through Syrian immigrants to Argentina.
yerevan: Yerevan lies on the banks of the Hrazdan River, in the north-east of the Ararat Plain, in the central-western part of Armenia and the heart of the Armenian Highland. Its average height is 990 metres. The upper part of the city is surrounded by mountains on three sides, and the Hrazdan divides it in two through a canyon. Mount Ararat, visible from any part of the city, is its principal symbol.

The origin of the name is unknown. One theory ties it to the Armenian king Yervand (Orontes) IV, but it more likely derives from the Urartian fortress of Erebuni, founded in 782 BCE, and the name evolved through Erevani and Erevan into Yerevan as Urartian and Armenian elements blended.

The territory has been inhabited since approximately the second half of the 4th millennium BCE. The southern district of Shengavit was populated from at least 3200 BCE in the period of the Kura–Araxes culture of the early Bronze Age, and excavations there found a series of large round buildings and ritual installations. King Argishti I of Urartu founded the fortress of Erebuni in 782 BCE at the western extreme of the Ararat Plain, as a great administrative and religious centre. By the late ancient Armenian Kingdom new capital cities were founded and Yerevan declined.

The Safavid Empire forcibly deported hundreds of thousands of Armenians to Iran in the Great Surgun of 1603–05, which mostly depopulated the city. An earthquake mostly destroyed it in 1679, and it was rebuilt on a smaller scale. It later became part of the Russian Empire. After the First World War it became the capital of the First Republic of Armenia in 1918, as thousands of survivors of the Armenian genocide in the Ottoman Empire arrived. It grew rapidly in the 20th century within the Soviet Union.

Yerevan is the capital and largest city of Armenia and one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, with 1,086,677 people. It has been the capital since 1918, the fourteenth in Armenia's history. It is the seat of the Araratian Pontifical Diocese, the largest diocese of the Armenian Apostolic Church.

Erebuni Fortress is considered the birthplace of the city, and Saint Gregory Cathedral is the largest Armenian cathedral in the world. Tsitsernakaberd is the official memorial to the victims of the Armenian genocide. The Matenadaran holds one of the largest depositories of ancient books and manuscripts in the world.
yermak-timofeyevich: Little is securely known of Yermak. No contemporary description exists, and the Remezov Chronicle, written more than a hundred years after his death, describes his looks although its narrator never saw him. The main sources are the Stroganov Chronicle, commissioned by the Stroganov family and so exaggerating their part, and the Sinodnik, written forty years after his death by Archbishop Cyprian of Tobolsk, who wished to have him canonised. The only account of his upbringing is the Cherepanov Chronicle, compiled by a Tobolsk coachman in 1760, which says he was born by the Chusovaya River and that his grandfather came from Suzdal.

According to that chronicle his father Timofey moved to the Stroganov lands on the Chusovaya, and Yermak worked on the Stroganovs' river fleet as a porter and sailor carrying salt along the Kama and Volga. He then gathered a gang and moved to the Don region as a river pirate, where he acquired the nickname Yermak. Before Siberia his combat experience consisted of leading a Cossack detachment for the tsar in the Livonian War of 1558-83 and plundering merchant ships.

In 1552 the army of Ivan the Terrible toppled the Khanate of Kazan, and the tsar granted the Stroganov merchant family the province of Perm and permission to expand along the Tobol and Irtysh rivers, which belonged to Kuchum Khan. Yermak led a force of 840 men, 540 of his own followers and 300 supplied by the Stroganovs, made up of Russians, Tatars, Lithuanians and Germans. W. Bruce Lincoln describes matchlock muskets, sabers, pikes and small cannons set against Tatar bows, arrows and spears, while Yuri Semyonov says Yermak had no cannon and only a few firearms. On 26 October 1582 he overthrew Kuchum's power at Qashliq and went on fighting the Tatars in Siberia.

Accounts of his death differ. The most common says Kuchum leaked false news that Bukharan merchants were held up on the river. Yermak set out to free them, camped on an island in the Irtysh without posting a guard, and Kuchum's men attacked at night in a storm and killed nearly all of his party. Legend says Yermak drowned, weighed down by armour the tsar had given him. The survivors left Qashliq, reinforcements arrived, and the Russians founded Tyumen in 1586 and Tobolsk in 1587. A monument to him was begun in 1903 at Novocherkassk, and two icebreakers have been named after him.
yervandashat: Also known as Erevandashat and Marmet, the city stood on a rock hill about 100 metres high at the meeting of the Araxes and Akhurian rivers, inaccessible from the river side and from the north. Movses Khorenatsi explains the move from Armavir by a change in the course of the Araxes, which had left the old capital short of water when its tributary froze in long, cold winters. Yervand, he writes, enclosed the hill with high walls, fitted the gates with copper doors reached by iron stairways with hidden traps for conspirators, and cut passages through the rock down to the river so that water could be drawn during a siege.

According to Khorenatsi, Yervand brought the royal treasury and part of the people of Armavir to the new city, but because the nobles and the people were discontented with him he moved the temple treasures and the statues of the gods to Bagaran. North of the river he planted a walled cedar forest, Tsnndots, stocked with deer, boars and other game for his hunting. Finds there are mostly medieval, with very little Hellenistic pottery.

The city prospered on an important trade route, a junction on the road to Satala, Trebizond, Phasis and Sebastopolis-Dioscurias, with ample water and rich fishing. Part of the population that Tigranes II brought from Hellenistic cities settled there, and in the 1st century BCE and the 1st century CE new districts grew on both banks of the Araxes. During the Arsacid period it was held by the princely house of the Kamsarakans and apparently ranked among the leading centres of Armenia beside Artashat and Vagharshapat. It survived until the 360s CE.

The architect and researcher Toros Toramanian noted that the ruins still stand, impressive for their strong position and for the many dwellings within the fortress walls, which he took as a sign that Yervand gathered many loyal followers inside for his own security.
yeshaq-i: Yeshaq, whose throne name was Gabra Masqal II, was of Amhara lineage, the second son of Emperor Dawit I, probably by Seyon Mogasa, one of Dawit's wives. In 1414 he succeeded his brother Emperor Tewodros I; his younger brothers included the later emperors Takla Maryam and Zara Yaqob.

His reign saw a revolt of the Beta Israel, which he ended by defeating the rebels at Kossoge, some 30 kilometres north of Gondar, where he built the church of Debre Yeshaq to mark the victory. He invaded the Shanqella region beyond Agawmeder and fought Mansur ad-Din and Jamal ad-Din II to the south-east. According to the historian al-Maqrizi he hired Mamluks led by al-Tabingha to train his army in gunnery and swordfighting, the earliest reference to firearms in Ethiopia, and an unnamed Copt from Egypt reorganised the kingdom and introduced splendid court dress for the emperor. George Wynn Brereton Huntingford suggests that it was in his reign that the court ceased to have a permanent capital and moved with the royal encampment.

Yeshaq made the earliest known contact between post-Axumite Ethiopia and a European ruler, a letter carried by two dignitaries to Alfonso V of Aragon proposing an alliance against the Muslims sealed by a double marriage. It is not clear whether Alfonso replied. A panegyric addressed to Yeshaq survives, which Enrico Cerulli called a gem of Ethiopian poetry, and a victory hymn of his reign holds the first mention of the name Somali.

E. A. Wallis Budge states that Yeshaq was assassinated and buried at Tadbaba Maryam in Sayint, while the historian Tadesse Tamrat believes the sources mask his death in battle against Jamal ad-Din II of Adal; al-Maqrizi records that he was killed when Jamal ad-Din defeated his exhausted army at Harjah. According to Jean-Claude Garcin, his capture of Zeila in 1415 prompted the Arabic epic Sirat Sayf ibn Dhi-Yazan, whose villain Sayf Ar'ed was probably modelled on him.
yeshe-o: Born as Khor-re, Yeshe-Ö was the son of King Tashi-gon and was drawn to religious matters from a young age. He was the second king in the succession of Guge, on the southwestern Tibetan Plateau, and ruled the merged kingdoms of Tashigon and Detsugon, which covered Purang and Guge together with Zanskar, Spiti, Lahaul and Upper Kinnaur. He held the combined Purang-Guge Kingdom from 967, and with his brother he ruled the whole Western Himalayan region.

His first act as king was to issue commands under the title bka’ shog chen mo, the Great Dictums, which set out his aim of ruling the kingdom theocratically and earned him the name of a king and monk. He ordered farmers and nomads to pay an endowment towards the upkeep of the monastery, founded temples and encouraged the nobility. Classical Tibetan historiography attributes to him the second diffusion of Buddhism in Tibet and the restoration of an organised monastic tradition.

Following the practice of Kashmir and India, he chose twenty-one young novices to be trained as monks in Kashmir and other Buddhist centres, where they were to study under teachers and translate scriptures from Sanskrit into Tibetan. Only two survived, Rinchen Zangpo and Lekpai Sherap; the others died in the harsh climate of northern India. Rinchen Zangpo was then put in charge of further translations and of building monasteries. Besides Tholing, Tabo Monastery and the Khochar monastery were built on the king's initiative.

Yeshe-Ö opposed the esoteric tantric practices, mostly of unorganised groups, that were widespread in Tibet, and he was repelled by the introduction of Tantrism into the country's new Buddhist culture. He wanted a purer and more rationalistic form of religion, and his views are quoted in the Blue Annals, written in the fifteenth century.

Many bronze works of art of the period are credited to Nagaraja, one of his two sons. The tenth-century Yeshe-Ö temple was damaged by the Red Guards in 1967, during the Cultural Revolution, and was later put under reconstruction. In the Lotsava Lakhang at Riba, in Ngari Prefecture, field research found a painting of eight monks, Rinchen Zangpo among them, whom Yeshe-Ö had sent to Kashmir to bring texts of Mahayana Buddhism back to western Tibet.
yeshwantrao-ghorpade: Yeshwantrao Hindurao Ghorpade was born on 13 November 1908 at Sanduru, the capital of Sandur, to Bhujangrao Yeshwantrao Raje Ghorpade, the jagirdar of Gajendragad, and his wife Tarabai Sahib Ghorpade. He was educated at Baldwin High School in Bangalore and Holkar College in Indore and graduated from Allahabad University. On 5 May 1928 he succeeded his late cousin Venkata Rao III as raja, and he was formally installed on 20 June 1928.

His reign is remembered for its social and administrative reforms as well as for his work for wildlife conservation. An administrator governed the state until 5 February 1930, when Yeshwantrao took full powers. In 1931 he set up a legislature of an upper and a lower house, the Sandur State Council, and in 1932 he abolished untouchability by law and opened the Hindu temples of the state to all castes.

The writer and naturalist Madhavaiah Krishnan, then an employee of the Sandur State Civil Service, drew his attention to wildlife conservation; the raja was also a member of the Bombay Natural History Society. He ruled until the state's accession to India on 10 August 1947 and received the King George V Silver Jubilee medal in 1935, the King George VI coronation medal in 1937 and the Indian Independence Medal in 1948.

After independence he served as vice-president of the Expert Committee of Wildlife Conservation in India. In 1954 he took over the General Sandur Manganese company, renamed Sandur Manganese and Iron Ore, which was listed as a public limited company in 1964. He died on 11 October 1996; his sons were Murarirao and Shivarao.
yesugei: Yesügei, also called Yesükhei Baghatur, belonged to the Borjigin family, and his name means "like nine": he was held to have the auspicious qualities of nine, a lucky number to the Mongols. He was the son of Bartan Baghatur, the second son of Khabul Khan, whom the Jin dynasty recognised as a khagan. Khabul was in turn the great-grandson of the Mongol chief Khaidu, the first to try to unite the Mongols.

With the help of his elder brother Negün Taishi and his younger brother Daritai Otchigin, Yesügei abducted Hö'elün, a daughter of the Olkhunut forest people, from her newlywed husband Chiledu of the Merkits. She became his chief wife. He had four sons by her, Temüjin (later Genghis Khan), Qasar, Hachiun and Temüge, and a daughter, Temülün.

Yesügei was a major chief of the Khamag Mongol confederation. After its khan Hotula died, the confederation had no elected king, but Yesügei ruled it in practice. He had a blood brother, or anda, in Toghrul Khan, later known as Wang Khan and Ong Khan, and helped Toghrul defeat his uncle Gurkhan.

By his second wife Sochigel he had two more sons, Behter and Belgutei. The Secret History of the Mongols records that Temüjin and Qasar, in their youth, ambushed their half brother Behter after he withheld the spoils of hunts and shot him with arrows, sparing Belgutei at Behter's plea. Belgutei became close to Temüjin and later one of his generals.

Yesügei died in 1171, when Temüjin was nine. The Secret History records that he had left the boy at the home of Dai Setsen, a Khongirad noble, after the two men agreed that Temüjin and Dai Setsen's daughter Börte would marry. On the way home he came upon Tatars holding a wedding feast. He was known among them as the man who had killed their relative Temüjin Uge in a battle eight years earlier, and the boy was named after that victory. The Tatars recognised him and poisoned his food. He reached his family's camp and died three days later.

After his death Toghrul at first helped Temüjin arrange his marriage to Börte and unite the tribes, but later turned to Temüjin's anda and rival Jamukha. During the Yuan dynasty Yesügei was given the temple name Liezu, meaning Ardent Founder, and the posthumous name Shenyuan Huangdi.
yevgenia-bosch: Yevgenia Bosch, born Meisch, came from near Ochakiv in the Kherson Governorate of the Russian Empire. Her father, Gotlieb Meisch, was a German colonist, mechanic and landowner, and her mother, Maria Krusser, a Bessarabian noblewoman. She attended the Voznesensk women's gymnasium and as a young woman married Peter Bosch, the owner of a small wagon shop, with whom she had two daughters. She joined the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party in 1901 and its Bolshevik faction in 1903.

After a police search of her house in 1906 she left her husband for Kyiv, where she worked in the underground with her sister Elena Rozmirovich and later with her partner Georgy Pyatakov. The two led the Kyiv committee until their arrest and exile to the Irkutsk Governorate in 1912, from which they escaped by way of Vladivostok, Japan and the United States to Switzerland. There they formed the Baugy group with Nikolai Bukharin and others, which opposed Lenin on the national question.

After the February Revolution she returned to Kyiv, came round to Lenin's position and headed party committees of the Southwestern region. She helped launch the First All-Ukrainian Congress of Soviets at Kharkiv in December 1917, which proclaimed a Soviet republic in federation with Soviet Russia and elected her to its People's Secretariat. In March 1918 she resigned in protest at the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk and joined the Red Army forces of Vladimir Antonov-Ovseyenko. She later chaired the party committee of the Penza Governorate, served on the Caspian-Caucasus front and was a political commissar in the war against General Denikin.

Suffering from tuberculosis and heart disease, Bosch was incapacitated from 1922. She joined the Left Opposition in 1923 and signed the Declaration of 46. Despairing after Trotsky was forced out as leader of the Red Army, and in pain from her illnesses, she shot herself in January 1925. The government played down her standing: she had only a local funeral and a short obituary in Pravda. Her memoirs, A Year of Struggle, appeared the same year, and a bridge over the Dnieper in Kyiv bore her name from 1925 until its destruction in the Second World War.
yevgenia-ginzburg: Yevgenia Solomonovna Ginzburg was born in Moscow on 20 December 1904, the daughter of Solomon Natanovich Ginzburg, a Jewish pharmacist, and Revekka Markovna Ginzburg. The family moved to Kazan in 1909. In 1920 she began to study social sciences at Kazan State University, later switching to pedagogy, and she worked as a teacher at a rabfak, a workers' faculty.

In April 1934 she was confirmed as a docent, roughly an associate professor, specialising in the history of the All-Union Communist Party, and was soon named head of a new department of the history of Leninism. By the autumn of 1935 she had been forced to leave the university. Around 1930 she married Pavel Aksyonov, the mayor of Kazan; their son Vasily Aksyonov, born in 1932, became a well-known writer.

After the assassination of Sergei Mironovich Kirov on 1 December 1934, Ginzburg was accused of taking part in a counter-revolutionary Trotskyist group said to be led by Professor Nikolay Naumovich Elvov and centred on the newspaper Krasnaya Tatariia, where she worked. She was expelled on 8 February 1937 and arrested on 15 February. Unlike most of those around her, she denied the charges from the first interrogation. Her husband was arrested in July and sentenced to 15 years of corrective labour.

On 1 August 1937 a closed session of the Military College of the Supreme Court sentenced her to ten years' imprisonment. She was shipped to Magadan and sent to the camps of the Kolyma valley, where heavy general work left her emaciated. A Crimean German doctor, Anton Walter, recommended her for nursing work at Taskan, and they later married. Released from the camp system in February 1949, she was ordered to stay in Magadan and began to write her memoirs in secret. She was arrested again in October 1949 and exiled, with Kolyma as her destination at her own request.

After Stalin's death in 1953 and her repeated appeals, she was released from exile and rehabilitated on 25 June 1955. She returned to Moscow, and finished her memoir after Walter's death in 1959. It could not be published in the USSR, but the manuscript was smuggled abroad and appeared in 1967 from Mondadori in Milan and Possev in Frankfurt, and has since been translated into many languages. She died in Moscow aged 72. Marleen Gorris directed a film of her story, Within the Whirlwind, with Emily Watson in the title role.
yevhen-petrushevych: Petrushevych was born on 3 June 1863 in Busk, Galicia, into the family of an Eastern Catholic priest of noble background. He studied law at Lviv University, where he was a leader of the student movement and headed the Academic Fraternity, and after a doctorate in law practised in Sokal, where he also headed the district Prosvita educational society. He became an active member of the Ukrainian National Democratic Party, formed in 1899.

Elected to the Reichsrat in 1907, he rose to head the Ukrainian Parliament Club, and in 1910 he entered the Galician Sejm, where he fought for a new election law that raised the Ukrainian mandates from 12 to 34 and then to 62. During World War I he opposed plans to annex Galicia to Poland, favoured its autonomy within Austria, and led the Galician delegation at Brest-Litovsk in February 1918. On 19 October 1918 a Ukrainian assembly in Lviv elected him president of the Ukrainian National Council.

After the Polish-Ukrainian War broke out and Lviv was lost, the government moved to Stanislaviv. On 9 June 1919, at Zalishchyky, he was granted the title of authorised dictator, acting as both president and head of government. When the Galician army retreated over the Zbruch in July 1919, the government settled in Kamianets-Podilskyi, where his relations with Symon Petliura worsened over the Ukrainian-Polish alliance. In autumn 1919 he left for Vienna, from where the exile government sent delegations to Riga and Geneva and appealed to the League of Nations.

On 15 March 1923 the Council of Ambassadors approved the annexation of the West Ukrainian lands by Poland. Disappointed, Petrushevych took an openly Sovietophile position and moved to Berlin, and the Politburo of the All-Union Communist Party decided in 1923 to fund his activities. He died on 29 August 1940 and was buried at the cemetery of St. Hedwig's Cathedral in Berlin; on 1 November 2002 his remains were reburied at the Lychakiv Cemetery in Lviv.
yi-hwang: Yi Hwang was born in 1501 in Ongye-ri, Andong, in the north of Gyeongsang Province, the youngest of eight children of the Jinbo Yi clan. A child prodigy, he learned the Analects of Confucius from his uncle at twelve and, admiring the poetry of Tao Yuanming, began to write verse. His poem Yadang, written at eighteen, is counted among his major works. About the age of twenty he immersed himself in the I Ching and Neo-Confucianism. He came to Seoul at 23, entered the national academy Sungkyunkwan in 1523, and passed the civil service examinations with top honours in 1534.

Yi held office under four kings: Jungjong, Injong, Myeongjong and Seonjo. His integrity made him relentless in purges of corrupt officials, and on numerous occasions he was exiled from the capital for his commitment to principle. Disillusioned by the power struggles at court in the later years of Jungjong's reign, he left political office, but he was repeatedly drawn back. He served as governor of Danyang at 48 and then of Punggi, where he improved the private academy Baekundong Seowon.

He was named head instructor of Sungkyunkwan in 1552 but turned down other prominent offices. In 1560 he established the Dosan seodang, devoted to meditation, study and teaching. King Seonjo appointed him minister of rites, which he declined at first, but he resumed office at 68 and wrote advisory documents including the Ten Diagrams on Sage Learning. He retired at 70 and died in 1570, and was posthumously promoted to the highest ministerial rank. His disciples reorganised the Dosan seodang as Dosan Seowon in 1574.

Yi followed the dualistic Neo-Confucianism of Zhu Xi, in which i and gi are the forces underlying the universe. He stressed i, the formative element, as the force that determines gi, in contrast to the school of his counterpart Yi I, which focused on gi. This emphasis became the core of the Yeongnam School, carried on by figures such as Yu Sŏngnyong and Kim Sŏngil.

The Ten Diagrams on Sage Learning, composed in 1568 for King Seonjo, presents the path to sagehood through ten chapters, each opening with a diagram and a text from Zhu Xi or another authority, and closing with a brief commentary. He also wrote sijo poetry. His thought influenced Japan, Taiwan and Vietnam, and research institutes devoted to him exist in several countries.
yi-i: Yi I was born in Gangneung, Gangwon Province, in 1536 into the Deoksu Yi clan. His father, Yi Won-su, was a Left Second State Councillor, and his mother, Shin Saimdang, was an accomplished artist and calligrapher. He was the grandnephew of Yi Ki, Chief State Councilor from 1549 to 1551. He studied under Baek In-geol, successor of Cho Kwangjo, and is said to have finished his lessons in the Confucian classics by seven and passed the Civil Service literary examination at 13.

After his mother's death when he was 16 he secluded himself on Kumgang-san for three years, studying Buddhism. He left the mountains at 20 and devoted himself to Neo-Confucianism. He married at 22 and the next year visited Yi Hwang at Dosan. His father died when he was 26.

He passed special examinations with top honours with a thesis called Cheondochaek, widely regarded as a literary masterpiece that displayed his knowledge of history, Confucian political philosophy and Taoism. He took top honours in civil examinations nine times in a row. He held government posts from the age of 29, went on a mission in 1568 as a document officer, took part in writing the Myeongjong Annals, and at 34 wrote Dongho Mundap, an eleven-article political memorial arguing that righteous government could be achieved.

By about 40 he had the deep trust of the king and was one of the central political figures. When political conflicts escalated in 1576 his efforts proved fruitless and he returned home to study and teach. He came back to office at 45 and held several ministerial posts, writing works that recorded crucial events and tried to ease the conflicts of the time. King Seonjo remained noncommittal, and Yi found it hard to stay neutral. He left office in 1583 and died the following year.

Yi did not fully agree with the dualistic Neo-Confucianism of Yi Hwang. His school stressed concrete, material elements and external experience and learning rather than inner spiritual perception. Unlike Yi Hwang, who disliked politics, he was an active official who wanted Confucian principles applied to administration, with sage learning and self-cultivation as its base. He proposed raising and strengthening an army against a possible Japanese attack, but the central government rejected it, and he died before the Imjin war began.

His works include Questions and Answers at East Lake, the Memorial in Ten Thousand Words, The Essentials of the Studies of the Sages, The Secret of Expelling Ignorance and the Daily Records of Lectures before the Throne. The Complete Works of Yulgok was compiled after his death. A street in Seoul, Yulgongno, is named after him.
yi-ja-gyeom: Yi was born in Kaegyŏng, the son of Yi Ho and grandson of Yi Cha-yŏn, father-in-law of King Munjong. Related to the royal house, he entered court service through eumseo, a path for nobles that spared them the civil service examination, and rose to high office when his sister married Sunjong of Goryeo. After Sunjong's early death he lost office when the widowed queen was found to have had a relationship with a slave.

He returned to power in 1107 by marrying his second daughter to Yejong of Goryeo, a match that helped the king calm officials opposed to his campaign against the Jurchens. In 1109 she bore the future Injong of Goryeo. When Yejong died in 1122, Yi placed his young grandson on the throne and ruled as regent, removing rivals, naming himself Duke of Hanyang in 1122 and Duke of Joseon in 1124. He married two more daughters to Injong, set up a court office of a kind reserved for princes or the queen, and sent an envoy to the Song dynasty to seek recognition as regent without the king's knowledge.

In 1126 Injong's advisers moved against him. Their forces stormed the palace on 25 February and killed the brother and son of Yi's ally Ch'ŏk Chun-gyŏng, who in revenge set the whole palace ablaze. Injong offered to abdicate, but Yi, unwilling to be seen as a usurper, urged him to stay, and scores of the king's supporters were executed or exiled. Trusting a divination that the eighteen would take the throne, a reading of the characters of his surname, Yi tried to poison the king with rice cakes, a plot the queen revealed.

Injong then won Ch'ŏk over with a letter of regret he had written on the night before the palace turmoil. In May 1126 Ch'ŏk's forces took the palace, and Yi surrendered without resistance, only three months after the fire. He was exiled to Yeonggwang and died there. Injong kept respect for his grandfather and former guardian, sending tribute to him and his wife Lady Ch'oe and 600 seok of rice to each of his sons. Tradition credits Yi with naming the dried yellow corvina of Yeonggwang, Yeonggwang gulbi, in defiance during his exile. The Goryeosa gives him a biography among the dynasty's traitors.
yi-sun-sin: Yi Sun-sin was born on 28 April 1545 in Hanseong, the present Seoul, to Yi Chŏng and a lady of the Ch'ogye Pyŏn clan. His family belonged to the Deoksu Yi clan. His grandfather had entered government service but was later impeached in the Gimyo literati purge, and his father did not pursue a government career. As a child Yi played war games and was always chosen as leader.

In 1576 Yi passed the military examination at thirty-two, after first failing when he broke a leg in the cavalry test. He was posted to the northern frontier in Hamgyeong province, defended border settlements against Jurchen raiders and became known for his strategy and leadership. In 1583 he lured the Jurchen into battle and captured their chief, Mu Pai Nai.

In 1592 Toyotomi Hideyoshi ordered the invasion of Korea as a base for conquering Ming China. The Japanese landed at Busan, met no naval resistance and reached Seoul in nineteen days. Yi began naval operations from Yeosu. Though he had never commanded a naval battle, he won the Battle of Okpo, the Battle of Sacheon and several others, and is generally accepted to have fought at least 23 naval battles and won them all. At Myeongnyang he led a fleet of 13 ships against at least 133 Japanese ships. Court factionalism led ministers to portray him to King Seonjo as a potential traitor, and he was arrested and tortured, but Prime Minister Yu Sŏngnyong's defence saved him from execution twice.

Yi died of a gunshot wound on 16 December 1598 in the Battle of Noryang, the last major battle of the Imjin War. After his death he received the title Chungmugong, Duke of Loyalty and Warfare, and the posthumous office of prime minister. His wartime journals, the Nanjung Ilgi, are part of UNESCO's Memory of the World initiative. Some military historians, among them Joseph Cummins and George Alexander Ballard, place him on a par with Horatio Nelson. A shrine to him stands in Asan, where he spent his youth.
yiddish: Yiddish, historically called Judeo-German or Jewish German, is a West Germanic language that originated in the Holy Roman Empire in the Middle Ages. By the 10th century a distinctive Jewish culture had formed in Central Europe, centred on the Rhineland (Mainz) and the Palatinate (notably Worms and Speyer), an area that came to be known as Ashkenaz.
