Yiddish gave the nascent Ashkenazi community a vernacular based on High German, fused with many elements from Hebrew, notably Mishnaic Hebrew, and to some extent Aramaic. Most varieties also include Slavic elements. It has traditionally been written in the Hebrew alphabet, and its orthography developed towards the end of the High Middle Ages.

The earliest surviving references, from the 12th century, call the language loshn-ashknaz, the language of Ashkenaz, or taytsh, a variant of the name for Middle High German. Colloquially it is mame-loshn, the mother tongue, as against loshn koydesh, the holy tongue, meaning Hebrew. The oldest surviving literary document in Yiddish is a blessing in the Worms machzor, a Hebrew prayer book, first recorded in 1272. Eastern Yiddish, far more common today, differs from Western Yiddish, which Ethnologue classifies as endangered, by its size and its extensive Slavic vocabulary.

Printing in the 16th century allowed cheap large-scale production of Yiddish works. Elia Levita, the earliest named Yiddish author, composed the Bovo-Bukh about 1507-08, printed from 1541. From the late 18th century, under the Haskalah, or Jewish Enlightenment, the language lost prestige, stigmatised by assimilationists and later by Zionists in favour of national languages and Hebrew.

In the early 20th century, especially after the October Revolution, Yiddish emerged as a major Eastern European language, with a flourishing literature, theatre and cinema, and the Yiddish Scientific Institute, YIVO, was founded in 1925. Before the Second World War there were 11 to 13 million speakers. About 85 per cent of the approximately six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust were Yiddish speakers, and the language declined massively. It is still spoken in Haredi communities, and a 2021 estimate counted 600,000 speakers in all.
yigael-yadin: Yigael Yadin was born Yigael Sukenik in Jerusalem on 20 March 1917, when the city was part of Ottoman Palestine. His father was the Polish-Jewish archaeologist Eleazar Sukenik, and his mother, Hasya Sukenik-Feinsold, was a teacher and women's rights activist. He joined the Haganah at the age of 15. In 1946 he left it after an argument with its commander, Yitzhak Sadeh, over whether a machine gun should be standard squad equipment.

In 1948 Yadin interrupted his university studies to return to active service and was Israel's Head of Operations in the 1948 Arab–Israeli War, responsible for many of its key decisions. In April he oversaw the secret biological warfare operation Cast Thy Bread, a campaign to poison the wells of Palestinian villages with bacteria and prevent the return of the evicted, probably with David Ben-Gurion's authorisation. He became Chief of Staff of the Israel Defense Forces on 9 November 1949 and resigned on 7 December 1952 over Ben-Gurion's cuts to the military budget.

He then turned to archaeology. In 1956 he received the Israel Prize in Jewish studies for his doctoral thesis on the Dead Sea Scrolls: his father had bought three of the seven scrolls found in 1947, and Yadin bought the other four in New York in 1954. He excavated the Qumran Caves, Masada, Hazor, Tel Megiddo and caves in the Judean Desert where objects of the Bar Kokhba revolt were found, and he thought the Solomonic Gate at Tel Gezer the high point of his career.

Yadin was military adviser to Prime Minister Levi Eshkol on the eve of the Six-Day War, and after the Yom Kippur War he sat on the Agranat Commission. In 1976 he founded the Democratic Movement for Change, known as Dash, in response to alleged corruption in the Labor Alignment. In the elections of 1977 Dash won 15 of the 120 seats in the Knesset and joined Menachem Begin's coalition after a few months.

As Deputy Prime Minister he played an important part in the contacts with Egypt that led to the Camp David Accords and the peace treaty. Dash broke into splinter factions, and he sat as an independent for the rest of his term. He retired from politics in 1981, and died on 28 June 1984 of a heart attack.
yigdal: Leopold Zunz held that the hymn was written by Daniel ben Judah, who spent eight years improving it before completing it in 1404. Some read its final line as bearing the signature Yechiel b'Rav Baruch, though who that was remains uncertain. Hartwig Hirschfeld attributed it to the poet Immanuel the Roman, who made several verse renderings of the 13 principles, among them a 72-line Poem Based on the 13 Articles that shares Yigdal's rhythm, rhyme and phrasing.

Ashkenazi Jews sing thirteen lines, one for each principle, repeating the last, on the resurrection of the dead, to complete the antiphon between hazzan and congregation. Sephardic Jews sing it in unison and add a fourteenth line naming these as the 13 bases of the Law of Moses. In the Sephardic rite it is often sung to a melody that represents the day, and in the Eastern Ashkenazic rite it opens Shacharit. In London a fixed tradition of antiphonal tunes for each occasion has lasted two centuries, among them the Friday evening tune and three for the Pilgrimage Festivals; Isaac Nathan used the Sukkot tune in 1815 for Lord Byron's The Wild Gazelle.

Not everyone sings it. Most Hasidic Jews leave it out because Isaac Luria reportedly omitted it from his siddur, rejecting poems he dated after the Talmudic era, though following Isaiah Horowitz most still consider it sacred. Syrian Jews omit it at the end of the services but sing it before Kiddush on Friday night, and Rabbi Joseph B. Soloveitchik opposed reciting it at the end of prayers as an imitation of the Christian custom of reciting a catechism.

The Methodist Thomas Olivers heard the hazzan Myer Lyon, who also sang in London opera as Michael Leoni, at the Great Synagogue of London, and around 1770 adapted his tune for the English hymn The God of Abraham Praise, a paraphrase that took a strongly Christian form when first printed in John Wesley's hymnbook of 1785. In the late 19th century Rabbi Max Landsberg and the Unitarian minister Newton M. Mann made the translation Praise to the Living God for the Reform Union Hymnal, which many Christian hymnals also adopted, all keeping close to the tune known as Leoni.
yin-rugeng: Yin was a native of Fuzhou with ancestral roots in Wenzhou, Zhejiang province. In 1902 his wealthy father sent him to Japan, where he studied the language and in 1905 enrolled at the First Higher School in Tokyo, a preparatory school for the Imperial Universities; the following year he moved to the Seventh Higher School Zoshikan in Kagoshima. In Japan he joined the Tongmenghui, the movement to overthrow the Qing dynasty, and married a Japanese woman.

On the orders of the Tongmenghui leader Huang Xing he returned to China to oversee revolutionary work in Hubei, and after the Republic of China was founded he joined the Kuomintang. In 1913 he went back to Japan to study law at Waseda University. From 1916 he served the Beiyang Government, helping to establish the Bank of China, and later took charge of foreign affairs for the Fengtian clique general Guo Songling, fleeing to Japanese territory after Guo was killed.

In 1926 he joined Chiang Kai-shek's Northern Expedition and took part in the capture of Nanchang. His knowledge of Japan made him a negotiator: he served the Shanghai mayor Huang Fu, was the chief Chinese negotiator after the Jinan Incident in 1928 and helped to negotiate the Shanghai Ceasefire Agreement of 1932. In 1933 he became commissioner of the Luantung Area of the demilitarised zone that agreement created in Hebei, the area he later declared autonomous with the encouragement of the Kwantung Army general Kenji Doihara.

In July 1937 about 800 soldiers of the Chinese 29th Army under General Song Zheyuan camped outside Tongzhou; Song had a secret agreement with Yin, who hoped to use them to rid himself of the Japanese. The result was fighting with the Japanese garrison, a mutiny of the East Hebei Army and a massacre of the town's Japanese and Korean inhabitants. Yin was captured by the Japanese but spared through the intervention of Toyama Mitsuru, and after five years of exile in Japan he held minor posts under the Wang Jingwei Government before resigning in 1944.

After Japan's surrender he was arrested and tried in Nanjing for treason, protesting that everything he had done had been out of patriotism for China. The Supreme Court sentenced him to death on 8 November 1947, and he was executed by firing squad at Nanjing on 1 December 1947.
yinchuan: Yinchuan lies in the middle of the Yinchuan Plain, sheltered from the deserts of Mongolia by the Helan Mountains to the west. The Yellow River runs through the area from south-west to north-east, and the plain has been irrigated by a canal system developed as long ago as the Han and Tang dynasties, which makes it very productive. The climate is a cold desert one, with about 194 mm of rain a year, dry cold winters and short hot summers.

The area was home to Shuidonggou, an early Paleolithic site more than 30,000 years old, and rock art was later made in the Helan Mountains. In the 1st century BCE the place was a county called Fuping, renamed Huaiyuan in the 6th century CE. After the fall of the Tang dynasty in 907 it came under the Tanguts, and in 1038 their leader Yuanhao declared himself emperor of the Great Xia. Many of the native Han population emigrated in response. The Pagoda of Chengtian and the Western Xia mausoleums were built in this period.

In the autumn of 1209 the Mongols besieged the city, by then called Zhongxing. A garrison of 150,000 held out, though Western Xia submitted to Mongol suzerainty. After the Xia tried to reassert its independence, the Mongols returned in 1227 and slaughtered the city's entire population; Genghis Khan died during the siege in circumstances that are debated. Under the Ming and Qing the city was the seat of the prefecture of Ningxia. In 1739 the Yinchuan–Pingluo earthquake levelled it, killing over 15,300 people.

Yinchuan became the capital of Ningxia province when it was formed from part of Gansu in 1928. In 1954 the province was abolished and the city passed to Gansu, but with the creation of the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region in 1958 it became the capital again. About a quarter of its people are Hui Muslims, and most of the rest are Han Chinese. The city is the chief market for the plain's grain, wool and animal products. Among the sights are the Western Xia imperial tombs, where nine imperial tombs and 253 lesser tombs have been unearthed since 1972, and the Haibao and Chengtiansi pagodas.
ying-bu: Ying Bu was born into a family of commoners in Lu County, present-day Lu'an in Anhui. A fortune teller told him in childhood that he would be a convict before becoming a king, and when he was later sentenced under Qin law to qing, the tattooing of a criminal's face, he laughed and recalled the prophecy; hence his other name, Qing Bu. Sent to Mount Li to labour on Qin Shi Huang's mausoleum, he befriended other convicts, escaped with them and became the leader of a bandit gang.

When the Dazexiang Uprising broke out in 209 BCE, he joined his father-in-law, the rebel leader Wu Rui, rallied several thousand men and later joined Xiang Liang, whose figurehead King Huai II of Chu named him Lord Dangyang. Under Xiang Yu he fought at the Battle of Julu in 207 BCE and afterwards, at Xin'an, oversaw the burial alive of Zhang Han's 200,000 surrendered Qin soldiers. When Xiang Yu divided the Qin empire into the Eighteen Kingdoms, Ying Bu became King of Jiujiang, and on Xiang Yu's secret order he killed the exiled Emperor Yi of Chu at Chen County.

In 205 BCE he twice pleaded illness rather than help Xiang Yu, and Liu Bang's envoy Sui He persuaded him to change sides. Defeated by Long Ju, he fled to Liu Bang, who made him King of Huainan in 203 BCE. He helped defeat Xiang Yu at the Battle of Gaixia in 202 BCE and ruled Huainan from Lu, over the commanderies of Jiujiang, Lushan, Hengshan and Yuzhang.

The executions of Han Xin and Peng Yue in 196 BCE alarmed him. When his official Ben He, suspected of an affair with one of Ying Bu's concubines, fled to Chang'an and accused him of plotting rebellion, Ying Bu killed Ben He's family and rose in revolt. He defeated and killed Liu Gu, Prince of Jing, and scattered a Chu army, but Emperor Gaozu, leading the Han army himself, defeated him at Zhui; asked why he rebelled, Ying Bu is said to have replied that he wanted to be emperor.

Left with about 100 men, he trusted a false offer from Wu Chen, Wu Rui's son, to help him escape to Nanyue, and was killed by peasants in Zi Village at Poyang. He is sometimes venerated as a door god in Chinese and Taoist temples, usually paired with Peng Yue.
yingya-shenglan: To the foreword he wrote in 1416, together with a poem, Ma Huan later added the posthumous title of the Yongle Emperor, which was conferred in 1424. A second foreword was written by Ma Jing in 1444. The afterword of 1451 came from the imperial clerk Gu Po, whom Guo Chongli, helped by his friend Lu Tingyong, persuaded to write it, and the book was published the same year.

The version in the Guochao Diangu was edited by Zhu Dangmian at an unknown date between 1451 and 1644 and fills 42 folios in chapter 106 of that work. The National Library in Beijing holds this edition, possibly the only surviving example; it has no foreword, poem or afterword, and nothing is known of the documents on which it was based. A copy at the Columbia University Libraries in New York shows that its copyist drew on other texts, since it adds the forewords of Ma Huan and Ma Jing, the poem, corrected readings and a few words.

The version in the Jilu Huibian, published by Shen Jiefu and Chen Yuting, fills 47 folios in chapter 62 and includes Ma Huan's foreword, his poem and Gu Po's afterword. Copies are held at Cambridge University Library, the Institut des Hautes Études Chinoises in Paris, the Library of Congress, Harvard Library and the National Palace Museum in Taipei, and manuscripts at the British Museum and the Sinological Institute in Leiden.

Zhang Sheng's condensed rewriting appeared in a posthumous edition of his works published by his son in 1522, and in 22 folios of chapter 63 of the Jilu Huibian. A further version, based on an unknown manuscript, fills 48 folios in the first chapter of the Shengchao Yishi, published by Wu Miguang in 1824.
yining: Yining stands on the northern side of the Ili River in the Dzungarian basin, about 70 km east of the border with Kazakhstan and about 710 km west of Ürümqi. The Ili valley is far wetter than most of Xinjiang and has rich grazing land. The city is the modern successor to the nearby ruined city of Almaliq. It is known as Ghulja in Uyghur and as Kulja in Kazakh, and in the 19th and early 20th centuries Russian and Western writers used Kulja for the whole Chinese part of the Ili basin and its two main cities.

The area was under the Chagatai Khanate from the 13th to the 15th century. Erdeni Batur, the first Khong Tayiji of the Dzungar Khanate, built a city here called Khobak Sari as the Dzungar capital, with a monastery, warehouses and settlements. Under Tsewang Rabtan and Galdan Tseren, Uyghurs were sent to farm the land and irrigation was introduced, producing wheat, barley, millet, melons, grapes, apricots and apples. Galdan Tseren built a monastery that was destroyed in the rebellion of Amursana and rebuilt in 1764 by the Qianlong emperor as the Anyuan temple.

Under the Qing the fort of Ningyuan was built in 1762 for settlers from southern Xinjiang, followed by the forts of Huining and Xichun. The Sino-Russian Treaty of Kulja of 1851 opened the area to trade. The city suffered severely in the Dungan Revolt of 1864–66. Russia seized the Ili basin in 1871, and the Treaty of Saint Petersburg of 1881 restored it to China. A 1911 reference work distinguished Old Kulja, the commercial centre, which is today's Yining, from New Kulja or Suiding, the Chinese fortress and regional capital.

Ningyuan County was renamed Yining County in 1914 to avoid confusion with other places of that name. The East Turkestan Revolution began at Ghulja on 7 November 1944, and the city was the capital of the Second East Turkestan Republic from 12 November 1944 until 22 December 1949. Yining became a separate city from Yining County in 1952, and in 1962 major Sino-Soviet clashes took place along the Ili. It is the administrative seat of the Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture and a commercial and agricultural centre of the valley, long a trading place for tea and cattle.
yinxu: Yinxu, Chinese for Ruins of Yin, lies in northern Henan, near modern Anyang and the borders Henan shares with Hebei and Shanxi. It corresponds to Yin, the final capital of the Shang dynasty. The name Yin appears not to have been used for the dynasty or its capital until the succeeding Zhou dynasty; the oracle bones call the state Shang and the capital Dayi Shang, the Great Settlement Shang. At 30 square kilometres the site is the largest archaeological site in China.

Ancient texts describe Yin as the last Shang capital but disagree on when the move took place. The Book of Documents and the Bamboo Annals say that King Pan Geng moved the capital to Yin, and the Annals add that he moved from Yan, present-day Qufu. In Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian Pan Geng instead moves it to Bo, south of the Yellow River, a location inconsistent with Yin. Yin was clearly the capital by the time of King Wu Ding, who launched numerous campaigns from it.

According to traditional accounts the last Shang king, Di Xin, was a tyrant, and Kings Wen and Wu of Zhou built support against him until the Battle of Muye ended the dynasty. The Zhou made their capital at Fenghao, and Yin was largely abandoned.

The site was then forgotten for millennia. In 1899 Wang Yirong, director of the Imperial Academy, recognised carvings on so-called dragon bones as ancient Chinese writing; by one account he found them in medicine bought for malaria. Illegal digs took tens of thousands of pieces before the source was traced to the village of Xiaotun, outside Anyang. In 1910 Luo Zhenyu identified the area as the last Shang capital. In 1917 Wang Guowei read the kings' names in the inscriptions and built a genealogy that closely matched Sima Qian's, confirming the Shang's historical authenticity.

Li Ji led the first official excavations in 1928-37, and work by the Institute of Archaeology has continued since 1950, uncovering palaces and temples, royal cemeteries, and bronze and bone workshops.

The best preserved royal tomb at Yinxu is that of Fu Hao, a military leader and wife of Wu Ding. Zheng Zhenxiang discovered it in 1976, and it has been dated to 1250 BCE. It was undisturbed and held six dog skeletons, 16 human slave skeletons and many grave goods. The tomb is open to the public, and nearby chariot pits hold the earliest animal-drawn carts found by Chinese archaeology. UNESCO selected Yinxu as a World Heritage Site in 2006.
ymer-prizreni: Ymer Prizreni, also called Ymer Drini, came from a family of müderris, teachers of Islamic learning, who held land around Zgatar near Prizren. His father, Sylejman Ali Nuhi, served as imam of the Bajrakli Mosque in Prizren and owned land, stores and mills; his grandfather Ali Nuhi founded the first mosque in Zgatar on 10 May 1814. Ymer studied Islamic theology and law in Istanbul and then taught at the madrasa of Prizren, where he became known as a supporter of the lower classes against the injustices of the Ottoman administration.

When the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878 began, he worked with other Albanian leaders to protect the territorial integrity of Albania and to press its national rights abroad, organising a self-defence committee for the Sanjak of Prizren and other committees in Kosovo. In 1877 he was elected to the first Ottoman Parliament, and he helped found the Central Committee for Defending Albanian Rights in Istanbul, chaired by Abdyl Frashëri, with whom he remained connected for the rest of his life.

In the spring of 1878 he chaired the committee that organised the general assembly at Prizren which founded the League of Prizren. He was elected chairman of the League in October 1879, and in January 1881 he became head of its Autonomous Provisional Government. In that office he directed the League's political work for a Vilayet of Albania and organised its armed resistance to the Ottoman armies sent to crush it in the spring of 1881.

After the League was suppressed he escaped capture by the Ottoman authorities and, refusing to submit, settled in Ulcinj, where he died on 12 June 1887 and where his tomb lies. He is said to have been murdered, and his archive of documents was reportedly stolen. The family's only descendants come from his brother Ali.
ynglinga-saga: Snorri Sturluson, Icelandic poet and historian, built the saga on the older Ynglingatal, a poem attributed to the 9th-century Norwegian skald Þjóðólfr of Hvinir, which also appears in Historia Norwegiae. It tells the most ancient part of the story of the House of Ynglings, the Scylfings of Beowulf, and describes the descent of the kings of Norway from this royal house of Sweden. References to historical events are woven into the narrative. The saga was first translated into English and published in 1844 by Samuel Laing.

The saga opens with a description of the world, which the Black Sea divides into Asia, Europe and Swithiod the Great, or the Cold, in the north, also called Godheim, the home of the gods, as against Mannheim, where people live. East of the river Tanais, the modern Don, lies Asaland, whose chief city is Asgaard, where Odin is chief. Odin wages war on the people of Vanaland but cannot defeat them; the two sides make a truce and exchange hostages, Njord the Rich, Frey and Freya going to Asaland. When the Vanaland people behead the wise Mime, Odin preserves his head with herbs and incantations so that it reveals secrets to him.

Foreseeing a new home in the north, Odin travels through Gardarike and Saxland to Fyen, sends Gefion to win land from King Gylve, and settles at Old Sigtun by Lake Maelare. Snorri presents him as a great sorcerer who shape-shifts, speaks only in verse and makes his warriors go berserk; he lays down laws on burning the dead, raising mounds and holding sacrifices. After Odin's death Njord rules, then Frey, who makes Upsal his capital; his other name, Yngvi, gives the Ynglings their name. When Frey dies his men hide his body in a mound with three windows, and the people go on paying tribute to him.

The kings who follow die in strange and often violent ways. Fjolne drowns in a vat of mead, Swegde is lured into a stone by a dwarf, Vanlande is killed in his sleep by the Mara, Domald is sacrificed by his people in a famine, and Agne is hanged by his wife Skjalv. King On sacrifices his sons to Odin, one every tenth year, to lengthen his life. The line runs through Ingjald, after whom the descendants settle in Norway, and on to Rognvald the Mountain-High.
ynglings: In the Scandinavian sources the Ynglings are the descendants of Yngvi-Frey of Vanaheim, and the name itself means descendant of Frey; Saxo Grammaticus calls them the sons of Frey. The dynasty claimed descent from the gods Freyr and Njörðr. In his Skáldskaparmál Snorri Sturluson also names Yngvi, a son of Halfdan the Old, as their ancestor, and elsewhere names Erik and Alrik, sons of Skjalf, as the forefathers of the house, so that the medieval genealogies offer more than one beginning.

When the poem Ynglingatal and the Old English Beowulf were composed, sometime in the eighth to tenth centuries, their authors expected their audiences to know a great deal about these kings, as the allusiveness of their references shows. In Beowulf the family appears as the Scylfings, and several of its kings are named there: Ongentheow, Onela, Ohthere and Eadgils, the Ale, Ottar and Adils of the Norse sources. Some of the early kings were likely mythical, while these, mentioned in both traditions, may have been real.

According to Snorri the dynasty led the settlement of the Swedish provinces and ruled them under the overlordship of the king at Uppsala, until it all but destroyed itself with Ingjald Ill-Ruler. A survivor, Olof Trätälja, became the ancestor of the Norwegian branch. Ynglingatal and Íslendingabók make the Fairhair dynasty of Oppland, from which came Harald Fairhair, the first king of all Norway, a branch of the Ynglings. Both Snorri and Saxo nevertheless describe the clan as remaining in Sweden as well.

Saxo Grammaticus counted Eric the Victorious, usually the first king in modern regnal lists, and his descendants among the Ynglings, though the Icelandic sources do not agree. Saxo's account of the Battle of Bråvalla, around 750, names among the Swedes Ingi, Oly, Alver and Folki, sons of Alrek, who served King Sigurd Hring and held the god Frey to be the founder of their race. The name Skilfing also lived on as a kenning for a king and, in the eddic poem Grímnismál, as one of Odin's names.
yodo-dono: Chacha was the eldest of three daughters of the daimyō Azai Nagamasa and Oichi, the younger sister of Oda Nobunaga. When Nobunaga's army besieged Odani Castle in 1573, she, her mother and her sisters Ohatsu and Oeyo were sent out safely, and her father and her only brother, Manpukumaru, died in its fall. In 1583 Oichi died with her husband Shibata Katsuie when he set fire to Kitanosho Castle under siege by Hideyoshi, having first placed her daughters in Hideyoshi's care. Ohatsu later married Kyōgoku Takatsugu, and Oeyo became the wife of the shōgun Tokugawa Hidetada and mother of Tokugawa Iemitsu.

When she became pregnant in 1588, Hideyoshi, who had no sons, was greatly pleased, and in 1589 he gave her Yodo Castle, remodelled by his brother Toyotomi Hidenaga. Her first son, Tsurumatsu, died in 1591, and her second, Hideyori, born in 1593, became Hideyoshi's designated successor. After Hideyoshi's death in 1598 she took tonsure as the nun Daikōin, founded the temple Yogen-in in memory of her parents and became the effective head of Osaka Castle as Hideyori's guardian. In 1600 she and three commissioners wrote urging Tokugawa Ieyasu to hasten to Kyoto against Ishida Mitsunari's rising, and she gave the Western Army no warrant in Hideyori's name; Ieyasu used her letter to brand Ishida's cause a rebellion.

After Ieyasu became shōgun in 1603 she resisted him, refusing in 1605 to let Hideyori pay homage. The inscriptions on the bell of Hōkō-ji, which the shogunate read as a curse on Ieyasu, and the gathering of rōnin at Osaka deepened the quarrel, and she banished Katagiri Katsumoto, who had proposed sending her to Edo as a hostage.

In the siege of 1614 she hired rōnin with gold and silver when no daimyō would help, and took part in the defence before agreeing to a peace. When Ieyasu attacked again in 1615 she and Hideyori killed themselves as the castle burned. No eyewitness account survives and her body was never found, which gave rise to stories of escape to Satsuma or Utsunomiya. Writers seeking to exalt the Tokugawa often portrayed her as a wicked and wanton woman, and James Clavell's Shōgun drew its Lady Ochiba from her.
yodo-river: The Yodo River is the principal river of Osaka Prefecture on Honshu, and it carries different names along its course. It leaves the southern outlet of Lake Biwa at Ōtsu, where a dam regulates the lake's level, as the Seta River. In Kyoto Prefecture it becomes the Uji River, and after it meets the Katsura River and the Kizu River it is called the Yodo. It then flows south through Osaka into Osaka Bay; part of it runs in an artificial channel, and the old course through the city is called the Kyū-Yodo River.

The basin has been a centre of Japanese politics, culture and economy since ancient times, and floods were frequent despite repeated works that began, by tradition, with the Ibaraki embankment of Emperor Nintoku's reign. Gyōki, a monk of the Nara Period, planned to cut away a hill that narrowed the Seta but gave up for fear of flooding downstream. Heian-kyō was chosen as capital partly for the river's route to the Seto Inland Sea, and the Uji River has a prominent place in the Uji chapters of The Tale of Genji by Murasaki Shikibu.

Toyotomi Hideyoshi rerouted the Uji and Yodo rivers when he built Fushimi Castle, completed in 1594, raising the Taikō Embankment and making Fushimi a transport hub. In the Edo period deforestation sent sediment into the riverbeds and caused floods, so the shogunate banned the digging of tree stumps in 1660, dredged the Seta from 1670 and in 1699 carried out the large works of Kawamura Zuiken. The river remained the main route for goods between Osaka and Kyoto until the first railways of the 1870s; in 1858 about 50 boats a day carried some 1,500 people from Osaka to Fushimi.

The river supplies water for irrigation and powers hydroelectric generators, and more than 50 bridges cross it. The surviving remains of the Taikō Embankment in Uji were designated a National Historic Site in 2009.
yohannes-iv: Yohannes IV was born Kahssai Mercha. His father, Mercha Wolde Kidan, came from the ruling family of Tembien, and his mother, Silas Dimtsu, was a niece of Sabagadis Woldu, so that he descended from the ruling families of Tembien, Agame and Enderta. The first half of his life is poorly documented, and the date of his birth is given as anywhere between 1831 and 1837. He was the youngest of his siblings and is first recorded in politics during a visit to the court of Tewodros II in 1864–1865, with his brothers Gugsa and Maru.

When a British expedition marched on Magdala in 1868 to free the European captives held by Tewodros, Yohannes agreed to help its commander, Sir Robert Napier, protecting supply routes from the coast. Tewodros killed himself three days after the expedition arrived at Magdala, and British officers admitted that they could not have reached it without the help of the chiefs and people of the country. Yohannes was rewarded with ammunition and artillery.

Yohannes continued the policy of Tewodros of unifying Ethiopia. He toured each region and met the governors he appointed, usually local nobles, so long as they submitted. In his first six years he united the mainly Christian provinces, including Lasta, Semien, Begemder, Gojjam, Wollo and Shewa. He crowned Menelik King of Shewa in 1878 and Tekle Haymanot King of Gojjam in 1881, and punished both after they fought at Embabo in June 1882.

He regarded divisions in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, Islam and foreign missionaries as threats to the state. At a council at Boru Meda in 1878 supporters of one disputed doctrine who protested had their tongues cut out, and he told the Oromo chiefs of Wollo to become Christians if they wished to live in peace. It is estimated that 550,000 Oromos and Jebertis were converted by force.

Khedive Isma'il Pasha of Egypt sought to bring the whole Nile basin under his rule, and Egyptian forces occupied Harar on 11 October 1875 and entered northern Ethiopia from Massawa. Yohannes appealed to the British, then marched against them. Later, under the Hewett Treaty, he allowed Egyptian garrisons to leave the Sudan across his lands. Ras Alula defeated a Mahdist army at Kufit on 23 September 1885, but Italy took Massawa.

When Mahdist forces sacked Gondar, Yohannes marched against them and was mortally wounded at the Battle of Gallabat on 9–10 March 1889, after going beyond the lines as victory neared. He named Ras Mengesha as his son and heir before dying, but Tigray fell into rebellion, and Menelik of Shewa was proclaimed emperor as Menelik II. His descendants ruled Tigray as hereditary princes until 1974.
yohl-ik-nal: Yohl Ikʼnal belonged to the royal Bʼaakal dynasty of Palenque and descended from its founder, Kʼukʼ Bahlam I. Her parentage is unclear because the hieroglyphic records are ambiguous: most scholars hold that she was the daughter either of Kan Bahlam I, her immediate predecessor, or of Kʼan Joy Chitam I, who ruled earlier in the sixth century. Her tie to Janahb Pakal is also uncertain; inscriptions describe a parent-child bond, and scholars are divided over whether he was her consort or her son. Through Lady Sak Kʼukʼ, the second woman to rule Palenque, she was an ancestor of Kʼinich Janaab Pakal I.

Classic Maya kingship passed almost always through the male line, and the circumstances of her accession have not survived. Scholars have suggested that no son of the previous ruler was old enough to reign, that a disputed succession or outside threat called for the strongest claimant, or that she first served as regent for a young male who died. The first sixteen years of her reign appear to have been stable, though the record for them is thin.

On 23 April 599 Palenque suffered an och kʼahkʼ, fire-entering, the standard Maya expression for the sacking of a city. Some inscriptions name a lord of Santa Elena as the direct attacker, suggesting that Calakmul acted through a dependent polity while claiming the victory. The city and its dynasty survived, and there are indications that either Yohl Ikʼnal in her last years or her successor Ajen Yohl Mat threw off Calakmul's dominance before 611.

She died on 7 November 604, recorded in the Long Count as 9.8.11.6.12 2 Eb 20 Keh, after twenty-one years on the throne; the cause of her death is not recorded. The archaeologist Merle Greene Robertson has suggested that an intact vaulted tomb beneath Temple 20, near the Temple of the Inscriptions, may be hers, pointing to its date, its rich burial goods and the small size of the skeleton, though other scholars identify it differently. Besides her two images on Pakal's sarcophagus, she was sculpted among the ancestors on the walls of his tomb, and she is named on the Palace Tablet, on three panels of the Temple of the Inscriptions and at Temple 17.
yokoi-shonan: Yokoi Shōnan, born Yokoi Tokiari on 22 September 1809, was a samurai of Kumamoto in Higo Province and a distant descendant of Hōjō Takatoki. The domain sent him to Edo in 1839 to study, and there he made contacts among the pro-reform members of the Mito domain. Back in Kumamoto he formed a group to reform the domain's administration along Neo-Confucian lines and opened a domain school, the Shōnan-do. He married Yajima Tsuseko, with whom he had two children, Miyako and Tokio.

As political adviser to Matsudaira Yoshinaga, the daimyō of Echizen, Yokoi wrote in Fukui the Kokuze Sanron, a treatise on state policy. In it he argued that Japan, though it had Buddhism, Shinto and Confucianism, lacked a true national religion of the kind Western nations had, and that this was a weakness of the Japanese kokutai; the idea later provided one rationale for State Shinto. He also stressed the need for a strong navy. Historians have labelled him pro-Western, yet he was harshly critical of Christianity as false and heretical.

When Matsudaira became acting prime minister of the Tokugawa administration in 1862, Yokoi went with him to Edo. He called for a complete reform of the shogunate, reconciliation with the Imperial Court, the full opening of Japan to foreign trade, economic reform and a modern army on Western lines. Wei Yuan's Illustrated Treatise on the Maritime Kingdoms convinced him that a cautious, gradual opening would spare Japan the mistake China had made in the First Opium War. He also proposed a national assembly of the major domains, with the shōgun becoming something like a prime minister.

Conservatives stripped him of his posts and even his samurai status and confined him to house arrest in Kumamoto, but he kept in touch with Katsu Kaishū and other reformers. After the Meiji Restoration he was freed and given the title of san'yo, councillor. On 15 February 1869 he was killed by conservative samurai who suspected him of being a Christian and of secret republican sympathies.
yolande-duchess-of-lorraine: Yolande was born at Nancy on 2 November 1428, the daughter of Isabella, Duchess of Lorraine, and René of Anjou, who was King of Naples, Duke of Anjou, Bar and Lorraine and Count of Provence. Her younger sister was Margaret of Anjou, Queen of England. In 1445, at Nancy, she married her second cousin Frederick II, Count of Vaudémont. The match was a dynastic alliance, arranged to end the dispute between her father and Frederick's father, Antoine of Vaudémont, over the succession to Lorraine.

The couple had several children. Besides René, who became Duke of Lorraine, there were Nicolas, Lord of Joinville and Bauffremont, who died in 1476; Jeanne, who married Charles IV, Duke of Anjou, in 1474; Yolande, who married William II, Landgrave of Hesse, in 1497; and Marguerite, who married René, Duke of Alençon, in 1488. Frederick died in 1470.

On the death of her nephew Nicolas in 1473 she inherited the Duchy of Lorraine and passed it at once to her eldest son René II. In 1480, after the death of her father, she did the same with the Duchy of Bar. Though she nominally held major territories, she ceded power and titles to her husband and son.

Yolande died at Nancy on 23 March 1483, aged 54, on the birthday of her sister Margaret, who had died the previous summer. In 1845 the Danish poet Henrik Hertz made her the heroine of the verse drama King René's Daughter, in which she is a blind sixteen-year-old princess kept in a garden paradise until a Moorish physician restores her sight and Count Vaudémont falls in love with her. There is no evidence that she was ever blind.

The play was translated into many languages, and a Russian version, adapted by Vladimir Zotov, became the basis of Tchaikovsky's opera Iolanta, with a libretto by his brother Modest Ilyich Tchaikovsky, first performed in St. Petersburg on 18 December 1892. A silent film was made of it in 1913. The book The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail later named her a Grand Master of the Priory of Sion, a claim resting on documents forged in 1967.
yom-kippur-war: The war was part of the Arab–Israeli conflict. In the Six-Day War of 1967 Israel had captured the Sinai Peninsula, the Gaza Strip, roughly half of Syria's Golan Heights and the West Bank. Four months before the fighting, Henry Kissinger offered Sadat's emissary Ismail an Israeli withdrawal from almost all of Sinai; Ismail never returned with a reply, and Sadat was already determined to go to war. The attack came on 6 October, the Jewish holy day of Yom Kippur, which coincided with the 10th day of Ramadan.

In Sinai the Egyptians deployed five divisions of 100,000 soldiers, 1,350 tanks and 2,000 guns against 450 Israeli soldiers in 16 forts along the canal. They armed their infantry with RPG-7 rockets and Sagger guided missiles, which proved devastating to the first Israeli armoured counterattacks. On the Golan the Syrians attacked with five divisions, 800 tanks and 600 artillery pieces against Israeli brigades of some 3,000 troops and 180 tanks. Dayan ordered the Jordan bridges prepared for detonation.

Arriving reserves turned the tide on the Golan from 8 October, and Israel pushed on towards Damascus. Jordan and Iraq sent forces to support Syria. In Sinai an Israeli force under Ariel Sharon crossed the Suez Canal at Deversoir, where a gap had been found between the Egyptian Second and Third Armies, and moved to encircle the Third Army. The Soviet Union airlifted 12,500 to 15,000 tons of supplies to its allies from 9 October. Resolution 338 of the Security Council demanded a ceasefire on 22 October, but fighting continued, and a second ceasefire took effect on 25 October.

After President Nixon authorised $2.2 billion in arms for Israel, Saudi Arabia declared an embargo against the United States, which led to the 1973 energy crisis. Kissinger pressed Israel not to destroy the trapped Third Army, hoping to draw Egypt away from Soviet influence. The war was a direct antecedent of the Camp David Accords of 1978 and the Egypt–Israel Peace Treaty of 1979, and the last Israeli troops left Sinai on 26 April 1982.

Israel lost between 2,521 and 2,800 killed. The shock to Israelis was severe, since the army had grown complacent after 1967. Historians differ over whether the outcome was an Israeli victory, an Egyptian victory or a stalemate.
yonago: Yonago lies in the far west of Tottori Prefecture and faces the Sea of Japan to the north and Lake Nakaumi to the northwest. It adjoins Shimane Prefecture and stands across the lake from the Shimane capital of Matsue. The city limits are mostly flat, with the Hino River flowing through the Yonago Plain, while the southern part is hilly country at the foot of Mount Daisen. An irrigation canal called the Yonekawa carries water from the Hino River to Sakaiminato. The name is written with two kanji, meaning rice and child.

The area belonged to the ancient province of Hōki. According to the Kojiki, the tomb of the creator kami Izanami lies on the border of Yonago with Izumo Province, and many remains of the Yayoi and Kofun periods have been found within the city limits.

In the early Edo period the Tokugawa shogunate appointed Nakamura Kazutada daimyō of the 175,000 koku Yonago Domain, and the castle was reconstructed. The centre of the modern city grew from the castle town. After Nakamura died without an heir the domain was abolished and its lands passed to the Ikeda clan of Tottori Domain, who kept the castle and gave it to their hereditary senior retainers of the Arao clan, who ruled it until the Meiji Restoration.

The town of Yonago was established in Aioi District in October 1889, under the new system of municipalities. A post office opened in 1872, a prison in 1877 and a courthouse in 1884, and railway services began in 1902. Yonago became a city on 1 April 1927 and absorbed the neighbouring town of Yodoe on 31 March 2005.

Yonago is the second largest city of Tottori Prefecture after Tottori and the commercial centre of its western part. Most of its workforce is employed in services, and Tottori University has a campus there. Its National Historic Sites include the ruins of Yonago Castle, the Mukoeyama Kofun Cluster, the Mukibanda Yayoi remains and the Kamiyodo temple ruins. Kaike Onsen, on Miho Bay, is said to be the birthplace of the triathlon in Japan. The city is twinned with Baoding in China and Sokcho in South Korea.
yonezawa: Yonezawa lies in the southeast corner of Yamagata Prefecture and covers 548.51 square kilometres. Its southern and eastern parts are river basins surrounded by large mountains, forming the Yonezawa Basin, and the Mogami River flows through the city. The south has complex terrain of several rivers and alternating ridges and valleys running east to west. Part of the city lies within the Bandai-Asahi National Park. The climate is humid continental, with warm to hot summers, cold winters and heavy precipitation from August to October.

The area was part of ancient Dewa Province and was controlled in the Sengoku period by the Date clan. The warlord Date Masamune was born in Yonezawa. In the Edo period the area became Yonezawa Domain under the Tokugawa shogunate, ruled by the Uesugi clan. After the start of the Meiji period it was organised into Minamiokitama District, Yamagata Prefecture.

Yonezawa is best known for its local delicacies, among them apples, Yonezawa beef and carp, and as a castle town that was once home to the Uesugi clan, including the daimyō Uesugi Yozan. Its economy rests on agriculture, horticulture, light manufacturing and tourism. Local attractions include Yonezawa Castle, Tateyama Castle, the Yonezawa City Uesugi Museum, Namegawa Great Falls and the hot springs of Shirabu Onsen and Yonezawa Onsen. Yamagata University has a campus in the city. Natives include the architect Itō Chūta, the statesman Hirata Tosuke and the admirals Yamashita Gentarō and Chūichi Nagumo.
yongle-emperor: Zhu Di was born on 2 May 1360, the fourth son of Zhu Yuanzhang, who in 1368 founded the Ming dynasty as the Hongwu Emperor. On 22 April 1370 he was made Prince of Yan, with his fief at Beiping, the present Beijing, and in April 1380 he moved there. In the 1380s and 1390s he proved a skilled military leader. After the Hongwu Emperor's death, the new Jianwen Emperor's advisors set out to limit the power of the princes, removing five of them, and regarded Zhu Di as the most dangerous.

In 1399 Zhu Di rebelled in the civil war known as the Jingnan campaign. He began with 100,000 soldiers and only the area around Beiping, but his troops were of higher quality. He ascended the throne on 17 July 1402 and took the era name Yongle. He erased the Jianwen Emperor's reign from the record, and tens of thousands of people were purged, among them Huang Zicheng and Qi Tai, who were put to death with their families and followers.

He made Beiping, renamed Beijing in 1403, a second capital, and its construction between 1407 and 1420 employed hundreds of thousands of workers. He had the Grand Canal rebuilt to feed the capital and the northern armies, finishing in 1415. He sponsored the Yongle Encyclopedia, which employed about two thousand scholars. Unlike his father, he avoided frequent purges. He led five campaigns into Mongolia, which failed to secure the northern border, and annexed Đại Việt in 1407 as Jiaozhi Province. In 1405 he appointed the eunuch Zheng He admiral of a fleet whose voyages reached India, Hormuz, Arabia and East Africa.

On 1 April 1424 the emperor set out on his last campaign into Mongolia, which failed. He died on 12 August 1424 at Yumuchuan, and private records suggest that a series of strokes killed him. He was buried in the Chang Mausoleum, the first of the Ming tombs north of Beijing, and his son Zhu Gaochi succeeded him as the Hongxi Emperor. Historians such as Chan Hok-lam, Edward Dreyer and Frederick Mote have described his reign as the second founding of the Ming dynasty.
yongle-encyclopedia: The Yongle Emperor, known for his military achievements, was also a reader who wished to categorise literary works into a reference encyclopedia to preserve rare books and simplify research. He raised the standing of the Hanlin Academy, which had handled clerical tasks such as drafting edicts, by selecting only top recruits and leaving clerical duties to imperial officers. In 1404, a year after the commission, a team of 100 scholars led by Xie Jin finished a manuscript called A Complete Work of Literature, but the Emperor rejected it and insisted on more volumes. In 1405 the number of scholars rose to 2,169, and they were sent across China to find books. The monk Yao Guangxiao was general editor.

The work was completed in 1408 at the Guozijian in Nanjing and filled 11,095 volumes, occupying about 40 cubic metres, with 370 million Chinese characters. It was meant to include every commentary written on the Chinese classics and all history, philosophy, arts and sciences, as a collation of excerpts and works from the whole of Chinese literature. It was handwritten, not printed, on special paper and bound in the wrapped-back style, with red ink, reserved for the emperor, for titles and authors. Entries were ordered by the sounds of characters under the Hongwu zhengyun, not by subject. Non-Confucian scholars wrote the Buddhist, Daoist and divination sections, and some Neo-Confucians dismissed the work as wheat and chaff.

The encyclopedia stood in Nanjing until 1421, when the capital moved to Beijing and it went to the Forbidden City. It narrowly escaped a fire in 1557, and the Jiajing Emperor had a manuscript copy made between 1562 and 1567. The original was lost afterwards, and theories include its burning in 1644, burial with the Jiajing Emperor, and the Qianqing Palace fire. Most of the copy was burnt or looted when Anglo-French forces invaded Beijing in 1860; about 5,000 volumes remained in 1875 and 800 by 1894, and the Boxer Rebellion and the Hanlin Academy fire cost more. The largest holding, 221 volumes, is at the National Library of China in Beijing, and the National Palace Museum in Taipei holds 62.
yongli-emperor: Zhu Youlang was the son of Zhu Changying, the seventh son of the Wanli Emperor, and of Empress Dowager Ma. He inherited the title Prince of Gui from his brother and lived obscurely as a minor member of the imperial family until the peasant rebel Li Zicheng took Beijing in 1644 and the Chongzhen Emperor killed himself at Coal Hill. Six weeks later the Manchu army entered the city and proclaimed the Qing dynasty, and over the next two years the loyalist Hongguang, Longwu and Shaowu emperors were captured and executed in quick succession.

Zhu Youlang became Caretaker of the State on 20 November 1646, after the death of the Longwu Emperor. When Longwu's brother proclaimed himself emperor as Shaowu, Youlang took the throne on 24 December 1646 with the era name Yongli, meaning perpetual calendar; their brief civil war ended a month later when the Qing captured and executed Shaowu. For his first five years his adoptive mother, Empress Dowager Wang, acted as his adviser, and it was said that he followed her wishes in everything.

Qing pressure drove the court from Guilin in Guangxi to Jiangxi and Hunan, then to Nanning. Youlang came to rely on local warlords and bandit chieftains, the most effective of whom, Li Dingguo, enlarged Southern Ming territory in the south-west for five years. The Qing answered by placing the region under the former Ming official Hong Chengchou as governor-general of five provinces, and by 1658 Youlang had been forced back into Yunnan.

Pindale Min, king of the Taungoo dynasty of Burma, allowed him to live at Sagaing, near Ava, if his men gave up their weapons. Fighting soon broke out between the exiles and their hosts; after Pye Min overthrew Pindale in May 1661, he ordered the Chinese followers killed, sparing only Youlang. In December 1661 Wu Sangui entered Burma with 20,000 men and demanded the emperor, and on 22 January 1662 he and his sons and grandsons were sent by boat to Wu's camp. Taken to Yunnanfu, he was strangled by Wu Sangui in June. Zhu Shugui, Prince of Ningjing, performed rites in his name in the Kingdom of Tungning until 1683.
yongzheng-emperor: Yinzhen, the future Yongzheng Emperor, was born on 13 December 1678, the eleventh recorded son of the Kangxi Emperor and the fourth prince to survive into adulthood. His mother, a court attendant of the Manchu Uya clan, was of low status and had no right to raise her own children, so Noble Consort Tong raised him. Kangxi gave his sons a rigorous education and took them on inspection trips; Yinzhen was made a beile in 1689 and a junwang, a prince of the second rank, in 1698.

In 1712 Kangxi deposed Yinreng a second time and named no heir, which set his sons against one another. Yinzhen had supported Yinreng, built his own base of support largely out of the limelight, showed no ambition and pleaded for mercy for other princes. When Kangxi died in December 1722 Yinzhen took the throne. Kangxi's choice was known only through a testament provided by Longkodo, and no decisive evidence showed it was not fabricated, so rivals such as Yinti, Yinzhi and Yinsi opposed him.

In 1723 he adopted the era name Yongzheng, "Harmonious Justice", and it has been suggested that the second character was meant to cover his disputed claim. Much of his early reign went on purging dissidents, and he grew increasingly fearful that his brothers would plot against him.

Nian Gengyao, commander of the Qing army in Xinjiang, was demoted and forced to take poison in 1726. Immediately after his enthronement Yongzheng cracked down on corruption and debt, relying partly on a secret report system in which trusted informants wrote privately to the emperor. He made meltage fees on silver an official source of local income, grouped the merchant houses of Canton into the Cohong in 1725 and removed all foreign priests from China. When civil war tore Tibet in 1727-1728 he intervened and left a Qing Resident, the amban, and a garrison.

Yongzheng ruled for thirteen years and died suddenly in 1735, aged 56, while reading court documents. It is likely that he died of poisoning from an elixir of immortality he was taking, and his successor, the Qianlong Emperor, evicted all Taoist priests from the palace. His reign was much shorter than those of his father and his son but achieved important reforms. Many consider it authoritarian, some calling him a benevolent despot and others holding that his autocratic policies went too far.
york: York lies in the Vale of York, a flat area of fertile arable land bordered by the Pennines, the North York Moors and the Yorkshire Wolds. The city was built at the confluence of the Ouse and the Foss on a terminal moraine left by the last ice age. It grew up as a river port, and the Ouse was originally a tidal river accessible to the seagoing ships of the time. The Roman name Eburacum or Eboracum is a Latinisation of a Brittonic word that may mean place of yew trees, or alternatively property of a man named Eburos.

Archaeological evidence suggests that Mesolithic people settled in the area between 8000 and 7000 BCE. By the time of the Roman conquest the land was held by a tribe the Romans called the Brigantes, whose territory first became a client state. Its leaders later grew hostile, and the Ninth Legion was sent north of the Humber into it. The city was founded as Eboracum in 71 CE. It became the capital of Britannia Inferior, a province of the Roman Empire, and was later the capital of the kingdoms of Deira and Northumbria and of Scandinavian York.

In 1068, two years after the Norman invasion, the people of York rebelled. The rising succeeded at first, but William the Conqueror suppressed it on arriving and at once built a wooden fortress on a motte. After a second rebellion in 1069 he built another timber castle across the Ouse. Both were destroyed in 1069 and rebuilt about the time of his ravaging of Northumbria, the Harrying of the North, when he destroyed everything from York to Durham.

York declined economically in the Tudor period. The Dissolution of the monasteries under Henry VIII ended its monastic houses. This contributed to the Pilgrimage of Grace, an uprising of northern Catholics, and Henry restored his authority by setting up the Council of the North in the dissolved St Mary's Abbey. The railway promoter George Hudson brought the railway to York in 1839, and the city was a major railway centre by the late 19th century.

York is a cathedral city in North Yorkshire, the traditional county town of Yorkshire. Its minster, castle and city walls are all Grade I listed. The walls are the most complete in England and incorporate part of the Roman fortress wall. York Minster is a large Gothic cathedral, and the Jorvik Viking Centre and the National Railway Museum are among the city's museums.
york-factory: York Factory stands on the north bank of the Hayes River, about 11 kilometres inland from the southwestern shore of Hudson Bay and some 200 kilometres south-southeast of Churchill. The much larger Nelson River, which drains Lake Winnipeg, reaches the sea just to the north, but the Hayes was the more practical canoe route. The bay was too shallow for seagoing ships to come close, so they anchored at Five Fathom Hole and smaller boats carried goods to the post.

The Hudson's Bay Company first set up Fort Nelson at the mouth of the Nelson River and then built York Factory on the Hayes, naming it after the Duke of York. New France contested the bay. Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville was driven off in 1690, captured the post in 1694 and renamed it Fort Bourbon, lost it the next year, and took it again in 1697 after winning the Battle of Hudson's Bay. The French held it until the Treaty of Utrecht returned it to the British in 1713.

For its first century the depot drew First Nations traders to it rather than sending traders out, until competition from the voyageurs of the North West Company pushed the company to build inland posts as far as the Oregon Country. From 1821 to 1873 York Factory was headquarters of the Northern Department, and from 1821 to 1846 the York Factory Express travelled twice a year to Fort Vancouver.

A stone and brick fort called the Octagon, built from 1788 to 1795, could not withstand the heaving permafrost and was razed in 1831, the year the present wooden building's centre was finished. By the mid-19th century the settlement had 50 buildings, though few liked it: the trader John McLean left in 1837 with little regret for its fogs, bogs and mosquitoes. Its role shrank after Rupert's Land passed to Canada, and in 1929 Churchill, joined to Winnipeg by rail, took its place.

The company closed the post in 1957, and its Cree residents were moved to York Landing, Split Lake and Shamattawa; Cree elders have recalled their wish to stay at Kihci-waskahikan, the Great House. Designated a National Historic Site of Canada in 1936, it has belonged to the Canadian government since 1968 and is run by Parks Canada. Its building of 1831 is the oldest and largest wooden structure built on permafrost in Canada.
york-maine: York lies on the Atlantic coast near the southern tip of Maine, on the Gulf of Maine, in York County. Its first name, Agamenticus, is an Abenaki term for the York River that was also given to the hill, visible from sea, now called Mount Agamenticus, whose summit stands 692 feet (211 metres) above sea level. The town is divided into the villages of Bald Head, York Village, York Harbor, York Beach and Cape Neddick, and lies about 65 miles (105 km) north of Boston.

In 1638 the settlers renamed it Bristol after the English city from which they had come. Sir Ferdinando Gorges, lord proprietor of Maine under the Plymouth patent, envisioned a great city rising from the wilderness and named the capital of his province Gorgeana. A charter from King Charles I made it the first incorporated city in America. After Gorges died, the Massachusetts Bay Colony claimed his territory, and in 1652 York was incorporated from part of Gorgeana, becoming the second oldest town in Maine after Kittery, incorporated two years before.

Control stayed contested. In 1662 the Crown ruled that Massachusetts Bay had exceeded its charter, and a royal commission visited in 1664. On 14 July 1668 John Leverett and Richard Waldron led twelve cavalrymen into York, deposed the officials and swore in new ones on the authority of Boston.

The first Congregational church was organised in 1672 under Shubael Dummer. In the Candlemas Massacre of 1692, during King William's War, Abenaki raiders destroyed York. Dummer was shot at his own front door, about 50 people were killed and nearly 100 were carried away captive. The last local attack came at Cape Neddick in 1723, during Dummer's War. Hostilities lessened after the French defeat at the Siege of Louisbourg in 1745 and ended with the Treaty of Paris of 1763. As provincial capital and site of the Royal Gaol, York prospered on trade with the West Indies, shipping lumber and farm goods for sugar and molasses; the merchant John Hancock kept a warehouse there. Jefferson's Embargo Act of 1807 crippled this trade.

After the Civil War, York's sea breezes and colonial houses drew tourists, and it became a fashionable summer resort, like Bar Harbor and Newport, with Gilded Age buildings in the Shingle style. Buildings in York Village are kept as museums by the Old York Historical Society. The Cape Neddick Light at Nubble Rock is among its best-known sights. The population was 13,723 at the 2020 census.
york-minster: A bishop of York was summoned to the Council of Arles in 314, which points to a Christian community in York at that time, though archaeological evidence for Christianity in Roman York is limited. The first recorded church was a wooden structure built hurriedly in 627 to baptise Edwin, King of Northumbria. Its location and that of its successors before 1080 are unknown. It was probably in or beside the old Roman principia, the military headquarters, and so near the present minster but not directly on the same site. Excavations in 1967-73 found no remains of the churches before 1080.

A song school was founded in 627 by Paulinus of York, the first Archbishop of York, and choir schools have been associated with the minster since the 7th century. The undercroft of the present building contains re-used fabric of about 1160.

York Minster is the seat of the archbishop of York and the mother church of the diocese and province of York. It is the second-largest Gothic cathedral of northern Europe and charts the development of English Gothic architecture, with Early English transepts, a Decorated nave and chapter house, and a Perpendicular eastern arm and central tower. Most of the building dates from between 1220 and 1472, and it is built of creamy magnesian limestone quarried at Tadcaster. It has a cruciform plan, an octagonal chapter house attached to the north transept and a central tower 72 metres high.

The minster keeps most of its medieval stained glass. The Dean and Chapter commissioned John Thornton in 1405 to design the Great East Window, for which he was paid £66. Its scenes come from the Book of Revelation, and it is the largest expanse of medieval stained glass in the country. The north transept holds the Five Sisters window, five lancets of grisaille glass.

Thomas Becket's shrine at Canterbury made it a rival draw for pilgrims, and York responded by seeking a saint of its own. On 18 March 1226 Pope Honorius entered the name of William Fitzherbert, a former archbishop, among the saints. In 1279 his remains were moved to a shrine behind the high altar, and King Edward I helped carry the chest.

On 9 July 1984 a serious fire damaged the south transept, and firefighters deliberately collapsed its roof to save the rest of the building. The heat shattered the glass of the rose window, but the lead held it together so that it could be taken down and restored. The 311 panels of the Great East Window were removed for conservation in 2008, and a renovation of the east front begun in 2007 was completed in 2018. An astronomical clock installed in the north transept in 1955 commemorates airmen killed in the Second World War.
york-river-virginia: The York River is formed at West Point, about 56 kilometres east of Richmond, where the Mattaponi and Pamunkey rivers meet. It widens from 1.6 kilometres at its head to 4.0 kilometres near its mouth and drains part of the coastal plain of Virginia north and east of Richmond. It enters the Chesapeake Bay about 8 kilometres east of Yorktown, which stands on its southern shore, while the Middle Peninsula lies to the north.

Native Americans called the river the Pamunkey, and the colonists of the Virginia Company first named it the Charles River. In 2002–2003 archaeologists found an extensive settlement at Purtan Bay, in what is now Gloucester County, which they have concluded is likely the site of Werowocomoco. The village was lived in from 1200 CE, with major earthworks built about 1400 CE. The site was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2006. The excavations have been carried out by the College of William and Mary, the Virginia Department of Natural History and representatives of the Powhatan descendant tribes.

The river's banks saw early settlements of the Virginia Colony. In October 1781 the British army under Cornwallis at Yorktown was cornered by the Americans under George Washington on land and the French fleet at sea, and its surrender ended the war in the east. In 1862 the same peninsula between the York and the James became the theatre of the Peninsular Campaign of the American Civil War.

The south shore holds York River State Park, Camp Peary and the Naval Weapons Station Yorktown, with wetlands and forest important to migratory waterfowl; the Colonial Parkway runs through part of it between Williamsburg and Yorktown. The only road crossing is the George P. Coleman Memorial Bridge, a swing bridge carrying U.S. Highway 17 between Yorktown and Gloucester Point, which charged tolls from 1952 to 1976 and again from 1995 to August 2025.
yorkshire: Yorkshire takes its name from the city of York, being York's shire. The name York is believed to come from the Brittonic Eburākon, probably meaning place of yew trees, which became Eboracum to the Romans, Eorfowīc to the Angles and Jórvík to the Vikings. The south-west includes Leeds, Sheffield, Bradford, Doncaster and Wakefield, and Hull lies in the south-east. The North York Moors fill the north-east, the Vale of York the centre, and the Pennines, including the Yorkshire Dales, the west. The historic boundaries were reasonably stable from 1182, when western areas went to the new county of Lancashire, until 1889.

By the late Iron Age the area was held by British Celtic tribes, the Brigantes in the north and west and the Parisi in what is now the East Riding. After the Romans left, small kingdoms arose, among them Deira in the east, Ebrauc around York and Elmet in the west. In 1066, shortly before the Battle of Hastings, Harold II marched north and defeated Tostig and Harald Hardrada of Norway at Stamford Bridge, where both were killed. Many castles, among them Richmond, Pickering, Skipton and York, were built in the Norman period.

In the Wars of the Roses, between the houses of York and Lancaster, battles were fought at Wakefield and Towton, the latter called the bloodiest ever fought on English soil. In the 16th and 17th centuries the wool textile industry moved from cottage work in the old market towns to mills in the West Riding powered by Pennine streams, helping Wakefield, Halifax, Leeds and Huddersfield to grow, while coal mining first came into prominence.

The county was divided into three ridings, East, West and North, a word of Viking origin from Threthingr, a third. Each was divided into wapentakes. York became a county corporate in 1396 and Hull in 1440, independent of the ridings. Each riding had its own lord-lieutenant from 1660, and from 1889 to 1974 the ridings were administrative counties.

Yorkshire's culture draws on Celts, Romans, Angles, Norse Vikings and Normans, and its dialect has roots in Old English and Old Norse. The white rose, once the badge of the Plantagenet House of York, is its emblem, and Yorkshire Day is observed on 1 August. York Minster is the largest Gothic cathedral in northern Europe.
yorkshire-wolds: The Wolds are the northernmost chalk hills in Great Britain, formed of marine limestones of the Cretaceous period. On the west they rise to an escarpment above the Vale of York, highest at Bishop Wilton Wold, also called Garrowby Hill, 246 m above sea level; to the east they flatten into the plain of Holderness. South of the Humber the same rocks continue as the Lincolnshire Wolds. At Flamborough Head the chalk ends in cliffs over 130 m high.

The plateau is cut by deep, flat-bottomed valleys, most of them dry because the chalk drains so well. This gives an upside-down farming system, with sheep and cattle grazing the valleys and crops grown on the hills. The Gypsey Race, which flows through the Great Wold Valley to Bridlington Harbour, is the northernmost chalk stream in Europe.

Fertile soils, good grazing, light tree cover and stone for tools drew early Neolithic settlers, and the Wolds are, with Wessex and Orkney, a key area for the study of the Neolithic in the British Isles. Long barrows at Fordon on Willerby Wold and at Kilham have been dated to around 3700 BCE; other monuments include Duggleby Howe, a henge at Rudston, the Rudston Monolith and four cursus monuments near the eastern end of the Great Wold Valley. More than 1,400 Bronze Age round barrows are known, and at Danes Graves some 500 small round barrows mark Iron Age burials, one of them with a chariot.

The Romans arrived around 71 CE and built roads across the Wolds from Brough to York and Malton; the native Parisi gradually adopted Roman ways, and villas stood at Rudston, Harpham, Brantingham, Welton and Wharram-le-Street. Walkington Wold holds the only known Anglo-Saxon execution cemetery in northern England, and Wharram Percy is one of the best-known deserted village sites in the country.

The largest town is Driffield, known as the Capital of the Wolds, a title Kilham held in the Middle Ages. Beverley, with its minster, lies on the eastern slopes. The Yorkshire Wolds Way, one of the nine National Trails of England, runs the length of the hills from the Humber Bridge at Hessle to Filey.
yorubaland: Yorubaland covers about 142,114 square kilometres, of which 74.6 percent lies in Nigeria, 18.9 percent in Benin and 6.5 percent in Togo. It runs north from the Gulf of Guinea and west from the Niger River, from near Lokoja into Togo in the north and along the coast to Porto-Novo, beyond which Gbe speakers predominate. Mangrove forests, estuaries and coastal plains rise northward to the Yorubaland plateau, whose highest point is the Idanre Inselberg Hills at over 1,050 metres. The south is tropical high forest and the north and west woodland savanna, with the harmattan blowing from the Sahara in the dry season.

Tradition regards Oduduwa as the progenitor of the Yoruba, and almost every Yoruba settlement traces its origin to princes of Ile-Ife, the cultural and spiritual homeland of the nation. Linguistic evidence suggests that the east of the region was settled earlier than the west. Ife had a golden age between 1100 and 1400 before the Oyo Empire surpassed it. Sixteen established kingdoms are said to descend from Oduduwa. Most states were ruled by Obas, priestly monarchs, with councils of chiefs called Oloyes; the balance of power varied, but a ruler who showed dictatorial tendencies could be sent an aroko, often parrot eggs in a covered calabash, ordering him to give up the throne, usually by taking his own life.

After the jihad of Uthman Dan Fodio, the Sokoto Caliphate overran Ilorin and sacked Oyo-Ile, the Oyo capital; Ibadan and the Ijebu kingdom checked further advance. The other city-states broke free of Oyo and fought among themselves, and in this period millions of Yoruba were forcibly transported to the Americas and the Caribbean, to Cuba, Brazil, Haiti, the United States and elsewhere. In 1892 the British went to war with the Ijebu Kingdom over its barriers to trade and occupied its capital, and protectorate treaties then brought the rest of Yorubaland under British rule. Almost a fifth of it, from Offa to Old Oyo and Kabba, was joined to Northern Nigeria.

In Nigeria Yorubaland comprises the states of Oyo, Osun, Ogun, Kwara, Ondo, Ekiti and Lagos and the west of Kogi, and it extends into the Ouémé, Plateau and Collines departments of Benin and the Plateaux and Centrale regions of Togo. It is home to an estimated 55 million people, most of them Yoruba.
yoshida-koriyama-castle: The castle stands in the Yoshida basin in northern Hiroshima Prefecture, ringed by the Chugoku Mountains and drained by two rivers, the Gonokawa flowing north to the Sea of Japan and the Otagawa flowing south to the Seto Inland Sea. It was also called Aki-Kōriyama Castle after the old province. The Mōri clan, descended from Ōe no Hiromoto, a leading retainer of the Kamakura shogunate, first built it as a small fort in the 14th century. Hiromoto's fourth son, Mōri Suemitsu, held a shōen estate in Aki Province, and his descendants became leaders of an alliance of local lords in eastern Aki and western Bingo.

Aki was a contested border between the Ouchi clan of Suo Province and the Yamana, and after the Onin War the Izumo-based Amago rose to challenge the Ouchi; the Mōri changed sides between them several times to survive. Under Mōri Motonari, who allied with the Ouchi, the castle was greatly enlarged into the clan's main stronghold, and the Amago siege of September 1540 ended in their defeat, with Ouchi help, in January 1541. Rebuilt to cover most of the mountain, it became an advanced mountaintop castle, or yamashiro, with inner and outer stone walls and a stone-walled fort.

Motonari gave the castle to his eldest son, Mōri Takamoto, and after the Amago were decisively defeated in 1566 he had it strengthened further. Mōri Terumoto began Hiroshima Castle as his new seat in 1589. After the Mōri sided with the western alliance at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, they lost Aki Province, and the castle was largely demolished early in the Edo period under the Tokugawa policy of one castle to a domain.

The ruins have been a National Historic Site since 1940 and are now a historical park, with low stone walls, moats and about 130 remains spread over the mountain. Artefacts excavated there are shown at the nearby Akitakata City Historical Museum, and in 2006 the Japan Castle Foundation listed the castle among Japan's Top 100 Castles.
yoshida-shoin: Yoshida Shōin was born Sugi Toranosuke in Hagi, in the Chōshū region, the second son of a modest-ranking samurai, Sugi Yurinosuke. At the age of four he was adopted by Yoshida Daisuke, whose house taught military studies to the daimyō, and he became heir of the Yoshida line at five when Daisuke died. His uncle Tamaki Bunnoshin hurried his education, and at eleven he impressed the daimyō Mōri Takachika with a lecture.

In 1851 he went to Edo and studied Western military science under Sakuma Shōzan, and at the end of that year he left on a four-month journey through north-eastern Japan without written permission. For this offence of dappan, fleeing the domain, he lost his samurai status and his stipend of 57 koku.

Allowed back to Edo in January 1853, Shōin saw the Black Ships of Matthew Perry at Uraga with Sakuma Shōzan and was deeply impressed by Western civilisation. He first tried to board a Russian warship at Nagasaki, but it sailed early. In 1854 he followed Perry's fleet to Shimoda and, with Kaneko Shigetske, rowed a stolen fisherman's boat out to the USS Powhatan on 27 March.

He was refused and handed to the authorities. His automatic death sentence was reduced after the intervention of Kawaji Toshiakira and two senior councillors. In the Noyama Prison at Hagi he lectured fellow prisoners on the Analects and Mencius and wrote a Record of Imprisonment.

Released into house arrest in 1855, he began lecturing in a small room of the Sugi house in 1856. In 1857 he took over the Shōkasonjuku Academy, which his uncle had run. His students included Kusaka Genzui, Takasugi Shinsaku, Itō Hirobumi and Yamada Akiyoshi, and since he could not travel, he sent them round Japan as investigators. In 1858 the shogunate signed a treaty without imperial sanction. Shōin proposed seizing the senior councillor Manabe Akikatsu on his way to Kyoto, killing him if he refused to act, but most of his disciples opposed it. He was imprisoned again.

Moved to Edo during the purge directed by the Tairō Ii Naosuke, Shōin confessed to the plot before the Council of State and was sentenced to death. He was beheaded on 21 November 1859, aged 29. Of his students, Takasugi Shinsaku led rifle companies against the shogunate's army in 1864, and Itō Hirobumi became Japan's first prime minister; Katsura Kogorō, Inoue Kaoru and Yamagata Aritomo also became known. He was enshrined in Setagaya in 1882, at Hagi, and at Yasukuni Shrine in 1888.
yoshino-nara: Yoshino (吉野町, Yoshino-chō) is a town in Yoshino District, in the central part of Nara Prefecture. The Ryumon Mountains run east to west in the north, the Omine Mountain Range spreads out to the south, and mountains extending from the Daidaka range lie to the east. Between them the Yoshino River flows from southeast to west through the centre of the town, and the Takami River flows from east to west. Settlements lie on the narrow stretches of flat land inside the meanders of the Yoshino River and on the more open land along its tributaries. The climate is humid subtropical, with an average annual temperature of 13.0 °C and about 1,893 millimetres of rain a year.

The area was part of ancient Yamato Province. The Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki mention Yoshino as a stopover on Emperor Jimmu's eastward journey to conquer Yamato. In the Asuka period, because it lay directly south of the capitals Asuka-kyō, Fujiwara-kyō and Heijō-kyō, it was a popular recreational spot for Emperor Ojin and other emperors and aristocrats, and Yoshino Palace stood there. During the Nara period the area was sacred to adherents of Shugendo. It was the capital of the Southern Court in the Nanboku-chō period.

After the Meiji restoration the village of Yoshino was established on 1 April 1889 under the modern municipal system. It became a town on 24 April 1928 and on 3 May 1956 annexed the town of Kamiichi and the villages of Kokusui, Nakasho, Ryumon and Nakaryumon. A local story holds that Prince Oama, later Emperor Tenmu, taught the people of the Kuzu district to make washi paper in the 7th century.

Mount Yoshino is known for its many thousands of cherry trees, which have inspired poetry by Chiyo, Uejima Onitsura and other writers. They were planted in four groves at different altitudes so that they come into bloom at different times in the spring. An account written about 1714 describes about 1,000 trees at the base, 1,000 in the middle, 1,000 higher up and 1,000 in the precincts of the inner shrine at the top.

The town has 5,874 people and covers 95.65 square kilometres. Its economy is based on forestry, sake brewing and tourism, and most of its forest is red cedar and cypress that have been planted and harvested in cycles for 500 years. Kinpusen-ji, Kinpu Shrine, Yoshino Shrine and Yoshino-Kumano National Park lie within it. In 2012 it was designated one of the Most Beautiful Villages in Japan.
young-italy: A few months after leaving Italy, in June 1831, Giuseppe Mazzini wrote a letter to King Charles Albert of Sardinia asking him to unite Italy and lead the nation. A month later, convinced that his appeal had not reached the king, he founded the movement at Marseille, in July 1831, while in exile. Its goal was a united Italian republic, to be won by a general insurrection in the reactionary Italian states and in the lands held by the Austrian Empire, since Mazzini believed that a popular uprising would create a unified Italy.

Its slogan was Union, Strength and Liberty. Members took nicknames from figures of the Italian Middle Ages and swore an oath to make Italy united, free, independent and republican, with every man considered equal.

The movement gathered about 60,000 members around 1833. In that year members plotting a revolt in Savoy and Piedmont were arrested and executed by the Sardinian police, and in Austria links with the movement were treated as treason, punishable by death. After a second failed revolt in Piedmont and Savoy in February 1834 it disappeared for a time, then reappeared in England in 1838.

Later insurrections in Sicily, Abruzzi, Tuscany, Lombardy-Venetia, Romagna (1841 and 1845) and Bologna (1843) failed. The short-lived Roman Republic of 1848 was crushed by a French army called in by Pope Pius IX, whom Mazzini had first hailed as a likely leader of liberal unification.

Giuseppe Garibaldi joined around 1833 after meeting Mazzini, took part in a failed revolt in Piedmont and was sentenced to death, and fled to Marseille. Young Italy became affiliated with Giovine Europa, founded in 1835, alongside similar movements such as Junges Deutschland, Młoda Polska and Giovine Svizzera. A last failed revolt against Austria in Milan in 1853 effectively ended it.

The failure of the Milan revolt of 1853 crushed hopes of a democratic Italy and favoured the Piedmontese monarchy, which achieved national unification in 1860 under Count Cavour.
